Old-connection batched merge leaks pooled `top_hits` when reduction trips the breaker

On a connection older than `batched_query_execution_delayable_writeable`, `QueryPhaseResultConsumer.MergeResult#readFrom` eagerly deserializes the aggregation tree, which retains slices of pooled `_source` buffers within any `top_hits` aggs in the tree. However this `DelayableWriteable.referencing` wrapper does not capture this ownership properly, instead (trappily!) expecting callers to set up the ownership of those buffer slices separately by calling `addTopHitsToReleaseList` or similar.

On this execution path, `reduce()` polls the batch out of the queue and then calls `addEstimateAndMaybeBreak` before recording the ownership of any `top_hits` aggs. If the circuit breaker trips, the `finally` block only does `Releasables.close` on the wrapper. The buffers retained by the `top_hits` aggs are never released back to their pools.

`releaseBatchedAggs` does release these hits, and it runs when the batch is discarded before `reduce`. That discard path was fixed in [elastic/elasticsearch#160484](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/160484). The description of that change calls out the remaining site: entries left in `remoteAggsList` when `reduce()` throws, described there as pre-existing and needing a separate fix. No issue tracks that follow-up. The hole is only the throw after the batch has been taken for the final reduce.

The coordinating node leaks the retained inbound buffer for each `top_hits` document in that batch. The request-breaker estimate itself is rolled back. The leak is the Netty buffer refcount, not breaker bytes.

It's super-tricky to actually get to this point today, although this isn't obvious without reading an awful lot of other code. Reaching it needs all of the following:

- A coordinating node and a data node on a version that batches query execution. The target node is `9.1.0` or newer, and the connection supports `batched_query_phase_version` (`9043000` / `8841019`).
- A transport version that does not support `batched_query_execution_delayable_writeable` (`9057000`, with no 8.19 patch id). An 8.19 proxy between two 9.x nodes (x≥1) negotiates that version on both hops and forwards the bytes.
- `ccs_minimize_roundtrips=false`, so the coordinator receives the batched `NodeQueryResponse` rather than a fully reduced remote response.
- At least two shards of the remote index on the same data node, so one batched node query is sent.
- The request breaker trips inside `reduce()` after that batch has been polled, on the batch estimate or on the extra 50% final-reduce estimate.

- [elastic/elasticsearch#160484](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/160484) releases these hits on the discard paths and leaves this `reduce()` throw unfixed.
- [elastic/elasticsearch#160363](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/160363) releases `top_hits` when `SearchResponseMerger` throws during a CCS final merge. Different owner, same missing close.
- [elastic/elasticsearch#164443](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/164443) leaks pooled hits when fetch fails after a successful query reduction, once `topHitsOwnershipTransferred` is set and `ReducedQueryPhase` has no cleanup.
- [elastic/elasticsearch#146431](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/146431) fixes a pooled `SearchHits` leak in `MergeResult#writeTo` on a transport-version mismatch. That is the write path.
- https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/164456 observes the more general pattern of problems with `Referencing` aggs.

`Referencing` aggregations do not own the resources inside them

`DelayableWriteable.Referencing` stores a live aggregation tree without taking ownership of its contents: its `close()` does nothing. That makes sense if the caller built the tree and already owns it, but it is trickier if the aggs are being deserialized from the wire, because at deserialization time there is no well-defined owner of this data. The caller is required to know to set up the ownership of the aggs, or release them properly, on all paths from deserialization onwards including exception paths. Many callers set this ownership up immediately by calling `InternalAggregations.addTopHitsToReleaseList` but it's hard for reviewers to know that this is required, and some callers may not even have access to the release list when creating the wrapper, forcing the ownership registration to be several frames away from the creation of the `Referencing` wrapper. This is very hard for reviewers to spot: see for instance #164457 and issues linked from there for some consequences of this trappiness. It also behaves very differently from `DelayedWriteable.Serialized` instances which do own their contents.

Today `top_hits` is the only reduced aggregation that retains a nontrivial resource: slices of the inbound network buffer captured in `_source`. However, I note that cardinality aggs copy their results into a `BigArrays.NON_RECYCLING_INSTANCE`, and t-digest aggs track their memory usage with the deprecated no-op breaker, and that to fix either of those things would mean attaching a nontrivial resource to them (respectively: recycled pages and a breaker reservation).

This is pretty related to #59892, #88128, #89437. I thought the specific problem I'm seeing with `DelayableWriteable.Referencing` deserved its own discussion, but I apologise if this duplicates existing discussions too much.

`wildcard` field can return fewer hits than `keyword` for `case_insensitive` queries on characters whose Unicode case folding differs from lowercasing (e.g. `ı`, `µ`, `ς`)

Term, prefix, wildcard and regexp queries with `"case_insensitive": true` on a `wildcard` field can miss documents that the same query finds on a `keyword` field. This doesn't look like a regression in the `wildcard` field itself but rather a result of an extended result set on the `keyword` field after switching to extended unicode lowercasing support in Lucene 10.2.0.

The `wildcard` field's own matching code did not change. What changed is the meaning of `case_insensitive`: it used to fold only ASCII characters and now applies Unicode case folding, first for `regexp` (Lucene 10.2.0) and later for `term`, `prefix` and `wildcard` queries (#153513). The `keyword` field and the exact verification step of the `wildcard` field follow the new behavior, but the `wildcard` field's ngram prefilter still only lowercases, so it can discard documents before verification sees them.

A `wildcard` field answers a query in two steps:

1. **Prefilter:** an ngram index (3-character pieces of the value, *lowercased*) quickly selects candidate documents.
2. **Verification:** the candidates are checked exactly against the original value.

Since `case_insensitive` was extended to Unicode case folding, step 2 treats the Turkish dotless `ı` and `I` as equal. Step 1 only lowercases, and lowercasing `I` gives `i`, not `ı`. So a stored `ISPARTA` is indexed as `isparta`, while a query for `ısparta` asks the prefilter for `ısp`, which is not in the index. The document is dropped before verification could accept it.

| Stored value | Query | Why they should match | `keyword` | `wildcard` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ISPARTA` (a Turkish city name in capitals) | `ısparta` (U+0131, dotless i) | `ı` ≈ `I` | found | **missed** |
| `10 µs` (U+00B5, micro sign) | `10 μs` (U+03BC, Greek mu) | `µ` ≈ `μ` | found | **missed** |
| `οδυσσευς` (U+03C2, final sigma) | `ΟΔΥΣΣΕΥΣ` | `ς` ≈ `σ` ≈ `Σ` | found | **missed** |

The affected characters are those whose case folding maps to a character that lowercasing does not: `ı` with `I`, `s`/`S` with the long s `ſ`, `µ` with `μ`/`Μ`, `ς` with `σ`/`Σ`. In practice the Turkish `ı` and the Greek final sigma are the most likely to matter: Turkish text is often stored in capitals while users type `ı`, and apparently many Greek word ends in `ς`, so an upper-case search for stored lower-case Greek text can miss.

```
PUT idx
{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "kw": { "type": "keyword" },
      "wc": { "type": "wildcard" }
    }
  }
}

[... 23 more lines]
```

(`\u0131` is `ı`, LATIN SMALL LETTER DOTLESS I.)

`responses[i].hits.total.value`, in order:

| Query type | `keyword` | `wildcard` (actual) | `wildcard` (expected) |
|---|---|---|---|
| term | 2 | **1** | 2 |
| prefix | 2 | **1** | 2 |
| wildcard | 2 | **1** | 2 |
| regexp | 2 | **1** | 2 |

The `wildcard` field's matching code did not change. What changed is what `case_insensitive` means, so `keyword` and the verification step became Unicode-aware while the ngram prefilter still only lowercases. Before that, both field types agreed. It happened in two upstream steps:

- **regexp:** Lucene 10.2.0 made the case-insensitive `RegExp` flags (including the deprecated `ASCII_CASE_INSENSITIVE`, which the `regexp` query used) do full Unicode folding. I checked the released jars: in 10.1.0 the regexp `s` does not match `ſ`, in 10.2.0 it does. Elasticsearch moved to 10.2.0 in #126594.
- **term / prefix / wildcard:** #153513 (July 2026) replaced Elasticsearch's ASCII-only case-insensitive handling with Lucene's Unicode simple case folding.

The Unicode test added with #153513 uses `Σ` / `σ`, which plain lowercasing already handles, so it does not exercise this gap.

Compared to the `keyword`field, users can see fewer results for case-insensitive searches on `wildcard` fields containing the characters above. Case-sensitive queries are not affected.

Columnar-only mapping parameters fail validation when a template switches to a columnar index mode, in three places

Some mapping validation depends on `index.mode`. Three code paths validate or merge mappings in a temporary index that does not have the `index.mode` from the template. In these paths, a valid columnar template fails with `parameter [multi_value] can only be used in columnar index modes`. The same gap is reached by root `dynamic: flattened` from #164147, which fails with `dynamic [flattened] is only supported in strict columnar mode`.

We reproduced all three cases with YAML tests. We ran them on the branch of #164147 (commit `b2c72f4`), not on `main`. The `multi_value` check is in `FieldMapper.checkTopLevelParse`, and #164147 does not change that code or the three code paths below. So we expect `main` to behave the same way, as the author of #164147 also reports. We have not run it there.

`DataStream.getEffectiveMappings` builds a temporary index from the write index. The write index keeps its old `index.mode` until the next rollover. The code then merges the template mappings into it. The code that corrects the index mode runs only if `index.routing_path` differs, and `IndexSettings.mode` is a final field.

Steps to reproduce:

1. Create a template with `data_stream: {}` and no `index.mode`. Create a data stream. The write index is a standard index.
2. Update the template to `index.mode: columnar`, with a keyword field `kw` that has `multi_value: false`. The template saves.
3. Call `GET _data_stream/<name>/_mappings` or `GET _data_stream/<name>/_settings`.

Actual result:
- Both calls return HTTP 400: `parameter [multi_value] can only be used in columnar index modes`.
- A wildcard GET fails for all matched data streams.
- The error stays until the next rollover.

The same steps with root `dynamic: flattened` (instead of `multi_value`) also return HTTP 400. In that case, `PUT _data_stream/<name>/_mappings` returns HTTP 200 with `applied_to_data_stream: false`. The stack trace goes through `DataStream.getEffectiveMappings` -> `MapperService.merge`. The settings API reaches the same code through `MetadataDataStreamsService.getEffectiveSettings`.

[CI] Harden run-bc-upgrade-tests.sh against transient snapshot manifest fetch failures

The `bc-upgrade` gate in `elasticsearch-intake` (and the equivalent PR pipeline step) hard-fails when the snapshot build **manifest** cannot be fetched, even when the failure is a transient availability issue on `snapshots.elastic.co`. This reds all intake builds on the affected branch until the manifest becomes reachable again, despite nothing being wrong with the commit under test.

All `main` intake builds in a ~40 min window on 2026-11-03 failed identically, e.g. [elasticsearch-intake #51958](https://buildkite.com/elastic/elasticsearch-intake/builds/51958) (also #51950, #51955, #51956, #51957):

```
Selecting the most recent build from branch [main].
Getting build manifest from ["https://snapshots.elastic.co/9.7.0-d08425c5/manifest-9.7.0-SNAPSHOT.json"]
Cannot get the build manifest from ["https://snapshots.elastic.co/9.7.0-d08425c5/manifest-9.7.0-SNAPSHOT.json"]
🚨 Error: The command exited with status 1
```

The manifest URL returned HTTP 200 again shortly afterwards, confirming this was a transient snapshot-publishing / CDN propagation race for the newly-advertised `9.7.0-d08425c5` snapshot — not a code change. The commit under test in #51958 was a mute-only PR.

In `.buildkite/scripts/run-bc-upgrade-tests.sh`:

```
MANIFEST="$(eval "curl -s $MANIFEST_URL")"
if [[ -z "$MANIFEST" ]]; then
   echo "Cannot get the build manifest from [$MANIFEST_URL]"
   exit 1
fi
```

A single `curl -s` with no retry. If the body comes back empty (5xx, CDN hiccup, or `future-releases.json` advertising a build id before its manifest finished publishing), the script treats it as a fatal `exit 1`. There is tolerance for an empty/`null` `MANIFEST_URL` (it skips), but not for a URL that resolves yet returns an empty body.

- Retry the manifest fetch a few times with backoff (`curl --retry` / explicit loop) before giving up.
- Use `curl -fsS` so HTTP errors are surfaced and distinguished from empty bodies.
- On persistent transient failure, prefer skipping the BC upgrade tests (`exit 0`, consistent with the existing "No snapshots or build candidates" skip) rather than reding the whole intake — or at minimum make the failure clearly distinguishable as infra, not a product regression.

Low-risk CI-tooling change; prevents upstream snapshot-infra blips from blocking all intake/PR builds on a branch.

Columnar batch indexing writes rows that failed with a version conflict

On an index with `index.mode: columnar` and `index.batch_indexing: true`, when a bulk is indexed through the columnar mapper path, a `create` item that conflicts with an existing id is reported as a version conflict (409), but the document is nevertheless written to the segment, without an `_id` doc value. This happens when the conflicting row is followed by at least one successful row of the same bulk.

Consequences:
- The document count is higher than the number of distinct ids.
- A search that fetches such a document fails an assertion (`_id doc value missing for docId 1`). With assertions enabled this is a fatal error and the node exits. I haven't checked what happens without assertions.

```
PUT dup
{
  "settings": {
    "index.mode": "columnar",
    "index.batch_indexing": true,
    "index.number_of_shards": 1,
    "index.number_of_replicas": 0
  },
  "mappings": { "properties": { "ints": { "type": "integer" } } }
}
[... 12 more lines]
```

Item statuses are `[201, 409, 409, 201]`, as expected. `_count` returns **3**, expected **2** (distinct ids `a` and `b`).

Fetching the documents then crashes the node when assertions are enabled (I used a dev node from `./gradlew run`):

```
GET dup/_search?size=10&seq_no_primary_term=true&version=true

[ERROR][o.e.b.ElasticsearchUncaughtExceptionHandler] fatal error in thread [elasticsearch[runTask-0][search][T#4]], exiting
java.lang.AssertionError: _id doc value missing for docId 1
	at org.elasticsearch.index.mapper.IdLoader$DocValuesIdLoader.leaf(IdLoader.java:608)
	at org.elasticsearch.search.fetch.FetchPhase$1.setNextReader(FetchPhase.java:461)
	at org.elasticsearch.search.fetch.FetchPhaseDocsIterator.doIterate(FetchPhaseDocsIterator.java:149)
	...
```

`create` items in one bulk request, 1 shard, columnar index with `index.batch_indexing: true` and the fields mapped. "Docs" is `_count` after refresh.

| Ids in the bulk | Item statuses | Docs | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a, a` | 201, 409 | 1 | 1 (OK) |
| `a, b, a` | 201, 201, 409 | 2 | 2 (OK) |
| `a, b, b` | 201, 201, 409 | 2 | 2 (OK) |
| `a, a, b` | 201, 409, 201 | **3** | 2 |
| `a, b, a, c` | 201, 201, 409, 201 | **4** | 3 |
| `a, a, b, c` | 201, 409, 201, 201 | **4** | 3 |
| `a, a, a, b` | 201, 409, 409, 201 | **3** | 2 |

So the count is wrong when the conflicting row is followed by a successful row. A conflicting row at the end of the bulk is fine, and a single `create` of an existing id is correctly rejected with no extra document.

I also saw the same extra documents when the conflict is with a document indexed by an earlier request, again when the conflicting row is followed by other rows. I observed that with a pre-built batch from an unreleased branch, not with a JSON bulk.

The columnar path is only taken when every field of the batch is mapped (see `ShardBatchMapper#resolveMappers`, which falls back for unmapped fields under a dynamic parent). I checked which path each bulk took with the `batch indexed [n] operations on primary shard` TRACE log of `ShardBatchIndexer`. Columnar index with `index.batch_indexing: true`, ids `x, x, y` where the second `x` conflicts:

| Bulk | Mapping state | Columnar path | Docs added | Expected |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `a, a, b`, index created with a mapping | all fields mapped | yes | **3** | 2 |
| `a, a, b`, index created without a mapping | unmapped (dynamic) | no | 2 | 2 (OK) |
| `c, c, d`, same index afterwards | now mapped by the first bulk | yes | **3** | 2 |
| `e, e, f`, using a new, unmapped field | unmapped | no | 2 | 2 (OK) |

So an index created without a mapping is not immune: the first bulk is fine because it takes the per-document path and creates the mapping, and later bulks with the same fields hit the problem.

The same bulks give the correct count with:
- `index.mode: columnar` and `index.batch_indexing: false`
- the standard index mode with `index.batch_indexing: true`
- bulks with fields that aren't mapped yet (per-document path, see above)

The wrong count is the same with these additional columnar settings: `index.recovery.use_synthetic_source: true`, and `index.mapping.source.mode: synthetic`.

[TSDB] Segment-scoped run-table ordinal encoding for dimension fields

In TSDB segments sorted by (`_tsid`, `@timestamp`), dimension values are piecewise-constant. Every document of a series carries the same ordinal. The ES95 codec encodes ordinals with block-scoped RLE, which has two problems:

- Storage and access cost scale with the number of documents (O(docs)) instead of the number of series (O(runs)).
- Runs reset at every block boundary, so compression depends on the ratio of run length to block size. The experiments under #141118 showed this ceiling. Larger blocks helped fields with long runs and did nothing for fields with short runs.

Dimension columns are therefore much larger than the information they hold. For `SortedSet` fields, the per-document `addresses[]` table adds further O(docs) overhead.

**Proposal**

Add a segment-scoped run-table layout for ordinal dimension fields, as a new doc values format.
- Sorted: store one `(startDoc, ordinal)` entry per run instead of one ordinal per document.
- SortedSet: store `startDoc[]` and a `setOffset[]` fencepost column that delimits each run's slice of the ordinal stream. This removes the per-document `addresses[]` table.
- Selection: a static check rejects fields where maxOrd * 2 > maxDoc. A dynamic check abandons accumulation when the run count grows too high. Rejected fields use the existing encoding.
- Sparse docs: Sorted reserves ordinal K as an "absent" sentinel. SortedSet uses an empty set.
- Readers: they implement the SortedDocValues and SortedSetDocValues contracts exactly, so ES|QL operators, ValuesSourceReader and the Lucene merge pipeline need no changes. A lookup costs `O(log N_runs)` per document.
- Upgrade path: existing ES95TSDB segments stay readable. Lucene SPI picks the right format from the codec name stored in the segment.
- Soft deletes: run boundaries ignore `LiveDocs`. Soft-deleted documents are masked at read time, so segments with soft deletes remain valid.

**Delivery plan**

#156068 is being split into stacked PRs:

Capture `dynamic`, `enabled` and `passthrough` of auto-flattened objects in `prefix_properties` for every index mode with `subobjects: false`

When `subobjects` is `false`, we flatten every plain object child into dotted leaf mappers, which means the object mapper itself (and with it any setting declared on it) no longer exists in the built mapping. In the strict columnar index modes we work around this by recording the settings of each dissolved object in the root's `prefix_properties`, keyed by the full dotted prefix, and by resolving them again at index time. In every other index mode we have no such place to put them, so we reject the mapping instead.

Note that the settings are not silently lost in the other modes: they are rejected with an `Auto-flattening [...] failed` error, so the practical effect is that a mapping that is valid in `columnar` or `logsdb_columnar` is invalid in `standard`, `logsdb` or `time_series` as soon as `subobjects` is `false`. The error from #151524 is the same one we would hit, for example, with this mapping in a standard index:

```
PUT test
{
  "mappings": {
    "subobjects": false,
    "dynamic": true,
    "properties": {
      "attributes": {
        "dynamic": false,
        "properties": { "host": { "type": "keyword" } }
      }
[... 3 more lines]
```

which we expect to fail with `Auto-flattening [attributes] failed because the value of [dynamic] (FALSE) is not compatible with the value from its parent context (TRUE)`.

We found this while reviewing #164260 (see [this thread](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/164260#discussion_r4441862559)), where child-first normalization has to move the `prefixProperties` of a dissolved object to the root. That PR is meant to be a pure refactoring, so we keep any behavior change out of it and track the change here.

Three places currently check the index mode, and all of them need to agree for the feature to work in other modes, while a fourth place needs a compatibility check:

- `ObjectMapper.Builder#asFlattenedFieldBuilders` only records `dynamic`, the `passthrough` priority and `enabled: false` into the collector when `parentContext.isStrictColumnar()` is true.
- `ObjectMapper.Builder#ensureBuilderFlattenable` rejects a differing `dynamic`, `enabled: false` and `passthrough` objects when the context is not strict columnar.
- `DocumentParserContext#resolveDynamic` returns the inherited `dynamic()` unchanged unless the index mode is strict columnar, so even a populated `prefix_properties` would be ignored at index time.
- `RootObjectMapper#doXContent` serializes `prefix_properties` whenever the map is non-empty, and the root parser accepts the key in any mode, so the serialization side is probably already mode-neutral. This is not a mode check, but we have not verified how a mapping with this key behaves on nodes that predate it.

Other auto-flattening restrictions (`synthetic_source_keep` on a dissolved object, an explicit `subobjects: true` below a `subobjects: false` parent) are not about prefix settings, and we would leave them as they are.

We would populate `prefix_properties` whenever an object is dissolved by auto-flattening, regardless of index mode, resolve `dynamic` and `enabled` from it at index time in every mode that has a non-empty map, and drop the corresponding rejections in `ensureBuilderFlattenable`. In general the work should be mostly removing mode checks rather than adding new logic, since the data structure, the merge rules (`PrefixProperties::merge`) and the lookup (`RootObjectMapper#resolveDynamic`) already exist.

Work items:

- Remove the `isStrictColumnar()` guard around the capture in `asFlattenedFieldBuilders` and the three matching rejections in `ensureBuilderFlattenable`.
- Make `DocumentParserContext#resolveDynamic` consult the root prefixes whenever `prefix_properties` is non-empty, keeping the early return for the common case so mappings without auto-flattened objects pay nothing.
- Decide how `passthrough` objects behave under `subobjects: false` outside columnar modes, since the alias resolution in `FieldTypeLookup` was written with the columnar root in mind.
- Add YAML tests that mirror `70_columnar_prefix_dynamic_properties.yml` for `standard` and `logsdb`, including put-mapping merges and composable templates, and add unit coverage that parses, normalizes and builds a non-columnar tree (`MappingBuilderNormalizeTests` currently only runs with the default index mode).
- Update the `subobjects` docs, which today describe auto-flattening conflicts as errors.

- Do we want `enabled: false` inside a dissolved object to drop the subtree in non-columnar modes too? In strict columnar modes the entire subtree is dropped at mapping time and ignored at index time, which differs from how a disabled object keeps its source in the other modes, so we should confirm the intended `_source` behavior first.
- What should happen for `dynamic: runtime` on a dissolved object? It is rejected in strict columnar modes today (`prefix_properties.<prefix>.dynamic` does not support `runtime`), and we would probably keep that rule.
- Is the change in observable behavior (mappings that fail today start to succeed) acceptable without an opt-in setting?

Benchmark synthetic `_source` reconstruction in strict columnar index modes

`columnar` and `logsdb_columnar` reconstruct `_source` from doc values (`synthetic`) or retrieve a materialized document (`columnar_stored`). The performance characteristics of these read paths have not been systematically quantified.

This issue tracks establishing a reproducible Rally benchmark to measure `_source` retrieval across index and source modes, identify potential bottlenecks, and provide a baseline for future optimizations. The benchmark should also detect regressions as more field types move to ColumNAR.

> [!NOTE]
> Columnar modes target analytical queries, which read a few columns across many documents and rarely fetch whole documents. `logsdb_columnar` also serves log workloads moving from `logsdb`, where retrieving individual documents is common. `_source` cannot be disabled in any columnar mode: it is always available, rebuilt at query time (`synthetic`) or written at index time (`columnar_stored`).

- **Index and source modes:** `logsdb` synthetic as a reference, `logsdb_columnar` synthetic and `columnar_stored`, and `columnar` synthetic.
- **Mapping and document width:** number of mapped fields versus populated fields, including sparse mappings.
- **Retrieval patterns:** single-document GET and search fetches of different sizes, as separate operations, and documents distributed across segments.
- **Field types and shapes:** keyword, text, numeric, date, `flattened`, `_unmapped`, and single-valued versus multi-valued fields.
- **Source retrieval:** full versus filtered `_source`, including whether filtering reduces reconstruction work.

- A reusable Rally benchmark, either dedicated or extending an existing track, covering representative combinations of these dimensions.
- Comparable measurements of fetch latency, throughput, CPU and allocations, with the same data and retrieval patterns across configurations.
- Profiling to distinguish `_source` reconstruction overhead from other fetch costs.
- Follow-up issues for significant bottlenecks identified by the measurements.

- #156317: ES|QL `LOAD` and `LOAD_ALL` in columnar mode.
- #161525: building the `columnar_stored` blob at index time.
- #164321, #164324: ColumNAR numeric adoption, which moves numeric and date fields to a new read path.

Evaluate block compression for ColumNAR numeric columns

Tracked in `numeric/meta` (#164320). Exploratory, not a release gate.

ColumNAR numeric blocks end with FOR bit-packing (`ForTerminal`), and no general-purpose compression runs after it. The column format already supports one: `BlockBytesCodec` compresses a block's packed bytes, the column metadata records its id, and readers decode both `IDENTITY_ID` and `ZSTD_ID`. String ordinal columns use Zstd this way. Numeric field columns always write `IDENTITY_ID` (`ColumNARDocValuesConsumer`).

Compare, per block:

- No compression (today).
- Zstd through the existing `ZSTD_ID`. This needs no new persisted id.
- LZ4, only if the measurements show that Zstd decode cost is a problem. It needs a new frozen `BlockBytesCodec` id and a `FormatVersion` bump, so it is not implemented just for the comparison.

FOR already removes unused bits, so the gain depends on the data. Measure on representative numeric columns from `elastic/logs`, including different value distributions and cardinalities.

Reindex relocation can fail due to race between node shutdown and relocation

9.5+

_bundled_

Reindex relocation will select the node to relocate the reindex to right before relocation, and once the reindex is running on the target node, then shutdown should wait for this reindex to complete or be relocated again, but there is a race between target node potentially shutting down before the reindex task is registered and stops shutdown.

Solving this shouldn't be too difficult, and it would entail making target respond with a specific exception that the source knows is safe to retry, and source can pick another node, and retry the relocation.

But intuitively it seems rare to hit, network would have to take a while, and shutdown generally first puts in a shutdown marker into cluster state, and then shuts down once a set of activities have happened.

Came out of https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/164014.

Shutdown a node when a reindex relocation is in-flight.

Tracked in `flattened/meta` (#164335). Depends on the ColumNAR storage for `flattened` keys (#155883).

ColumNAR stores each `flattened` key as its own string column. In the strict columnar modes, `ES819` stores all keys of a document in one keyed BINARY blob. Per-key columns may improve selective keyed reads, but introduce per-column metadata and potentially different costs for wide or sparse documents. This issue adds JMH benchmarks that measure how both formats scale with the number of keys. The `elastic/logs` Rally benchmark (`flattened/rally`, #164293) measures end-to-end performance on real logs and does not vary the number of keys.

Add JMH benchmarks in `:benchmarks` that compare `ES819` and ColumNAR on the same generated `flattened` data, in two scenarios:

- **Wide documents:** increase the keys per document, with every key present in every document, so the distinct keys grow with it. This measures the cost of wider documents at constant density.
- **Sparse schema:** increase the distinct keys in the segment and keep the keys per document fixed. Each key becomes sparser as the schema grows. This measures the cost of more columns and their metadata.

In both scenarios, keep the document count, the values per key and the value cardinality fixed. Sweep each scenario to the largest key count that is practical to generate and measure, with 10,000 distinct keys as a target, and report where the overhead becomes significant rather than assuming a threshold.

Measure:

- Indexing: flush throughput.
- Merging: merge throughput.
- Reader open: segment open time and heap per segment, to quantify per-key metadata overhead.
- Reads: one key out of N, and many keys out of N.
- Storage: encoded doc-values size after a force merge, including metadata. Report it explicitly, for example with `@AuxCounters`, not through heap allocation or throughput.

`FlattenedFieldExtractBenchmark` already builds `flattened` data with N keys, but it writes `SortedSetDocValuesField` directly and so measures neither codec. Reuse its data generation where it fits.

The `ES819` side can be built before the ColumNAR storage lands.

In the strict columnar index modes, fields that the mapping does not cover go into the `_unmapped` sink, a hidden `flattened` field. This makes the sink a main source of `flattened` data in these modes, and no Rally benchmark covers it yet. This issue tracks extending `elastic/logs` to index into the sink and comparing `ES819` with ColumNAR on it. Rally validation of ColumNAR `flattened` is currently limited to this scope.

Map dynamic decimals as `double` in strict columnar index modes

main (9.7.0-SNAPSHOT, `736f515bed1d`). The same code path is on `9.6` (`b470db715010`) and `9.5`; reproduced on `main` only.

None (default `rest-api-spec` YAML test cluster)

_bundled_

In the `logsdb_columnar` and `columnar` index modes, a dynamically mapped decimal number becomes a `float` field, and the `float` rounding becomes the stored document. The original value cannot be recovered.

The rounding itself is generic synthetic source behavior: `logsdb`, `time_series`, and `standard` indices with synthetic source return the same rounded value. The difference is that those modes can opt out with `index.mapping.source.mode: stored`, while strict columnar modes accept only `synthetic` and `columnar_stored`, both rebuilt from doc values. A dynamic template or explicit mapping with type `double` is the only escape. This issue proposes mapping dynamic decimals as `double` by default in the strict columnar modes only.

Elasticsearch has always mapped dynamic decimals to `float`, as a deliberate storage trade-off. In a `standard` index with stored `_source`, that trade-off affects only the indexed value: `_source` keeps the original JSON. Columnar modes do not retain the original JSON representation. Both synthetic and `columnar_stored` source expose the precision loss introduced by the dynamically selected `float` mapping.

| Scenario | Current `float` | With `double` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `_source` after indexing `123456789.123` | `1.2345679E8` | `1.23456789123E8` |
| `range` with `gt: 1730544000.0` over docs `1730544000.0` and `1730544000.123` | 0 hits, the values cannot be distinguished | 1 hit |
| Index `1e39` | rejected: `[float] supports only finite values` | accepted |

The last row shows that `double` also widens the range of accepted values, so the change affects indexing behavior, not only source fidelity.

The columnar documentation states that dynamic decimals are mapped as `double` (Dynamic mappings section of `docs/reference/elasticsearch/columnar/index.md`), which does not match the behavior above.

Mapping decimals as `double` substantially reduces the precision loss: `123456789.123` round-trips through binary64 and synthetic source, while the current `float` mapping loses significant digits. Arbitrary decimal literals are not guaranteed to round-trip exactly.

The decimal type comes from `DynamicFieldsBuilder.Concrete#newDynamicDoubleField`, which always builds `NumberType.FLOAT` and does not check the index mode. A fix must preserve dynamic `dense_vector` promotion, keep mappings consistent during rolling upgrades (using an index creation version gate), and decide whether `{dynamic_type}` templates should follow the same behavior. Regression tests should cover vector promotion boundaries and source reconstruction.

> [!NOTE]
> `float` is the default because it is more space-efficient. Mapping dynamic decimals as `double` may increase doc values storage in the columnar modes. The storage cost of `double` in the columnar codec should be measured before deciding.

```
PUT test
{
  "settings": { "index.mode": "logsdb_columnar" }
}

PUT test/_doc/1?refresh
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-02T00:00:00Z",
  "value": 123456789.123
}
[... 2 more lines]
```

Returns `"value": { "type": "float" }`.

```
GET test/_doc/1
```

Returns `"_source": { "value": 1.2345679E8 }`.

The same happens with `"index.mode": "columnar"` (no `@timestamp` needed) and with `"index.mapping.source.mode": "columnar_stored"`.

Use ranges for nested kNN retry exclusions

Agent discovered issue of unreleased post filtering knn issue. I'll review soon.

>
> ### Problem
>
> Nested kNN post-filter retries currently represent every previously seen document as
> an individual global doc ID. When a child survives the post-filter,
> `KnnQueryUtils.expandToParentBlocks` expands its parent block into every child doc ID
> in that block so that later rounds cannot return another child for the same parent.
>
> This makes the retry exclusion state proportional to the total number of documents
> under matched parents rather than to the number of matched parents. A parent with a
> very large nested block can therefore create a large `int[]`, and each later retry
> uses `sortedMerge`, which temporarily allocates another array sized to both inputs.
> The result is avoidable request heap pressure and potentially an OOME.
>
> The expansion itself should not suffer integer overflow while each block is emitted
> once: the result is bounded by the reader's `maxDoc`. The practical problem is the
> amount of materialized state and the additional full-array allocations while merging
> rounds.
>
> This behavior predates #162790, but that PR makes repeated post-filter retries a
> normal path and therefore makes it more important that exclusion state remain
> compact.
>
> ### Proposed direction
>
> Represent retry exclusions as sorted, disjoint, half-open global doc-ID ranges:
>
> * A filtered-out individual document contributes `[doc, doc + 1)`.
> * A matched nested parent contributes `[blockStart, parentDoc + 1)`, preserving the
> current behavior of excluding the entire block.
> * Merge overlapping or adjacent ranges across candidates and retry rounds.
> * Teach `ExcludeDocsQuery` (or a replacement) to skip these ranges directly while
> retaining its reader identity check and optional per-leaf search mask.
>
> This changes storage from O(total documents in matched parent blocks) to O(number of
> matched parents plus individually filtered candidates), without changing which
> documents a retry may visit.
>
> Important correctness invariants:
>
> * Expand only a parent that already produced a post-filter match. A child that was
> filtered out remains a singleton exclusion so untried siblings stay eligible.
> * Preserve sorted/deduplicated behavior across leaves and retry rounds.
> * Preserve global doc-ID/reader identity semantics and per-leaf retry masking.
> * Handle singleton/range overlap and ranges intersecting leaf boundaries.
>
> Tests should include a very large parent block whose exclusion representation remains
> constant-sized, overlapping singleton and parent-block exclusions, merging across
> rounds, multiple leaves, and parity with the existing `expandToParentBlocks` and
> `ExcludeDocsQuery` behavior tests.

Nested kNN post-filtering can miss a parent's best passing child

Had an agent find this problem. I will investigate further sometime soon.

>
>
> kNN post-filtering is enabled for nested vector queries that use the diversifying-children query. The unfiltered delegate returns at most one child per parent, and `PostFilterKnnQuery` applies the user filter to those returned children afterward.
>
> If a parent's highest-scoring child fails the filter, a lower-scoring child from the same parent may pass. That passing child is hidden behind the filtered-out representative and is not necessarily recovered. On `main`, retries only run when the filtered pool is short, so another parent can fill the pool and cause the incomplete result to be accepted.
>
> This means post-filtering can change the result set relative to the ordinary pre-filtered nested kNN query.
>
> ### Minimal scenario
>
> For `k = 1`, consider one segment with these nested children:
>
> | Parent | Child | Score | Filter |
> | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
> | A | A1 | 0.99 | fail |
> | A | A2 | 0.98 | pass |
> | B | B1 | 0.80 | pass |
>
> Add enough passing filler children so the shard-wide filter selectivity reaches the post-filter threshold.
>
> The unfiltered diversifying query chooses A1 for parent A and B1 for parent B. Post-filtering removes A1, leaving B1 to fill the `k = 1` pool. Because the pool is full, `main` does not retry. The post-filtered query returns parent B, while the pre-filtered query can see A2 and returns parent A.
>
> The same underlying problem remains with a leaf-floor completeness check: a leaf-wide floor does not bound the unreturned children hidden behind each parent's selected representative. Other parents can push the leaf floor below the global threshold even while A2 remains competitive.
>
> ### Expected behavior
>
> Post-filtering is an execution optimization and must not change which nested parents are eligible or hide a parent's best filter-passing child.
>
> ### Impact
>
> Filtered approximate kNN searches over nested vectors can return a lower-scoring parent than the corresponding pre-filtered search, even when enough matching documents exist. Post-filtering is enabled by default when estimated selectivity is at least `index.dense_vector.post_filter_selectivity_threshold` (default `0.7`).
>
> ### Suggested mitigation and fix
>
> Short term, do not wrap diversifying/nested kNN queries in `PostFilterKnnQuery` when `parentFilter != null`; keep them on the pre-filter path.
>
> Long term, nested post-filtering needs parent-aware frontier state. A parent whose returned representative failed the filter must remain unresolved while that representative is competitive. Retry until the parent produces a passing child, has no children left, or its next-child upper bound is below the global boundary. A leaf-wide minimum score alone is insufficient.
>
> ### References
>
> - #162790 improves leaf-level retry completeness but intentionally does not address this nested/diversifying case.
> - #148876 introduced the post-filtering path where this behavior originates.
>

ES|QL RERANK produces invalid rankings with listwise rerankers

ES|QL `RERANK` splits its input into many small, independent inference requests and then treats the returned scores as globally comparable. This is valid for pointwise rerankers (cross-encoders), but not for listwise rerankers, whose scores depend on which other documents are in the same request. With a listwise endpoint, including the preconfigured `.jina-reranker-v3` endpoint that the RERANK docs recommend, the final ranking can be wrong. #161191 (configurable batch size) would not fix this, and could make it worse.

- **Pointwise** rerankers (most cross-encoders, including `.rerank-v1-elasticsearch`) score each `(query, document)` pair independently. A document's score does not depend on the other documents in the request, so scores from separate requests can be merged and sorted.
- **Listwise** rerankers score documents relative to each other. For example, [jina-reranker-v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.25085) places the query and all candidate documents in one context window, so documents attend to each other during the forward pass (up to 64 documents and 131K tokens per pass). A document's score is a function of the whole candidate list.

Because of this, a listwise reranker only produces a valid ranking when it sees the entire candidate set at once. Scores from two requests with different candidate lists are not on a common scale and cannot be merged by sorting.

For comparison, the `text_similarity_reranker` retriever sends the entire `rank_window_size` in a single rerank request (`TextSimilarityRankFeaturePhaseRankCoordinatorContext#computeScores`).

1. **Row limit.** `RERANK` inserts an implicit `LIMIT esql.command.rerank.limit` (default 1000) below itself and runs on the coordinator.
2. **Pages.** The operator (`RerankOperator`, an `InferenceOperator`) processes each input compute page independently. A request never contains rows from more than one page, and each page produces its own output page.
3. **Batches.** Within a page, `RerankRequestIterator` cuts a new request every `RerankOperator.DEFAULT_BATCH_SIZE` (10) documents. Every non-blank value of every `ON` field is a separate document; the row's score is the max over its values.
4. **Concurrency.** Up to 10 pages and 50 requests are in flight at once.
5. **Scores.** `RerankOutputBuilder` writes each document's raw `relevance_score` into `_score`. A downstream `SORT _score DESC` compares scores across all requests and pages.

How many pages reach RERANK depends on what is upstream:

- **`SORT ... | LIMIT n | RERANK`**: the coordinator's `TopNOperator` re-chunks rows into pages of `max(32, 256KB / estimatedRowSize)` rows, also cut at `esql.values_loading_jumbo_size` bytes (default `max(heap/1024, 1MB)`). 100 rows with a typical schema arrive as 1 page; wide rows (many `text` fields) or large values split them into several pages (for example 32/32/32/4).
- **`LIMIT n | RERANK`** (no sort): pages are passed through from the data nodes as they arrive, roughly one or more per shard with matches. 100 rows can arrive as anywhere from 1 to 100 pages, and the split varies between runs.

Take `... | SORT _score DESC | LIMIT 100 | RERANK "query" ON body WITH {"inference_id": ".jina-reranker-v3"} | SORT _score DESC`:

- The 100 candidates are scored in 10 independent requests of 10 documents each.
- Each document is ranked only against the 9 other documents in its batch, chosen by upstream row order, not against the full candidate set.
- The final `SORT _score DESC` merges scores from 10 different candidate lists as if they were comparable. A document that scored highly against 9 weak neighbors can outrank a better document that was scored against 9 strong ones.
- The grouping depends on page boundaries, which depend on schema, value sizes, heap size, and (without a sort) data distribution and exchange timing. The same query can return different rankings across runs or clusters.

None of this is visible to the user: there is no warning, and results look plausible.

#161191 proposes a configurable batch size so users can "rerank their full candidate set together, for example all 80 retrieved documents in one inference request". For listwise rerankers this looks like the fix, but it is not:

- **Batch size does not control the candidate set.** Batches never span pages, so a batch size of 100 still splits 100 rows whenever they arrive in more than one page. Users who set the batch size to their `LIMIT` will reasonably believe they get a single listwise ranking, and will silently not get one in some cases (wide rows, large values, small heaps, unsorted input).
- **Splits become more uneven.** With a large batch size, the split follows page boundaries, which produces lopsided groups (for example 32/32/32/4, or one large group plus a few one-row groups from small pages). Documents in a tiny group are scored against almost no competitors, and their scores are then merged with scores from much larger groups.
- **Request size becomes unbounded.** RERANK applies no truncation to input values, and the row limit can be raised without a maximum. A batch size that matches the row limit allows a single request of `rows x values x value size`, which can exceed provider limits or the model's context window. jina-reranker-v3, for example, only processes 64 documents per pass, so the provider splits the request again internally.
- **Fewer, larger requests reduce concurrency**, which increases latency for pointwise endpoints that gain nothing from larger batches.

A configurable batch size could still be useful for tuning pointwise rerankers. But using it safely requires users to know whether their endpoint is pointwise or listwise, and to understand how that interacts with batching and page boundaries. Nothing in the endpoint configuration or the RERANK syntax exposes this. That is a significant cognitive load, and it is likely to lead to user error: a batch size that is a harmless performance knob for one endpoint silently changes the ranking for another.

The _terms_enum API fails on keyword field when index mode is columnar

The terms enum api is able to return values for non indexed and indexed fields in other index mode.

However for columnar index modes, we can no longer do this. With columNAR the dictionary that powered the terms enum is different than the dictionary used by doc value field using sorted doc value types. Not all values may appear in the dictionary and some segments may not have a dictionary at all.

Supporting the terms enum api for non indexed fields in strict columnar index mode while retaining api semantics means doing cpu intensive operations at runtime. This while terms enum api is meant to respond with very low latencies. This means supporting terms enum api for the columnar index mode can't be supported and should fail.

The terms enum api does fail today, but the error is not descriptive and that should be updated. We also need to make sure that terms enum api should keep working for indexed fields in columnar index mode.

ESQL golden tests: detect stale suite directories (renamed, moved or deleted test classes)

#163784 makes every golden suite fail on directories under `golden_tests/<Class>/` that name no test method of the class. That check runs from the class's own `@AfterClass`, so it can only see its own directory. A suite that is renamed, moved to another package, or deleted leaves `golden_tests/<OldClass>/` behind, and no class ever claims that directory. Nothing notices.

Raised by @ivancea in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/163784#discussion_r4426051828.

Nothing is stale today: every `golden_tests/*` directory under `x-pack/plugin/esql/src/test/resources` has a matching class. This is preventive.

The resource path mirrors the package. `GoldenTestCase#goldenRoot` already relies on `src/test/resources/<package>/golden_tests/<SimpleName>/`, so each suite directory maps back to exactly one class name: `<package>.<SimpleName>`.

- One standalone test (next to `GoldenGcTests`) that walks `src/test/resources` for every `golden_tests/*` directory, derives the class name from the path, and fails if `Class.forName` finds nothing or finds something that does not extend `GoldenTestCase`.
- Same contract as the method-level check: compare against what exists, not what ran; normal mode fails with the directory list, `goldenGc` (fix mode) deletes.
- A suite moved to another package keeps its class alive but orphans the old directory. The path-derived lookup resolves in the old package, so it is caught too.
- Document it in `GoldenTestsReadme.MD` next to the existing stale-directory bullet.

ES|QL: Breaker trip during SwissHash grow fails STATS BY with a 500 (IndexOutOfBoundsException) instead of a 429

main (`9.7.0-SNAPSHOT`, 7720ab831efd). The 9.6 branch has the same code. `BytesRefSwissHash` has grown this way since it was added (#139343, in 9.4), but as far as I can tell only the parallel hash aggregation (#158508, on 9.6 and main) keeps using a hash after its grow failed.

None beyond the default distribution.

_bundled_

Under memory pressure, a `STATS ... BY <keyword>` query can fail with a 500 `IndexOutOfBoundsException` instead of a 429 circuit breaker error, and `BugLogger` reports it as a bug:

```
[ERROR][o.e.c.o.Driver] [runTask-0] Error running driver [final]java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 117282 out of bounds for length 4097
	at jdk.incubator.vector/jdk.incubator.vector.ByteVector.fromArray(ByteVector.java:3042)
	at org.elasticsearch.swisshash.BytesRefSwissHash$BigCore.addImpl(BytesRefSwissHash.java:648)
	at org.elasticsearch.swisshash.BytesRefSwissHash$BigCore.addWithHash(BytesRefSwissHash.java:635)
	at org.elasticsearch.swisshash.BytesRefSwissHash.addWithHash(BytesRefSwissHash.java:248)
	at org.elasticsearch.swisshash.BytesRefSwissHash.add(BytesRefSwissHash.java:235)
	at org.elasticsearch.compute.aggregation.blockhash.BytesRefBlockHash.add(BytesRefBlockHash.java:120)
	at org.elasticsearch.compute.aggregation.blockhash.BytesRefBlockHash.add(BytesRefBlockHash.java:94)
	at org.elasticsearch.compute.operator.HashAggregationOperator.addInput(HashAggregationOperator.java:577)
	at org.elasticsearch.compute.operator.ParallelHashAggregationOperator$Worker.processOnePage(ParallelHashAggregationOperator.java:490)
[... 2 more lines]
```

Two problems combine.

**1. A failed grow leaves the hash corrupted.** `growTracking()` doubles `capacity`, `mask` and `nextGrowSize` before the new core is built, and the `finally` closes the old core whether or not the new one was built:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/7720ab831efd44db2e8fd456e34c314a5b713048/libs/swisshash/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/swisshash/BytesRefSwissHash.java#L754-L763

If `new BigCore()` trips the breaker (on its control bytes, or on a page from `grabPage()`), `bigCore` still points at the old core, which is now closed. Its control array is sized for the old capacity while `mask` is for twice that, and its `idAndHashPages` went back to the `PageCacheRecycler`. `SmallCore.transitionToBigCore()` has the same shape and leaves both `smallCore` and `bigCore` null:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/7720ab831efd44db2e8fd456e34c314a5b713048/libs/swisshash/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/swisshash/BytesRefSwissHash.java#L465-L474

The next `add` or `find` on that hash then does one of three things:

- it probes past the end of the old control array and throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException`;
- after a failed small-to-big transition, it throws `NullPointerException` on `bigCore`;
- when the probe stays inside the old control array, it reads and writes `idAndHashPages` that were already returned to the recycler and may belong to another hash by then. I haven't observed this case, but nothing prevents it, and it would silently corrupt another query's data instead of failing.

`LongSwissHash` and `LongLongSwissHash` grow the same way. That's from reading the code; I only tested `BytesRefSwissHash`.

**2. `ParallelHashAggregationOperator` can add to a hash after its worker failed.** When a background `WorkerTask` throws from `processOnePage`, the `finally` releases the worker's lock before `AbstractRunnable.onFailure` records the failure:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/7720ab831efd44db2e8fd456e34c314a5b713048/x-pack/plugin/esql/compute/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/compute/operator/ParallelHashAggregationOperator.java#L384-L398

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/7720ab831efd44db2e8fd456e34c314a5b713048/x-pack/plugin/esql/compute/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/compute/operator/ParallelHashAggregationOperator.java#L444-L450

In that window the driver thread can take the same lock in `finish()`, which checks `hasFailure()` once at the top and then drains pages into every worker it can lock:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/7720ab831efd44db2e8fd456e34c314a5b713048/x-pack/plugin/esql/compute/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/compute/operator/ParallelHashAggregationOperator.java#L222-L254

That matches the stack above: the driver thread's `finish()` adds a page to a hash whose grow had just failed on a background worker.

**Expected:** the query fails with the 429 `CircuitBreakingException`. A failed grow should leave the hash in its previous, usable state, for example by committing the new capacity and closing the old core only after the new core is built and rehashed. The parallel operator also shouldn't hand pages to a worker whose previous `processOnePage` threw.

**Unit test (deterministic).** Add this to `BytesRefSwissHashTests`:

```
public void testAddAfterBreakingOnGrow() {
    BytesRef[] v = randomValues(PageCacheRecycler.PAGE_SIZE_IN_BYTES).toArray(new BytesRef[0]);
    TestRecycler recycler = new TestRecycler();

main

none

_bundled_

A top-level `knn` search on a nested `dense_vector` field with `inner_hits` returns 500 when a filter has to be rewritten against the shard's mappings before it can be built.

Examples:
- A `term` query on a field the index doesn't map, inside a clause that still matches documents, such as `must_not`
- A `semantic` query

The same searches work without `inner_hits`, and the hits themselves are filtered correctly.

Expected: hits with inner hits, filtered as requested.

Cause: in the query phase, each top-level `knn` becomes a `KnnScoreDocQueryBuilder`.

The filters are only used to build inner hits.
They go through an `InnerHitsRewriteContext` rewrite, which has no mappings, and then `InnerHitContextBuilder` calls `toQuery` on them.
Any filter that only becomes buildable after a rewrite against mappings fails at that point.
The main hits are unaffected, because the DFS phase builds a `KnnVectorQueryBuilder`, which does rewrite its filters.

Possible fix: rewrite `filterQueries` in `KnnScoreDocQueryBuilder.doRewrite`, as `KnnVectorQueryBuilder.doRewrite` does.

[ES|QL] PROMQL: `a/(b)` fails to parse ("extraneous input ')'") — the lexer reads `/(` as an index-pattern token

9.5.0-SNAPSHOT (`ca18acd4`, 2026-08-03), 9.6.0-SNAPSHOT (`eba6e093`, 2026-10-01), 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT (`679b3d8f`, 2026-10-28)

_none_

_bundled_

In the ES|QL `PROMQL` command, a division operator immediately followed by an opening parenthesis (`a/(b)`) fails to parse:

```
parsing_exception: line 1:109: extraneous input ')' expecting <EOF>
```

The same expression with a space after the `/` parses and returns the right value. Every other binary operator works without a space.

| PromQL expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `6/(2)` | ❌ `extraneous input ')' expecting <EOF>` |
| `vector(6)/(vector(2))` | ❌ same |
| `6 /(2)` | ❌ same |
| `6/ (2)` | ✅ `3` |
| `6 / (2)` | ✅ `3` |
| `6/2` | ✅ `3` |
| `6*(2)`, `6+(2)`, `6-(2)`, `6%(2)`, `6^(2)` | ✅ |
| `ROW x = 6/(2)` (plain ES|QL, not PROMQL) | ✅ `3` |

**Expected:** `a/(b)` parses like `a / (b)`. It is valid PromQL, and Grafana dashboards write ratios like `sum(a)/(sum(a) + sum(b))` all the time.

**Likely cause:** in `PROMQL_MODE`, the lexer reuses `UNQUOTED_SOURCE` for the index pattern (`x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/antlr/lexer/Promql.g4`). `UNQUOTED_SOURCE_PART` in `lexer/From.g4` allows `'/' ~[*/]`, which is meant for date-math index names. That alternative also matches the two characters `/(`. ANTLR prefers the longest match, so `/(` becomes one `UNQUOTED_SOURCE` token instead of `PROMQL_OTHER_QUERY_CONTENT` (`/`) followed by `PROMQL_LP` (`(`). The swallowed `(` never calls `incPromqlDepth()`. Its matching `)` is then lexed as `PROMQL_QUERY_RP`, which ends the query text one parenthesis early, and the final `)` is extraneous.

```
PUT promql-paren-repro
{"mappings": {"properties": {"@timestamp": {"type": "date"}}}}

POST _query
{"query": "PROMQL index=promql-paren-repro start=\"2026-10-30T00:00:00Z\" end=\"2026-10-30T01:00:00Z\" step=1h value=(6/(2))"}
```
→ `400 parsing_exception: line 1:109: extraneous input ')' expecting <EOF>`

```
POST _query
{"query": "PROMQL index=promql-paren-repro start=\"2026-10-30T00:00:00Z\" end=\"2026-10-30T01:00:00Z\" step=1h value=(6 / (2))"}
```
→ `200`, value `3.0`

The error does not depend on data or the index: the bare form (`… step=1h 6/(2)`) and real metric selectors (`sum(a{job="x"})/(sum(a) + sum(b))`) fail the same way.

ES|QL: Share the hash join build side across drivers and shard batches

`INLINE STATS`, `IN` and `NOT IN` subqueries materialize the sub-plan result as a local relation and join it back to the source rows with a hash join. The relation travels inside the plan, so the join runs on every data node.

Every driver builds its own lookup hash table from the relation's key columns, and deep-copies each value column it loads. A data node also runs its shards in batches of `max_concurrent_shards_per_node` (10 by default) and plans each batch separately, so every batch builds the table and copies the columns again.

So a data node holds one table and one copy of the value columns per driver, and builds them once per driver per batch. For a large relation, the memory grows with the number of drivers, and the build time with the number of drivers times the number of batches.

- Build one lookup table that every driver probes. The first driver to receive input builds it, and the others hold a bounded amount of input until it is ready.
- Make one copy of each loaded value column and share it the same way.
- Keep both across the shard batches of a data node request, and release them when the request finishes.
- Charge both to the request breaker once.

Sharing the table needs lookups that are safe to run concurrently. `PackedValuesBlockHash.lookup`, used for joins on several keys, encodes probe keys into the hash's own scratch buffer, so concurrent lookups return wrong rows.

ES|QL: unmapped_fields="load" loses old values of an unmapped object once it is mapped as an object-valued type

This affects unmapped fields stored in both the `_unmapped` sink and `_ignored_source`.

When a document holds an unmapped object such as `{"location":{"lat":1.5,"lon":2.5}}` and `location` is later mapped with a type that takes an object as its value (`geo_point`, a range type, `histogram`, `aggregate_metric_double`, `flattened`, ...), `SET unmapped_fields="load"` returns `null` for `location.lat` and `location.lon` on the old document, although it returned their values before the mapping. The mapped field `location` is read from its own doc values, which the old document doesn't have, so it is `null` too. The old values are then unreachable from ES|QL under any name.

The two storages differ only in what `_source` shows for the old document:

| Storage | How the unmapped object is stored | `_source` after the mapping |
|---|---|---|
| `_unmapped` sink (strict-columnar index modes) | one key per leaf, under its full dotted path | `{"location.lat": "1.5", "location.lon": "2.5"}` |
| `_ignored_source` (`dynamic: false`, synthetic `_source`) | the whole object as one entry at `location` (`DocumentParser.parseObjectDynamic` -> `FallbackPostMapper.capture`) | `{"location": {"lat": 1.5, "lon": 2.5}}` |

On the sink, `_source` keeps showing `location.lat` as a field that ES|QL refuses to load. Under `subobjects: false`, the children of a `dynamic: false` object are flattened instead of being captured as one entry, so `_ignored_source` may store and show dotted leaves the same way (not verified).

Both the columnar index modes and the sink are behind feature flags; the `_ignored_source` case is in released versions.

`UnmappedFields.mayExist(name)` calls `skipped("", name)`, which returns `true` when a prefix of the name resolves to a field mapper with `supportsParsingObject() == true`. `UnmappedFields.blockLoader(name, walk)` returns `ConstantNull` when `mayExist(name)` is `false`, before it decides between the sink and a walk of `_source`, so the rule applies to both storages.

ES|QL: Prune STATS ... BY keys that are a function of another single-valued key

Part of #142176. Follows #164026 and #164027.

`STATS ... BY x, x + 1` groups by two keys, but the second key is a function of the first. The rule can drop the second key and compute it after the aggregation. That makes the grouping cheaper.

This is only correct if the keys are single-valued. When an input column can hold a list, each value becomes its own group, and the derived key no longer follows from the first one. A version of this rule was added before without a proof. It was removed in #161531 for external data sources.

- Add `PruneRedundantAggregateGroupings`. It drops a `BY` key that is a function of another key, if `ValueCardinality` proves the input keys single-valued.
- Add optimizer tests for the cases that must rewrite, and for the cases that must not (multi-valued fields, lists from `VALUES`, unknown nodes).
- Add csv-spec or YAML tests that check query results do not change.

ES|QL: Add ValueCardinality to prove that a column is single-valued

Part of #142176. Follows #164026. Followed by #164028.

A rule often needs to know if a computed column is single-valued, not only a mapped field. For example, after `EVAL k = MV_MAX(languages)` or `STATS ... BY k`. #164026 gives the proof for mapped fields. This ticket extends it to the rest of the plan.

`ValueCardinality` is a plan walk. It answers "at most one value per row?" for a column or an expression, with `SINGLE` or `MAYBE_MULTI`.

- Mapped fields use `EsField.isStaticallySingleValued()`.
- `EVAL`, `RENAME`, `ROW` and `MV_EXPAND` are resolved to their definition.
- `STATS` proves group keys and `COUNT`. Other aggregate functions can return a list (`VALUES`, `TOP`), so they are unknown.
- `Filter`, `Limit`, `OrderBy` and `TopN` pass the question to their child.
- Any other node gives `MAYBE_MULTI`. A wrong proof gives wrong results, but a missing proof only loses an optimization.

No rule uses it in this ticket.

More aggregate functions, arithmetic such as `a + 1`, and a general allow-list of scalar functions that never return a list. `SPLIT` returns a list from one input, so this must be an allow-list.

Window functions (OVER, PARTITION BY, LAG/LEAD)

Summary

ES|QL has no window functions, so analytical calculations that depend on a row's position or neighbors in an ordered, partitioned set cannot be expressed. The immediate need is a moving average over a time series, but the same gap blocks ranking, running totals, period-over-period deltas, and anything else that needs LAG / LEAD. Window functions are high on our list of analytical capabilities.Upstream tracking issue: elastic/elasticsearch#116213. It had no visible activity for almost a year. Elastic support said LAG / LEAD are in planning and that the work is internal, and that they raised it with the product team on several occasions. As of the last update in the conversation, the product team has not given a timeline or a scope for what would be released.

Ask

  1. A firm timeline for window function support in ES|QL.
  2. Clarity on planned scope. At minimum we need the ES|QL equivalent of the standard SQL window clause:
RANK() / COUNT() / ... OVER (
    [PARTITION BY column1, column2, ...]
    ORDER BY column3 [ASC | DESC], column4 [ASC | DESC], ...
)
  1. Support for aggregate functions as window functions (so a moving average can be written directly), plus ranking functions and LAG / LEAD.
  2. A way for customers to vote on or prioritize upstream feature requests.

Example use case

Moving average of events per hour over the previous 3 hours, per host. In SQL:
SELECT host, hour, events,
       AVG(events) OVER (
           PARTITION BY host
           ORDER BY hour
           ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
       ) AS moving_avg_3h
FROM hourly_events
Splunk equivalent with streamstats:
index=web-logs
| bin _time span=1h
| stats count AS events BY host, _time
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats window=3 avg(events) AS moving_avg_3h BY host
ES|QL has no equivalent of the OVER clause today. The closest it can do is the per-host, per-hour aggregation itself:
FROM web-logs
| STATS events = COUNT(*) BY host, hour = BUCKET(@timestamp, 1 hour)
| SORT host, hour

Input data

Hourly event counts per host, as returned by the aggregation step in all three platforms: host | hour (UTC) | events -- | -- | -- host-a | 00:00 | 4 host-a | 01:00 | 6 host-a | 02:00 | 8 host-a | 03:00 | 2 host-a | 04:00 | 10 host-b | 00:00 | 1 host-b | 01:00 | 3 host-b | 02:00 | 2 host-b | 03:00 | 6 host-b | 04:00 | 4 For example, host-a at 03:00 is (6 + 8 + 2) / 3 = 5.33. The same shape applies to LAG / LEAD: a period-over-period delta for host-a at 03:00 would need the 02:00 value (8) alongside the current row (2) to give -6, which ES|QL also cannot do without window functions.

Zero-filled time bins (gap fill) for BUCKET / TBUCKET

1. Zero-filled time bins (gap fill) for BUCKET / TBUCKET

Summary

STATS ... BY BUCKET(@timestamp, ...) only emits rows for buckets that contain at least one document, so periods with no events are missing rather than zero-valued. Any downstream aggregation over the bucketed series, such as AVG of per-bucket counts or rates, is computed over only the non-empty bins. If 6 hourly buckets are expected and 3 are empty, the average of a per-hour count is divided by 3 instead of 6. This overstates the average for sparse data and also distorts percentiles, minimums, and any threshold or baseline comparison built on the series. It is a correctness problem for detection and alerting use cases, where "no events" is itself the signal.Splunk's timechart returns every bin in the search range with a zero for empty ones, so results are correct by default. ES|QL has no equivalent, and no native way to generate the full set of bins and join counts onto them.

Ask

A gap-fill capability that emits every bin in the search range with a configurable default (zero or null). For example, an option on BUCKET/TBUCKET, or a dedicated command.

Example data

Index web-logs, search range 2026-10-29T00:00Z to 2026-10-29T06:00Z, 1-hour bins. Events exist in only three of the six hours: Hour (UTC) | Events -- | -- 00:00 | 3 01:00 | 2 02:00 | 0 03:00 | 0 04:00 | 5 05:00 | 0

Workarounds today

  • Fill gaps in the consumer after the ES|QL query returns.
  • Fixed, known bin lists can be built with ROW plus MV_EXPAND, but ES|QL has no range-generating function, and LOOKUP JOIN only joins against an index, not a stats result, so counts cannot be joined onto the generated bins.

Notes

  • The queries above are illustrative and have not been run against a cluster.

[ML] Nightly maintenance should delete emptied rolled .ml-anomalies-* results indices

Nightly ML maintenance rolls `.ml-anomalies-*` indices at `xpack.ml.results_index_rollover_max_size` (#131014, #136065), but nothing removes a rolled results index once retention has emptied it. This is a design gap: the state indices already have the cleanup (`EmptyStateIndexRemover`), the results indices do not. The nightly maintenance should delete emptied rolled results indices.

- `ExpiredResultsRemover` runs one delete-by-query per job through the job's read alias. It never drops an index.
- `EmptyStateIndexRemover` deletes empty `.ml-state*` indices that are not behind the write alias. It is wired into `TransportDeleteExpiredDataAction`. No equivalent exists for `.ml-anomalies-*`.
- `JobDataDeleter` drops a results index only on job delete, and only if no other job's documents remain in it.
- After each roll, `MlIndexAndAlias.addResultsIndexRolloverAliasActions` re-adds every job's filtered read alias to the new index, from the earliest index that had it (`addReadAliasesForResultsIndices`). A job's read alias therefore spans every backing index.

With `results_retention_days` set, old backing indices end up with no retained results documents. The retention delete excludes `model_size_stats`, `forecast` and `forecast_request_stats`, so those can remain. The indices stay in the cluster, keep their shards, and keep one read-alias entry per job, forever.

Example: a shared custom index for ~1,700 jobs at ~8.6 GB/day rolls about every 6 days. That is ~60 backing indices a year, each carrying ~1,700 read-alias entries (~100k alias entries a year), and every job's read alias searches all of them.

Add a results-index counterpart to `EmptyStateIndexRemover` to the delete-expired-data step of the nightly maintenance. It deletes a rolled results index when:

- it is not the latest index of its family (no job's write alias points at it), and
- it holds no documents that retention keeps.

Points to settle in the implementation:

- Treatment of `model_size_stats` and forecast documents in an otherwise empty index. A job that stopped writing before the roll must keep its latest `model_size_stats`.
- A stopped job's results are never expired, because the retention cutoff is relative to the job's latest bucket. Its index is not empty and is kept, which is correct.
- Respect indices with an ILM policy, as the rollover does (`hasIlm`).
- Naming is safe: `MlIndexAndAlias.nextSuffix` uses the highest existing suffix + 1, so deleting old indices does not cause reuse.

The failure has nothing to do with how I resolved the conflicts. The merge itself is correct, and the upper bounds files are exactly main's.

Workflow

lucene_snapshot is a long-lived branch that mirrors main with a newer Lucene snapshot. A scheduled Buildkite job (elasticsearch-lucene-snapshot-update-branch) merges main into it once a day and pushes straight to the branch, so there is no PR and no PR checks. When that merge hits a conflict, the job fails and someone has to do the merge by hand and open a PR. That is the case where this check runs. It happens fairly often, because lucene_snapshot keeps edits to files like muted-tests.yml, etc.

Why it fails

The task decides what a PR changed by diffing against merge-base(<elastic remote>/<PR base branch>, HEAD). For a PR into lucene_snapshot, that is the tip of lucene_snapshot, which can be many commits behind main. So everything main has added since then looks like it was added by the PR. The task requires every newly added definition to be referenced by an upper bounds file, but only the newest definitions on main are. In this PR, 7 definitions come in from main and only 2 are upper bounds, so the rest fail. The task stops at the first one, so only one is reported. I reproduced it locally: with the base set to lucene_snapshot it fails, and with the default base of main it passes.

Motivation

A manual main-to-lucene_snapshot merge PR currently cannot pass CI on its own. Whoever does the merge has to bypass the check each time, and a real transport version problem on the branch could be missed. The check does not seem to have been meant for this case.

Possible solution

When the target branch is lucene_snapshot or a branch with that prefix, compare against main instead of the target branch. In TransportVersionResourcesService, findUpstreamRef() could use main in that case. That would make the git base for a merge PR the main commit that was merged. Definitions that come from main would then not look new, and a definition that is really new on lucene_snapshot would still need an upper bound. The patch branch detection also uses the target branch name, so it should keep using the real target branch.

There is also a smaller option, which is to skip definitions that already exist on main in the added definition check only. That fixes the error above but leaves the other rules exposed.
