Batch scoring of multiple query vectors in `dense_vector` brute-force search to improve IO efficiency

Relates to https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/160367

When we perform a multi-search over `dense_vector`, query execution runs independent searchers. This is likely sufficient for many use cases, especially if the system is not memory constrained, as long as the touched files are memory mapped. However, if we exceed the page cache capacity and start to churn, we may go to disk many times to fetch the same data. This will be most noticeable when doing brute force search via a `dense_vector` query. In such cases, reworking query execution to push down the multi-vector score will improve IO efficiency by utilizing the fetched vectors across multiple search vector comparisons.

This design is an open ended question. Based on some quick checking with a 🤖, this kind of change might be non-trivial due to the current implementation of search execution. As such, this is just a backlog item for now.

Note: "multi-query" here means multiple *query* vectors scored against the same document vectors, not multiple vectors per document.

analysis from my agent 🤖

> This analysis was produced by AI assistants (Claude) from web searches and code review. Items marked *(unverified)* were not confirmed against current source. Treat it as a starting point.

Exact (brute-force) scoring via `DenseVectorQuery` scores one query vector per search. When many exact searches target the same field (e.g. through `_msearch`), each one independently reads every vector in every segment from disk / blob cache into memory. Scoring Q query vectors in a single pass would read each vector once instead of Q times, which should help when exact scoring is I/O or memory-bandwidth bound.

Scope is exact scoring only (`DenseVectorQuery.Floats`/`Bytes`/`DocValuesFloats`/`DocValuesBytes`, including the `FilteredDenseVectorQuery` path). Approximate HNSW search is out of scope: each query traverses a different part of the graph, so there is little overlap to amortize.

Whether the bottleneck is IO or CPU/memory bandwidth depends on whether the field fits in page cache. When it fits, repeated scans are served from cache and the gain is mainly cache and bandwidth efficiency. When it does not, repeated scans re-read the same pages from disk, and batching saves IO.

`TransportMultiSearchAction` fans out independent `client.search(...)` calls. Each sub-search has its own query phase, `Weight` and `ScorerSupplier`, so any sharing of vector pages is incidental (page cache / shared blob cache), not planned. *(class-level detail unverified; an older Elastic staff forum answer also states msearch items execute as independent single searches, and the documented `max_concurrent_*` parameters only control concurrency)*

No precedent was found in Elasticsearch for sharing scan or scoring work across `_msearch` sub-searches. This does not rule out an existing proposal. The nearest related work is the batched query phase, which batches a single search's shard requests per data node to reduce transport overhead, and is not cross-query fusion. Outside Elasticsearch, Faiss flat-index search accepts a matrix of queries and uses BLAS matrix multiplication, and Qdrant and Milvus expose batch search APIs *(unverified here)*.

Process each segment in doc-ID windows and run all Q targets over a window before advancing:

```
for window in [min, max) step W:
    for t in targets:
        scorer[t].nextDocsAndScores(windowEnd, liveDocs, buf)
        offer buf to heap[t] if above its min-competitive score
```

- The first target pulls the window's vectors into memory; the remaining targets hit L2/L3 or the page cache.
- Size `W` so `W * dims * elemSize` fits in L2.
- Each target keeps its own `VectorScorer` (`rescorer`, `RawVectorScorer`, doc-values), so quantized fields that rescore against raw vectors are covered.
- A shared filter is evaluated once per leaf; per-target filters fall back to un-batched execution.

To verify against the forked Lucene: whether `VectorScorer.Bulk#nextDocsAndScores` honors `upTo` strictly, its internal batch size, and any prefetching it does.

Once I/O is amortized, a "1 doc x N targets" or tiled dot-product kernel in `ESVectorUtil` could avoid reloading the doc vector per target. Applies to raw float/byte paths only.

1. Library-only prototype: `MultiDenseVectorQuery` plus collector manager, benchmarked directly (JMH or `ESSingleNodeTestCase`) with Q = 1 / 8 / 32 vs. Q separate searches on a cold cache. This decides whether the rest is worthwhile.
2. Explicit batched API carrying `query_vectors[]` and returning Q result sets.
3. Keep `_msearch` as the surface: the coordinator groups compatible sub-requests (same index, field, similarity, size, filter, `denormalize`), sends one shard request with Q targets, and demuxes Q `TopDocs` into the original slots. Needs a new transport version and a fallback for incompatible sub-requests; fetch-phase features (`explain`, `profile`, etc.) would need to fall back or be rejected.

#160367 proposes prefetch in the `VectorScorer.Bulk` path for larger-than-memory deployments. The two are complementary: prefetch makes a single query's pass cheaper, while batching amortizes that pass across queries. Prefetch may reduce the benefit of batching when IO is the only bottleneck, so the prototype benchmark should be run both with and without prefetch.

- Memory scales with Q (Q heaps plus Q targets); cap the batch size (about 16-64?).
- Per-target min-competitive pruning is needed to keep heap traffic from dominating.
- `denormalize` magnitude doc values should be read once and shared across targets.
- Different filters or similarity functions can't be batched together.

Build the leaf scorer (section 1) and measure the Q-scaling curve before committing to any API change.

Adapt to Dutch stemming changes

For years the default Dutch stemmer was Porter-style. Kraaij-Pohlmann was the other one (dutch-kp), removed by Lucene 10.
Lucene 11 upgraded the bundled Snowball stemmers ([apache/lucene#15505](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/15505)). Snowball replaced the default Dutch stemmer with Kraaij-Pohlmann (the old dutch-kp). Lucene now ships both:

- DutchStemmer — Kraaij-Pohlmann. Used by DutchAnalyzer and language="Dutch".
- Dutch_porterStemmer — the Lucene 10 algorithm. Lucene’s migrate note is language="Dutch_porter".

The name Dutch now means KP. The old algorithm was renamed Dutch_porter and kept as a leftover class.

The same Elasticsearch names (dutch analyzer, stemmer language: dutch, dutch_stem, snowball language: Dutch) now emit different tokens. A pre-11 Dutch index still opens but requires reindexing.

Elasticsearch should not break analysis compatibility on a Lucene 11 upgrade. Existing dutch names need to keep Lucene 10 Porter stems. The `lucene_snapshot_11` branch currently follows Lucene’s default (KP). Yaml tests expectations were updated to the new tokens so the suite stays green. That is not the product behaviour we want.

Note: `dutch_kp` is not a viable way back. Lucene 10 removed `KpStemmer`, so 8.16 deprecated the registered name and made the filter a no-op ([#113143](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/113143)). Lucene 11 then made Kraaij-Pohlmann the default `Dutch` stemmer once it ugpraded its snowball library.

- Decide whether Kraaij-Pohlmann is still offered under a new name (dutch_kp is already a no-op).

ESCF batch indexing must preserve the lexical form of floating-point numbers

Follow-up to #162922 and #163401 (closed as a known limitation; we think it needs a fix).

When a document goes through the ESCF batch indexing path, JSON floating-point numbers are stored as `double`. A `keyword` sub-field of such a number is then built from the double, so the original text is lost. The sequential path keeps the original text.

Example from the `employees` csv-spec dataset (`salary_change` is a `double` with a `salary_change.keyword` sub-field):

| Source value | Sequential path | Batch path |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-1.90` | `"-1.90"` | `"-1.9"` |

#162922 makes batch indexing the default for strict columnar index modes (`columnar`, `logsdb_columnar`, `vectordb_columnar`) when the `batch_indexing` feature flag is on. The same document indexed into a columnar index now produces different `keyword` sub-field values than it did before, and different values than a non-columnar index gets. This is a limitation of the ESCF transport format, not of the columnar format on disk, so the on-disk format can hold the correct value once the encoder passes it through.

- `EscfEncoder`, `VALUE_NUMBER` case: floats and doubles are stored with `row.doubleField(fieldName, val)` (around line 341). The parsed text is dropped.
- `EscfColumnTransforms`, `SourceValueType.DOUBLE` cases: the value is rendered for string consumers with `Double.toString(...)` (around lines 159 and 221).

Keep the raw text of a floating-point value when a string consumer (for example a `keyword` sub-field or a dynamic template that maps numbers as strings) needs it. The encoder already has a `rawTextMode` that passes `parser.optimizedText()` to the sink, so one option is to store the text next to the double, or to store the text only when the mapping has a string sub-field for that path. The cost is extra bytes per float in the batch; we can measure that with the existing bulk benchmarks.

- `CsvColumnarIT.modeSettings()` no longer sets `index.batch_indexing: false`, and the `TODO` that points to this issue is removed.
- `topN.sortingOnNumbersFromStrings`, `drop.whereWithEvalGeneratedValue_DropHeight` and `rename.renameIntertwinedWithSort` pass with batch indexing on.
- A unit test in `EscfEncoderTests` (or `EscfColumnTransformsTests`) covers a float with trailing zeros that has a `keyword` sub-field, and asserts the original text.

- #162922 (per-index `index.batch_indexing` setting, adds the workaround)
- #163401 (original report)
- #162057, #159025 (earlier PRs where `CsvColumnarIT` failed for this reason)

ES|QL: Support TS over views whose body is TS <index> | WHERE

A view is planned as a subquery, and subqueries lose time series semantics, so `TS <view>` does not work. Views that contain `TS ... | STATS` already compose fine. This issue is about the other end: a view that only scopes raw time series data, with no aggregation.

Treat a view whose body is `TS <index>` plus optional `WHERE` as a virtual time series source. The timestamp comes from the underlying data, so `TBUCKET` and the time series functions keep working without the caller declaring anything. Start narrow (`TS` plus `WHERE` only) and widen from there.

An SRE owns the checkout service. Its OTel metrics land in `metrics-otel-*`, shared with every other service and environment.

```
// view: checkout_prod_metrics
TS metrics-otel-*
| WHERE service.name == "checkout" AND deployment.environment.name == "production"
```

```
TS checkout_prod_metrics
| STATS rate(http.server.request.count) BY TBUCKET(5m)
```

The consumer references the view by name, so editing the filter or renaming an attribute reaches every query. Other uses: a stable name for a renamed attribute (schema evolution), and views as a reusable catalog, where "views work everywhere except `TS`" will surprise users.

Operations that are only valid after `TS` with a `STATS` could be hidden inside a view and produce cryptic errors, especially with nested views. For the first cut, the narrow `TS` plus `WHERE` rule avoids this. Options to discuss: validate on view save, or an opt-in `SET` as an initial workaround. We'd prefer inferring it automatically, since users would hit the same limit.

Adapt to DictionaryCompoundWordTokenFilter changes

Lucene 11 dropped the `DictionaryCompoundWordTokenFilter` constructor that took `onlyLongestMatch` and `reuseChars` ([apache/lucene#14356](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/14356). The replacement is `onlyLongestMatchIgnoreSubwords` ([apache/lucene#14278](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/14278),
  [apache/lucene#14311](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/14311)).

  The old `onlyLongestMatch` flag did not skip characters already used in a longer hit, so `schwein` still produced `wein`. Lucene treated that as broken longest-match. `reuseChars=false` was the skip-forward behaviour;
  `onlyLongestMatchIgnoreSubwords` is roughly old `onlyLongestMatch=true` plus `reuseChars=false`. The superclass always gets `onlyLongestMatch=false`.

  Elasticsearch never exposed `reuseChars` (it was hard-coded `true` on `main`, with a TODO pointing at ([apache/lucene#14278](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/14278)). `dictionary_decompounder` still documents and parses `only_longest_match` (default `false`). Hyphenation is unchanged and still uses
  that setting.

  `lucene_snapshot_11` compiles against the 6-arg constructor. This issue tracks the long-term adaptation of the dictionary filter — settings, docs, and token-filter sharing.

What changed, and what Elasticsearch still assumes:
    - **Constructor**: was `(…, onlyLongestMatch, reuseChars)`. Now `(…, onlyLongestMatchIgnoreSubwords)`. There is no `reuseChars` and no old `onlyLongestMatch` on this filter.
    - **`only_longest_match`**: still parsed on the shared compound factory (default `false`) and still in the dictionary sharing key. It is no longer passed to Lucene for `dictionary_decompounder`. Docs still list it. Hyphenation still honours it.
    - **What the branch passes**: `onlyLongestMatchIgnoreSubwords` is hard-coded `true`. That is not the documented dictionary default (`only_longest_match: false`, emit every matching subword). Nested hits such as `wein` inside `schwein` are dropped.
    - **`reuseChars`**: never a user setting. Do not put it back when merging `main`.

  Stop-gap commit:
    - [023d5002ab84](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/commit/023d5002ab84) — drop `reuseChars`; call the 6-arg constructor with `onlyLongestMatchIgnoreSubwords=true`

Adapt to updated LRUQueryCache

Lucene 11 comes with a refactored `LRUQueryCache` ([apache/lucene#15558](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/15558), [apache/lucene#14222](https://github.com/apache/lucene/issues/14222)) for improved scalability under concurrent search.

The new cache is partitioned (separate locks per partition) and keyed by `(query, segment)` so a lookup hashes to one partition.
Stale-segment cleanup moved off the search thread and onto a background task.

Lucene also turned the default query cache off ([apache/lucene#14187](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/14187)); Elasticsearch does not use that default and still installs its own node-level cache.

Elasticsearch wraps Lucene's cache in `IndicesQueryCache` so `_stats` / node `query_cache` can be attributed per shard.
The `lucene_snapshot_11` branch has the minimum set of changes needed to compile, plus some muted tests. This issue tracks the adjustments required to adapt Elasticsearch long term.

What changed in Lucene, and what Elasticsearch still assumes:
- **Cache keys**: was `segment → query → DocIdSet`. Now one key per `(query, segment)`. One query on N segments is N entries, not one.
- **Stats hooks**: The old two-level map had two events: unique query vs per-segment `DocIdSet`. `onQueryCache` / `onDocIdSetCache` (and the eviction pair) matched that split. They are deprecated and now fire together for the same insert or evict.
  Replacements are `onCacheEntryInserted` / `onCacheEntryEvicted`. `ElasticsearchLRUQueryCache` still overrides the old pair, so published `query_cache` stats can over- or under-count. Filter caching on the search path still works.
- **`maxSize` / `indices.queries.cache.count`**: The setting (default `10000`) is still passed through as Lucene `maxSize`. It used to mean unique queries — a cap so query objects do not dominate RAM, next to `indices.queries.cache.size` (`10%`).
  Lucene's `maxSize` is now the number of `(query, segment)` keys. The same number is a tighter, different limit. Lucene no longer tracks unique queries.
- **Cleanup**: Dead-segment keys used to be dropped on the search thread when the segment closed. Cleanup is now async: a scheduler, or `cleanup()`. Without either, stale keys sit until LRU evicts them. The cache still stays within `maxSize` and
  does not serve stale data.
- **Default cache**: `IndexSearcher.DEFAULT_QUERY_CACHE` is null. Production searchers use `IndicesQueryCache`. Unit tests that rely on Lucene's default do not.

ES|QL: fail at planning time when a function is newer than a participating cluster

A cross-cluster query that uses a function the remote cluster's version doesn't have is shipped to that
remote anyway. The remote can't deserialize the plan, and with default settings the user gets a silently
skipped cluster instead of an error.

Coordinator on 9.5+ (or main), remote on 9.4.x, where `TO_TEXT` doesn't exist:

```
POST _query
{
  "query": "FROM remote:employees | EVAL x = TO_TEXT(first_name) | KEEP emp_no, x"
}
```

The argument has to be a field so `TO_TEXT` isn't folded away on the coordinator.

The coordinator serializes the remote fragment (`ClusterComputeRequest` → `RemoteClusterPlan.writeTo` →
`writeNamedWriteable(plan)`) with `ToText` inside it. The remote fails in
`NamedWriteableRegistry.throwOnUnknownWritable` with
`IllegalArgumentException: Unknown NamedWriteable [...Expression][ToText]`.

What the user sees depends on two settings (`ClusterComputeHandler`, `shouldSkipOnFailure ||
(allowPartialResults && canAllowPartial(e))`):

- `skip_unavailable=true` (the default, `RemoteClusterSettings.DEFAULT_SKIP_UNAVAILABLE`) or
  `allow_partial_results=true`: the remote is marked `skipped`, `is_partial` is true, and the response
  has no rows from it. The only clue is the `Unknown NamedWriteable` reason under `_clusters`.
- `skip_unavailable=false` and `allow_partial_results=false`: the query fails with that deserialization
  error, which doesn't name the function's minimum version or say what to change.

Both responses are only correct if the user reads `_clusters`. Nothing says "TO_TEXT isn't supported by
remote cluster [remote] (version X)."

In assertion-enabled builds (`assert ignoreDeserializationErrors` in `throwOnUnknownWritable`) the remote
node dies instead. That's how this surfaced in CI: #154471, where `casePartialFold*` specs using
`TO_TEXT` took down a 9.4.4 remote in `multi-clusters:v9.4.4#csvSpecTests#newToOld` and every later
test in the suite failed. #154474 gated the specs; the product behavior is unchanged.

The query fails during verification with a 4xx that names the function and says a participating cluster
is too old, the same way commands already do. `Verifier` has `checkTimeSeriesCollapseSupported`,
`checkHighlightSupported`, and `checkDenseVectorSupported`, which compare
`AnalyzerContext.minimumVersion()` to the command's `TransportVersion` and fail with "X is not supported
on every participating node; rolling upgrade in progress, or a remote cluster is on an older version".
`minimumVersion` already covers every node in every cluster the query targets (see `IndexResolver`).

Functions have no such check. Any scalar or aggregate function added after the oldest wire-compatible
version can reach a remote that doesn't know it, not just `TO_TEXT`.

Give `FunctionDefinition` an optional minimum `TransportVersion`, set when a function is added, and have
the `Verifier` walk the plan's expressions and fail when `minimumVersion` doesn't support one. That
replaces per-command checks with one rule for functions.

Things to decide:

- **Over-rejection.** The Verifier runs before optimization. A function that is constant-folded, or
  only runs on the coordinator after the remote fragment (for example, an `EVAL` after `STATS`), never
  reaches the remote. Rejecting those would break queries that work today. Checking the physical
  fragments actually sent to each cluster is more precise, but it fails later and needs a per-cluster
  version, not the global minimum.
- **Rolling upgrades.** The same gap probably applies within one cluster when a new coordinator sends a
  data-node request to a node that hasn't been upgraded. I haven't verified that path.
- **Existing functions.** Backfilling minimum versions for functions added since the oldest supported
  remote version, or only enforcing it for new functions going forward.

- #154471, #154474: the CI failure and the test-side gate
- #159672: version-gates the request filter on the functions it emits (narrower; request filter only)
- elastic/esql-planning#1474: csv-spec tests missing `required_capability` at merge time

Index Partitions by Shard

This is an idea based on looking at other systems and how they partition data, and dealing with many thousands of data streams. This would be a foundational shift for Elasticsearch, but one that I think would dramatically benefit it and users for any time-based use case (other reasons to partition exist, but scale is generally much lower), especially in Serverless.

The idea is simple at a high level, but the details make it complex:

1. Support partitioning on fields: specifically `@timestamp`, but ultimately however a user chooses to do index sorting.
    - It's easiest to reason about for time, where users could decide when to partition like practically every SQL database.
2. Partitioning changes the semantics of index management for Elasticsearch.
    - Instead of partitioning _by index_ (rolling over), the index sticks around just like tables in an SQL database that support partitioning. Elasticsearch could, instead, add new, empty shards to an existing index as a new "partition". This would get all of the advantages of prefetch lookup from Lucene index sorting while simultaneously limiting the amount of metadata outside of shard management.
3. The old shards would then still exist in a way that allows them to be easily replicated, inherently isolated from other partitions, and scalable separately by nature of being shards.
    - Unlike data streams, the old shards do not need to become readonly unless you want them to be. If data comes in out of order, you can still write a shard from yesterday if the `@timestamp` wants it there and that still benefits from append-only features (but nothing should really stop edits either).
    - New handling would need to exist for partitions to allow old partition shards _for the same index_ to exist across data tiers in fundamentally the exact same way.
    - Deleting partitions is a "simple" matter of deleting shards.
    - The ES index would inherently need to somehow allow shard changes and the semantics of the shard number would change (the meaning of shard `0` is different in this context).
    - Data streams could be layered on top of this, if desired, to make it

Instead of having [tens of] thousands of indexes to support a very long tail of data, users would have one index with potentially thousands of partitions that could support years of data. APIs could exist to combine or split partitions for when a user realizes partitioning by day versus week / month / year was the wrong decision (either for bureaucratic reasons or performance).

To the end user, managing partitioned indexes would be much simpler. New day -> new shards, but the same index. ES is still stuck with shard management (like every large scale database), but for most time-based use cases the number of indexes would [be able to] drop dramatically.

Explore incremental dynamic mapping updates

Part of #163171.

Every dynamic mapping update does work proportional to the whole mapping, even when it adds one field. With about 10,000 fields per index this is what saturates the master after a rollover. It also still applies to label names once metric names leave the mapping.

| Step | What happens | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Master merge | copies the sibling mappers, rebuilds the mapper, re-serializes and compresses the whole mapping | `ObjectMapper.mergeChildMappers`, `DocumentMapper.mappingSource()` |
| Publication | the whole mapping is sent to every node | `MappingMetadata` is `SimpleDiffable` |
| Persistence | a new mapping hash means a new full mapping document on master-eligible nodes | `PersistedClusterStateService` (`mapping_hash`) |
| Apply | nodes holding a shard of the index re-parse the full source and rebuild `DocumentMapper` and `MappingLookup` | `MapperService.updateMapping` |

The mapping is one `CompressedXContent` blob, and every step uses it as the source of truth:
- the master's no-op check compares the old and new source;
- deduplication and persistence are keyed by its hash;
- it is the payload on the wire;
- it is the input of `MapperService`.

1. **Profile** a single dynamic update on an index with about 10,000 fields. Break the time down across master merge, serialization and compression, publication, persistence, and node apply, and include allocation and GC.
2. **Based on the profile**, evaluate incremental updates for the dominant steps:
   - `MappingMetadata` as entries keyed by field path, diffed like `aliases` and `inferenceFields` in `IndexMetadata`, with full mapping as the fallback when the base version is missing;
   - incremental apply in `MapperService` (path copying in `DocumentMapper` and `MappingLookup`);
   - persistence as entries, or a base plus deltas;
   - an incrementally maintained mapping hash.
3. **Write up** the cost and the risks: transport version and mixed clusters, immutability of the mapper structures read by indexing threads, and canonical source for no-op detection and `GET _mapping`.

Reducing the number of updates (#161615, #160644, merging concurrent updates on the master) and removing metric names from the mapping (#146989).

[Meta] Dynamic mapping overhead for metrics data streams

Metrics data streams (Prometheus remote write, OTel) map every metric name to a field. The set of names is open-ended, so the mappings are fully dynamic and can reach the `index.mapping.total_fields.limit` (10,000 fields) per backing index. This issue tracks the work that reduces the cost of that, so related issues and PRs can be found in one place.

- A rolled over backing index is created from the template only, so it rediscovers every metric field from scratch.
- Each document that adds a field makes the primary send a `put-mapping` update to the master and wait for it. The updates of a shard bulk request are serial. A new backing index with about 9,500 metric fields needs thousands of updates.
- Each update does work proportional to the total number of fields:
  - the master merges the update into a copy of the whole mapping and re-serializes and compresses the mapping source;
  - `MappingMetadata` is a `SimpleDiffable`, so the whole mapping is published to every node;
  - every node re-parses the full mapping on the cluster applier thread.
- `put-mapping` tasks run at `HIGH` priority, above rollover tasks, so a backlog can delay rollover.
- The mappings stay in memory: cluster state on every node, `MappingLookup` per shard, and per-field Lucene structures per segment.
- Once the field limit is reached with `ignore_dynamic_beyond_limit`, the fields that are kept depend on arrival order.

Observed on 9.4 with about 10,000 metric fields per backing index: master pending queue of 800 to 2,000 tasks for 15 to 40 minutes after rollovers, a single `put-mapping` taking 11.8s, about 105,000 mapping updates a day on one stream, and rollovers running late (suspected to be queueing behind `put-mapping`, not confirmed).

Fewer updates:

Cheaper updates:

No dynamic updates for metric names:

Field limit behavior:

- Map the metric fields explicitly in the index or component template. A `dynamic_template` still triggers dynamic updates.
- Move high-cardinality parts of metric names (class, method, percentile) into labels so they become dimensions instead of new fields.
- Fewer fields per data stream makes each update cheaper but adds streams and rollovers, which can coincide.

Unpromotable refresh reports shard failures due to relocation

An unpromotable (search-shard) refresh reports a shard failure when the target search shard is closed mid-request because cluster state removed it. The indexing primary has already refreshed successfully. The failure is `AlreadyClosedException: engine is closed`, raised while the search shard is waiting for the requested primary term and segment generation.

I suspect this is a bug because `TransportUnpromotableShardRefreshAction` already treats "search shard does not exist yet" as success, because the copy that recovers later reads the latest commit from the indexing shard. The mirror case is not handled: the search shard exists when the request arrives, registers a segment-generation listener, and is then closed by `IndicesClusterStateService` before that generation is reached. `SearchEngine.failSegmentGenerationListeners` completes the listener with `AlreadyClosedException`, and that exception is recorded as a shard failure on the refresh response.

The following test reproduces the issue:

```
diff --git a/x-pack/plugin/stateless/src/internalClusterTest/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/recovery/SearchShardRelocationIT.java b/x-pack/plugin/stateless/src/internalClusterTest/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/recovery/SearchShardRelocationIT.java
index 7f24985fd548..e43d5a1a3034 100644
--- a/x-pack/plugin/stateless/src/internalClusterTest/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/recovery/SearchShardRelocationIT.java
+++ b/x-pack/plugin/stateless/src/internalClusterTest/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/stateless/recovery/SearchShardRelocationIT.java
@@ -357,6 +357,70 @@ public class SearchShardRelocationIT extends AbstractStatelessPluginIntegTestCas
         assertAcked(updateSettingsRequest.get());
     }
 
+    /**
+     * An unpromotable refresh registers a segment-generation listener on the current search shard. Relocating that shard
[... 65 more lines]
```

A refresh whose indexing primary succeeds should not report a shard failure solely because the search copy it was waiting on was removed by a relocation or rebalance. The replacement search shard recovers from the indexing shard's commit. The same rationale is already documented for a search shard that has not been created yet:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/43d26a280f3b906bd0c48ce6789cb3efedf85147/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/admin/indices/refresh/TransportUnpromotableShardRefreshAction.java#L134-L136

That shortcut is only safe when the new copy will actually observe the refreshed generation. Responding success as soon as the old engine closes can return from refresh before the replacement shard is searchable, so a following search can miss the refresh. The in-flight refresh should be retried against the current routing table until the requested generation is visible on the search copy that owns the shard, or until the request times out.

Copy caller-owned bytes in the binary doc values queries

Follow-up to #163062. That PR makes `ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery` deep-copy each term it is given, because the query kept the caller's `BytesRef` objects. If a caller changed those bytes after construction, the hash code and the matches of the query changed. `ColumnarStringTermQuery` and `ColumnarStringRangeQuery` already copy their bytes, and so does `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermInSetQuery`, which serializes its terms into `PrefixCodedTerms`.

These seven queries still assign their `BytesRef` arguments in the constructor without a copy:

| Query | State kept from the caller |
|---|---|
| `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQuery` | `term`, also captured by `term::equals` |
| `ScanningBinaryDocValuesRangeQuery` | `lower` and `upper`, also captured by the range matcher |
| `BinaryDocValuesContainsTermQuery` | `containsTerm`, also captured by the matcher |
| `KeyedArrayOrderInlineNullTermQuery` | `term`, also captured by `term::equals` |
| `KeyedArrayOrderInlineNullPrefixQuery` | `prefix`, also captured by the matcher |
| `BinaryDocValuesRangeQuery` | `from` and `to`, used when scoring |
| `XSortedSetDocValuesRangeQuery` | `lowerValue` and `upperValue`, used when resolving ordinals |

All are in `server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/lucene/queries/`. `ScanningBinaryDocValuesPrefixQuery` takes a `String` and builds its own bytes, so it has no copy gap. Its gap is memory accounting, tracked in #163148.

An isolated probe built each query from a four-byte term that is a slice of a 1 MiB array, built an equivalent query from independent bytes, and then changed the first byte of the caller's term. Equality and hash code changed for all seven. For the first five, the stored matcher changed from accepting the term to rejecting it. The scoring paths of the last two were read but not run.

No existing production caller is known to change a `BytesRef` after building one of these queries, and I did not audit every caller. A caller's object can reach the query unchanged: `BytesRefs.toBytesRef` returns a `BytesRef` argument as it is, and `KeywordFieldMapper.indexedValueForSearch` skips conversion when no normalizer is configured. This is defensive hardening, for the same reason as in #163062: a query that is used as a cache key must not change when the caller does.

Deep-copy the `BytesRef` arguments in these constructors.

The copy has to happen before the matcher is built. In `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQuery`, `super(fieldName, term::equals, ...)` runs before the field is assigned, so copying into `this.term` afterwards leaves the matcher bound to the caller's bytes. Create the copy first, and use it for both the matcher and the fields that define equality. Keep `null` and open range bounds as they are. A shallow `BytesRef` clone is not enough, because it still shares the byte array.

For each query, change the caller's bytes, `offset` and `length` after construction, and check three things against a query built from independent bytes:

- equality and hash code are unchanged;
- the stored matcher gives the same result, for the queries that have one;
- a term that is a small slice of a large array is stored as its own bytes, not as a reference to the array it was sliced from.

Cover open range bounds for the three range queries.

`ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery` copies each incoming term before it is added to the sorted set, so repeated terms are copied and then dropped. For input with many repeated terms this allocates in proportion to the bytes supplied, not to the number of distinct terms. This is a consideration, not a known problem. It should be measured on realistic `terms` queries before any change.

Memory accounting for these queries, tracked in #163148. The copy fixes and the accounting changes touch the same classes and can be done together for the scanning queries.

Test large values and large term sets in the string query tests

The string query tests added in #163062 use many small documents. They do not use large individual values, documents with many slots, or large term sets. A review of that PR listed cases that are still missing. This issue tracks adding them as tests. It does not propose a production change.

A large value does not reach that buffer by itself. `span` returns a direct slice of the chunk for a compressed value inside one chunk, and for the identity codec when the stream is a single chunk. The fixtures must force a read that crosses chunks and the identity codec with several chunks. After the large read, read matching and non-matching small values through the same reader.

Cover a document whose real payload is above the threshold, so the method builds it in a buffer of its own, and one whose estimate is above it but whose payload is below, so it uses the shared buffer. A direct column query may not call `binaryValue()`, so call it, or run a query over the wrapped column that reads through it.
- An unsorted any-of input with thousands of distinct terms, repeated terms and terms that are absent from the column. Run it on the single-valued and multi-valued framings and on the column and fallback paths. `indexOneSegment` always writes framed multi-valued payloads through `slotsPayload`, so one slot per document does not cover the raw single-valued framing. Use a separate fixture for it, as `ColumnarStringRangeAndAnyOfQueryTests` already does, or extend the helper.

`ColumnarStringTermQueryTests`, `ColumnarStringAutomatonQueryTests` and `ColumnarStringRangeAndAnyOfQueryTests`, using `ColumnarStringQueryTestUtils.indexOneSegment`. Each check should state its expected document IDs explicitly. Keep the large cases deterministic and bounded, and do not repeat each large fixture across the full randomized matrix of layouts and framings.

Report the memory held by columnar and binary doc values queries to the circuit breaker

`ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery` is the query behind a `terms` query on a keyword field that uses the columnar codec. It holds one `BytesRef` per term. #163062 changes it to deep-copy every term it is given, so the query will own its bytes. It does not implement `Accountable`.

For the queries discussed here, `MaxClauseCountQueryVisitor` charges the request circuit breaker per leaf query. It also has special branches for other query types, such as fuzzy and point range queries.

- A leaf that is `Accountable` is charged `ramBytesUsed()`.
- A leaf that implements `BinaryDocValuesScanCost` (the scanning binary doc values queries) is charged its `ramBytesUsed()` if it is `Accountable`, or its shallow size if not, plus an estimate of the memory needed to decode the column. Without a reader that estimate is about 3 KB.
- Any other leaf is charged `shallowSizeOf(query)` plus 1 KB. The columnar `ColumnarString*Query` classes take this branch or the `Accountable` one.
- A query that was marked pre-charged with `markQueryMemoryPreCharged` is skipped entirely. The check returns before any of the branches above.

So a term set query with many terms is charged as if it were one small clause.

**Term sets.** The memory `ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery` holds grows with the number of distinct terms and their byte lengths, up to `index.max_terms_count` terms (65,536 by default). The query is charged about 1 KB however many terms it holds. Its retained size has not been measured. Nothing charges the terms up front on this path either. `KeywordFieldMapper.termsQuery` and `TextFamilyFieldType.termsLikeQuery` go straight to `binaryQueries().terms(...)`. `TermBasedFieldType.termsQuery` does it differently for `TermInSetQuery`: it charges `TermsQueryCostEstimator` with `query.ramBytesUsed()` and calls `markQueryMemoryPreCharged`.

**Case-insensitive prefixes.** `ScanningBinaryDocValuesPrefixQuery` builds a `ByteRunAutomaton` for a case-insensitive prefix and keeps it inside its matcher. The query is not `Accountable`, so the automaton is not reported. An isolated probe measured the automaton's own `ramBytesUsed()` for prefixes of repeated `a` characters, against the visitor's estimate for the query without a reader:

| Prefix length | Automaton bytes | Visitor estimate |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 16 | 5,009 | 3,112 |
| 256 | 27,153 | 3,112 |
| 4,096 | 381,393 | 3,112 |

These are the size of the automaton alone, not a measurement of the whole heap, and a 4,096 character prefix is an extreme input. The numbers come from a local probe run at commit `220fcdb2fe91`, the head of #163062 when it was audited. The probe built each query from the production sources and read the automaton's `ramBytesUsed()` and the visitor's estimate. The numbers were reproduced by running the same probe again, not by a separate implementation.

Already `Accountable`: `ColumnarStringAutomatonQuery`, `AbstractBinaryDocValuesAutomatonQuery` and its subclasses, and `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermInSetQuery`.

In priority order:

1. Make `ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery` implement `Accountable`. The query is immutable, so the size can be computed once in the constructor. It should include the query object, the `TreeSet` and its entries, each unique term and its byte array, the field name, and the container behind the membership set. Terms shared by the tree and the membership set are counted once.
2. Make `ScanningBinaryDocValuesPrefixQuery` report what its matcher retains: the automaton for the case-insensitive branch, and the encoded prefix bytes for the case-sensitive branch, plus the `String`. The matcher state needs to be exposed so `ramBytesUsed()` can include it.
3. Consider `Accountable` for the other queries that hold byte strings. One or two terms limits the object count but not the byte size. `ColumnarStringTermQuery` and `ColumnarStringRangeQuery` already own deep copies, so their size can be measured now. `ScanningBinaryDocValuesTermQuery`, `ScanningBinaryDocValuesRangeQuery`, `BinaryDocValuesContainsTermQuery` and the two `KeyedArrayOrderInlineNull` queries should get it together with the ownership fix in #163150. `BinaryDocValuesRangeQuery` and `XSortedSetDocValuesRangeQuery` are lower priority. `ColumnarNumericRangeQuery` and `BinaryDocValuesLengthQuery` hold primitives and gain little.
4. Decide whether the binary doc values term set paths should charge `TermsQueryCostEstimator` up front and call `markQueryMemoryPreCharged`, for both the scanning and the columnar implementations. Two cautions:
   - Marking a scanning query as pre-charged skips the whole visitor charge, including its decode memory estimate. Charging only the retained size up front would drop that estimate, so it has to be kept.
   - The existing `TermBasedFieldType` charge runs after `TermInSetQuery` is built, so it charges earlier than the visitor but does not cover the allocation peak inside the constructor.

- Two otherwise identical queries, one built from compact arrays and one from terms that are slices of a much larger array, report the same size. This also covers the copy.
- Repeated terms are counted once: a query built from a term list with duplicates reports the same size as one built from the distinct terms.
- A term set large enough to exceed the breaker limit makes the visitor trip the breaker for `ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery`.
- `MaxClauseCountQueryVisitor` charges `ramBytesUsed()` for `ColumnarStringAnyOfQuery`, not the flat 1 KB.
- `ScanningBinaryDocValuesPrefixQuery` reports a size that grows with the prefix length in the case-insensitive branch, and the visitor charge includes it plus the decode estimate.
- If item 4 is done, the up-front charge equals the estimate for the same terms and the decode estimate is still charged.

Changing `index.max_terms_count` or the breaker limits. Copying caller-owned bytes in the constructors, tracked in #163150.

Date fields do not store array offsets natively with synthetic source

With `synthetic_source_keep: arrays` (the logsdb default), numeric (#124594) and boolean (#125529) fields store array order in a `<field>.offsets` sorted doc value instead of putting the whole array in `_ignored_source`. `DateFieldMapper` has the plumbing for this since #149646: it resolves an `offsetsFieldName`, records offsets in `parseCreateField`, and uses `SortedNumericWithOffsetsDocValuesSyntheticFieldLoaderLayer` in its synthetic source loader. But it does not override `Mapper#getOffsetFieldName()`, so `supportStoringArrayOffsets()` is false and the document parser routes every date array to `_ignored_source`. Inside that capture scope no offsets are recorded, so the `.offsets` doc value is never written and the offsets loader layer is never exercised. Native offsets for date are effectively only active in strict columnar mode.

So date arrays in logsdb still pay the `_ignored_source` storage cost that numbers and booleans no longer pay.

- Override `getOffsetFieldName()` in `DateFieldMapper`, gated by a new `IndexVersion`, so indices created before the change keep their current behaviour.
- Add `DateOffsetDocValuesLoaderTests` extending `OffsetDocValuesLoaderTestCase`, like the number, boolean and ip variants.

The oversized-offsets fallback from #163007 then applies to date on this path as well; the fallback writer is already in place.

no_such_remote_cluster_exception fails the whole request even with ignore_unavailable=true and allow_no_indices=true

When an index expression contains a cluster alias that is not configured, CCS-enabled APIs (`_field_caps`, `_search`, `_resolve/index`, …) fail the entire request with `no_such_remote_cluster_exception`, regardless of `ignore_unavailable` / `allow_no_indices`. Other "unavailable target" cases are already handled leniently, which makes this the one case a client cannot opt out of.

Reproduced on 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT with no remote clusters configured (`GET _remote/info` → `{}`), `my_index` exists:

```
GET missing_cluster:logs-*/_field_caps?fields=*&ignore_unavailable=true&allow_no_indices=true
→ 404 {"error":{"root_cause":[{"type":"no_such_remote_cluster_exception","reason":"no such remote cluster: [missing_cluster]"}], ...}}

GET my_index,missing_cluster:logs-*/_field_caps?fields=*&ignore_unavailable=true&allow_no_indices=true
→ 404, same error - my_index is not returned

GET my_index,missing_index/_field_caps?fields=*&ignore_unavailable=true
→ 200 {"indices":["my_index"], ...}                 (missing local index is skipped)

GET missing_*:logs-*/_field_caps?fields=*&ignore_unavailable=true&allow_no_indices=true
[... 4 more lines]
```

With security enabled and a non-superuser the same error is wrapped in a 403 `security_exception` (the `no_such_remote_cluster_exception` is only in `root_cause`).

Kibana data views are index expressions that regularly reference clusters that aren't configured (yet, or anymore): data views shipped by integrations / created via API with `allowNoIndex: true` before the remote exists, or `logs-*,old_cluster:logs-*` after a remote is decommissioned. Today a single such alias breaks field fetching for the whole data view (elastic/kibana#228752, elastic/kibana#166812, elastic/kibana#197747).

The only workaround (elastic/kibana#299790) is to catch the error, parse the alias out of the `reason` string, drop the matching patterns and re-issue the request - one extra round trip per missing alias, since only the first one is reported, and dependent on the error message format.

Either of:

1. Treat an unconfigured cluster alias like an unavailable target: skip it when `ignore_unavailable=true` (and apply `allow_no_indices` if nothing remains), consistent with how missing local indices and non-matching wildcard aliases are handled today.
2. If implicit lenience is undesirable (cf. #138987), an explicit opt-in - e.g. a request parameter, or extending `skip_unavailable` semantics to unconfigured aliases.

As a smaller improvement, reporting *all* missing aliases in a structured way (not only the first one in the reason string) would at least make the client-side workaround a single retry.

ES|QL: LIMIT BY against a remote cluster older than 9.4

`LIMIT ... BY` becomes a `LimitBy` plan node. `LimitBy` is a pipeline breaker, so when the plan is split it stays in the `FragmentExec` sent to data nodes (`PlannerUtils.reductionPlan` maps it to `LimitByReduction`), including the data nodes of remote clusters. `LimitBy` was added in 9.4 (#143458), and nothing in `LimitBy` checks the remote's version. LIMIT BY has been GA since 9.6 (#159313). DEDUP, which the coordinator rewrites into `LIMIT 1 BY`, inherits the same exposure.

Not verified yet. Check what `FROM remote:idx | LIMIT 1 BY x` does against a remote on 9.3 or 8.19: a clear error, keeping the `LimitBy` on the coordinator, or a deserialization failure. If it fails badly, fix it in LIMIT BY and add a backwards-compatibility CCS test.

This started as a DEDUP GA story under https://github.com/elastic/esql-planning/issues/1760. It was moved out because the behavior belongs to LIMIT BY, which is already GA.

ES|QL: EMBEDDING fails with a server error when its input is a constant held in a ROW/EVAL variable

`EMBEDDING` throws `QlIllegalArgumentException: Should not fold expression` when its text or inference-id argument is a variable that holds a constant. The user gets a server error. `TEXT_EMBEDDING` rejects the same query during analysis with a clear message.

Found while working on #161305, assisted by 🤖 .

Either query fails. I reproduced both as `CsvIT` specs against `test_embedding_inference`:

```
ROW input="Who is Victor Hugo?"
| EVAL embedding = EMBEDDING(input, "test_embedding_inference")
```

```
ROW a = 1
| EVAL t = "Who is Victor Hugo?"
| EVAL embedding = EMBEDDING(t, "test_embedding_inference")
| KEEP t, embedding
```

The query fails with `QlIllegalArgumentException: Should not fold expression`. That exception is documented as a server error, meant for bugs. Stack trace (line numbers from main at `7865babebf98`):

```
QlIllegalArgumentException: Should not fold expression
  at Expression.fold(Expression.java:101)
  at Literal.of(Literal.java:209)
  at RuleUtils.collectFoldableRefs(RuleUtils.java:157)
  at RuleUtils.foldableReferencesSkipMVGroupings(RuleUtils.java:122)
  at PropagateEvalFoldables.apply(PropagateEvalFoldables.java:34)
  at LogicalPlanOptimizer.optimize(LogicalPlanOptimizer.java:158)
  at EsqlSession.optimizedPlan(EsqlSession.java:3055)
```

`TEXT_EMBEDDING` with the same shape fails cleanly during analysis:

```
first argument of [TEXT_EMBEDDING(text, "text-embedding-inference-id")] must be a constant, received [text]
```

The query should work, or it should fail with a validation error. A server error is wrong either way.

1. `Embedding.resolveType()` does not check foldability, so analysis accepts the variable.
2. `FoldInferenceFunctions` runs in the pre-optimizer, before the logical optimizer. It folds only functions that are already `foldable()`. `EMBEDDING(input, …)` is not, so it is skipped.
3. In the optimizer, `PropagateEvalFoldables` calls `RuleUtils.collectFoldableRefs`. That method substitutes known constants into each alias. The `Embedding` is now foldable, so it calls `Literal.of(...)`.
4. `Literal.of` calls `Embedding.fold()`. `Embedding` has no `fold()`, because inference calls run asynchronously through `FoldInferenceFunctions`. The default implementation throws.

Inline literals work, because the `Embedding` is already foldable when the pre-optimizer runs. Every existing `EMBEDDING` spec passes its text inline, even the specs with a `ROW` source. That is why nothing caught this.

`Embedding` checks constants in `postOptimizationVerification`. `TEXT_EMBEDDING` checks in `resolveType()` with `isFoldable`. This behavior has been present since EMBEDDING was added in #144484. [Comments in that PR](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/144484/changes#r2980001766) suggest a unified approach between EMBEDDING and TEXT_EMBEDDING, but that is deferred for future work.

1. **Check foldability in `Embedding.resolveType()`, like `TEXT_EMBEDDING`.** This is a small change and gives the unified approach asked for in #144484. Variables get a clear error, and nothing that works today stops working. `VerifierTests.testEmbeddingLiteralValues` (which accepts a `ROW` attribute) and the `OptimizerVerificationTests` cases would need updating.
2. **Make deferral work.** Run `FoldInferenceFunctions` after constant propagation, and stop `collectFoldableRefs` from folding inference functions. This is a larger change to the optimizer pipeline.

Starting with the first option as a targeted fix and following up with the second as a longer term improvement seems like a reasonable progression.

ES|QL grouping on ColumNAR keywords re-hashes the same terms on every page

ES|QL reads a single-valued ColumNAR keyword as an `OrdinalBytesRefBlock` (`ColumnarStringPageReader`). The ordinals and the dictionary are local to one page. For each page, the reader calls `termAt` and copies the bytes for every distinct term, and `BytesRefBlockHash` hashes each of them. The same terms are hashed again on the next page of the segment.

Carry the column's dense ordinal through the loader, with a segment-scoped handle to resolve terms (`StringColumnSource#termAt`). Let the bytes-ref block hash cache the group id for each segment ordinal across pages, as #162573 does for `terms` aggregations.

- This needs a new block type or sink call, and clear rules for the lifetime of the dictionary handle.
- The hash must know when the segment changes.
- Start with the single-key hash. Multi-key hashes and multi-valued pages can follow.
- Profile a `STATS ... BY <columnar keyword>` query first, to check that the per-page cost is large enough to matter.

Relates to #161260 and #162573.

ES|QL: INLINE STATS result over 512 KB crashes the coordinator under assertions (BigArrays not supported because we don't close) When the first phase of an `INLINE STATS` produces a result column larger than `esql.block_factory.max_block_primitive_array_size` (512 KB) that contains a null or a multivalue, the column is built as a `LongBigArrayBlock`, `IntBigArrayBlock`, `DoubleBigArrayBlock` or `BooleanBigArrayBlock`. The result is inlined into the second-phase plan as a `LocalRelation`, and sending that plan to another node goes through `PlanStreamOutput#writeCachedBlock`, which asserts that no big-array block is ever written. With assertions enabled the coordinator exits with a fatal error; without them the block is shipped and rebuilt on every receiving data node with a non-breaking, non-recycling factory, so that memory is outside every circuit breaker. A request to the local node is not serialized, so a single-node cluster never hits this. This is the node crash behind #148619, seen there on 2026-05-08 (`9.5.0-SNAPSHOT`, `IntBigArrayBlock`) and 2026-09-27 (`9.4`, `IntBigArrayBlock`); the reproduction below trips the `LongBigArrayBlock` assert on `9.4` and `main` today. Two nodes, an index with two shards pinned one per node, 70,000 documents with distinct `long` values of `k` plus one document without `k`: ``` FROM big | INLINE STATS c = COUNT(*) BY k | STATS rows = COUNT(*), docs = SUM(c) ``` With assertions enabled the coordinator exits (`main` at `3152445bc180`, 2026-10-22): ``` [ERROR][o.e.b.ElasticsearchUncaughtExceptionHandler] [test-cluster-0] fatal error in thread [elasticsearch[test-cluster-0][search][T#4]], exiting java.lang.AssertionError: BigArrays not supported because we don't close at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.io.stream.PlanStreamOutput.writeCachedBlock(PlanStreamOutput.java:142) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.local.ImmediateLocalSupplier.lambda$writeTo$0(ImmediateLocalSupplier.java:77) at org.elasticsearch.common.io.stream.StreamOutput.writeArray(StreamOutput.java:981) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.local.ImmediateLocalSupplier.writeTo(ImmediateLocalSupplier.java:77) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.local.LocalRelation.writeTo(LocalRelation.java:60) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.join.Join.writeTo(Join.java:146) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.Limit.writeTo(Limit.java:75) at org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.plan.logical.Project.writeTo(Project.java:101) [... 5 more lines] ``` The REST client retries on the surviving node, which answers from its own shard with `is_partial: true` and logs `partial failure at path: /_query`. On `9.4` the same assert is at `PlanStreamOutput.java:141`; the two CI traces under #148619 show `:142`, which on those commits is the `IntBigArrayBlock` assert. InlineStatsBigBlockIT, drop into x-pack/plugin/esql/qa/server/multi-node/src/javaRestTest/.../multi_node/ ``` /* * Copyright Elasticsearch B.V. and/or licensed to Elasticsearch B.V. under one * or more contributor license agreements. Licensed under the Elastic License * 2.0; you may not use this file except in compliance with the Elastic License * 2.0. */ package org.elasticsearch.xpack.esql.qa.multi_node; import com.carrotsearch.randomizedtesting.annotations.ThreadLeakFilters; [... 68 more lines] ``` Mechanism and evidence - `EsqlSession#resultToPlan` (`main:1500-1514`, `9.4:706-721`, identical) turns the first-phase pages into one `LocalRelation` with `SessionUtils.fromPages(schema, pages, blockFactory)`, one breaker-tracked builder per column. The only size check is `esql.intermediate_local_relation_max_size`, applied to the whole result and defaulting to `min(2% of heap, 100 MB)` (`PlannerSettings`, both branches). On `9.4` `INLINE STATS` is the only caller; on `main` the subquery paths reach it too (`EsqlSession.java:1289, 1310`). - `LongBlockBuilder#build` switches to `buildBigArraysBlock()` once the builder's `estimatedBytes` exceeds `blockFactory.maxPrimitiveArrayBytes()` (512 KB by default, `BlockFactory.DEFAULT_MAX_BLOCK_PRIMITIVE_ARRAY_SIZE`). A dense single-valued column becomes a `LongBigArrayVector` wrapped in a `LongVectorBlock`, which the assertion does not see but which is shipped and rebuilt untracked just the same; a column with a null or a multivalue becomes a `LongBigArrayBlock`, which the assertion catches. Same for `Int`, `Double`, `Boolean`. - `InlineJoin#inlineData` (`:69-84`) keeps the `LocalRelation` as the right side of the join whenever there are grouping keys; the join sits inside the `FragmentExec` that `DataNodeRequest#writeTo` serializes per data node. `TransportService` hands a request for the local node to the handler without serializing it (`sendLocalRequest`), which is why one node, or all shards on the coordinator, never trips it. - `PlanStreamOutput#writeCachedBlock` (`main:141-145`, `9.4:140-144`) asserts against the four `*BigArrayBlock` types with `BigArrays not supported because we don't close`; its Javadoc says plan blocks "are not tracked by BlockFactory ... so they should be small". `LongBlock#writeTo` has an explicit big-array branch, so without assertions the write succeeds. - `PlanStreamInput#readCachedBlock` (`:110-124`, both branches) rebuilds the block with `BlockFactory.builder(BigArrays.NON_RECYCLING_INSTANCE).breaker(new NoopCircuitBreaker(...))` under a `TODO track blocks read over the wire`. The heap is ordinary and garbage-collected, so this is unaccounted memory, not a leak: up to `min(2% of the coordinator's heap, 100 MB)` per data-node request. - CI evidence: elasticsearch-periodic #12843 (`9.4` at `772626126b7c`, job `openjdk25 / checkPart5 / java-matrix`): `test-cluster-0` log has the fatal error at `2026-09-26T17:55:41` node-local time (`2026-09-27T00:55:41Z`), `test-cluster-1` loses the master at 17:55:41,802, and `GenerativeUnmappedLoadIT.test` fails in `cleanUpCluster` with a 60 s timeout followed by `Connection refused`. The test cluster runs with `-Xmx512m`. The JUnit XML does not record the crashing query; that it was an `INLINE STATS` follows from `resultToPlan` being the only producer of a `LocalRelation` under a `Join` on `9.4`. The same assertion on `9.5.0-SNAPSHOT`, same `Join → LocalRelation → ImmediateLocalSupplier → DataNodeRequest` chain, is in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/148619#issuecomment-4408792506. - The later `9.4` re-mutes under #148619 (2026-10-13) are 60 s client timeouts, which `main`'s generative harness allows and `9.4`'s does not; they are not this crash. - Reproduced locally with the test above on 2026-10-22: `9.4` at `97722d84b647` (`PlanStreamOutput.java:141`) and `main` at `3152445bc180` (`:142`); in both the surviving node answers `is_partial: true`. Re-running `GenerativeUnmappedLoadIT` on `9.4` with the CI seed `7C6B4CED327345CA` passed. Found while triaging #148619. Assisted by Claude.

max_shards_per_node supported by platform

[Settings](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/elasticsearch/configuration-reference/miscellaneous-cluster-settings#cluster-max-shards-per-node) (`cluster.max_shards_per_node: 1000`, `cluster.max_shards_per_node.frozen: 3000`) are dynamic.

This can result in a quiet ticking time bomb where the cluster seems performant until a cluster fault detection occurs (or in ECH, a plan change is attempted) & then recovery struggle busses if it even successfully catches up (commonly related to elected-master sizing & frozen IO).

- Either hard coded value or dynamic value proportional to the master-eligible nodes' resources).
- This would need to be a new Elasticsearch static settings as dynamic settings cannot be user-override restricted.
- These settings could by called like `cluster.max_shards_per_node_for_platform` for normal+frozen (default: `-1`).
- Their logical effect would be the original dynamic settings would take effect up until this new static/hard limit.

Nested terms aggregations on ColumNAR keywords fall back to hashing

#162573 caches terms buckets by ColumNAR dictionary ordinal, but only for owning bucket 0. A `terms` aggregation under another bucket aggregation (for example `date_histogram` or `terms`) collects for other owning buckets. Those documents go to the per-document collector, which hashes their bytes.

Key the cache by owning bucket and ordinal, so nested aggregations use ordinals too.

- The cache is now one dense array sized by the dictionary. With many owners it would be a hash or a per-owner array. The memory must be charged to the request breaker.
- Cap the total cache size across owners and fall back to the per-document path above it.
- Segments with a small dictionary and many owners may cost more to cache than to hash. Benchmark before choosing the limits.

Relates to #161260 and #162573.

Multi-valued ColumNAR keywords fall back to hashing in terms aggregations

#162573 caches terms buckets by ColumNAR dictionary ordinal. A document with several values (`MULTI_VALUED`) still goes to the per-document collector, which hashes its bytes. The rest of the segment keeps the cache.

For a multi-valued document, read all its slot ordinals and de-duplicate them as ints. Then call `acceptExisting` for each distinct ordinal.

- A term repeated within one document must count once, as it does for a keyword field.
- Escaped values are not in the dictionary. They need byte comparison to de-duplicate, and they can repeat an ordinal-coded value's bytes.
- `StringColumnSource#denseTermOrdinal` answers for one value only. It needs a multi-valued variant, for example one that fills an `int[]`.

Check first how often `terms` runs on multi-valued ColumNAR keyword fields in `logsdb_columnar`, to confirm the gain.

Relates to #161260 and #162573.

Adapt to TieredMergePolicy.setMaxMergeAtOnce removal

Lucene 11 removed `TieredMergePolicy#setMaxMergeAtOnce` ([apache/lucene#14165](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/14165)). There is no replacement: the policy no longer bounds how many segments may be merged together.

`lucene_snapshot_11` stopped calling the Lucene setter so the branch compiles. Elasticsearch still accepts `index.merge.policy.max_merge_at_once` (dynamic, index-scoped, `ServerlessPublic`, default `16`), but it no longer passes the value to Lucene. Changing it has no effect on merges. Merges may combine more than 16 segments (the old default). `segments_per_tier` and `max_merged_segment` still apply. The cluster-state metadata index (`PersistedClusterStateService`) used to allow merges of up to 100 segments. That cap is gone.

This change is difficult to make transparent to ES users, as the setting is entirely gone. We should deprecate the setting in Elasticsearch and signal that it should not be used, at the same time we should not start rejecting the setting in a minor release. The best course of action is deprecation + silently ignore .

Adapt to RegexpQuery no longer taking a determinize limit

Lucene 11 stopped compiling regexp queries to a DFA up front ([apache/lucene#15939](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/15939)). `RegexpQuery` constructors no longer take `determinizeWorkLimit`. The query can run as an NFA.

`lucene_snapshot_11` dropped that constructor argument so the branch compiles. The Elasticsearch public parameter `max_determinized_states` is still accepted and documented as if Lucene always determinizes. That is only true on some paths.

What users see:
  - `_search` with a circuit breaker (the normal path): the limit still applies. ES builds the DFA in `AutomatonQueries` / the query circuit breaker and can still throw `TooComplexToDeterminizeException` (HTTP 400).
  - Paths that construct Lucene `RegexpQuery` directly ignore the limit: no-breaker construction (unit tests, some fallbacks), `query_string` with a forced analyzer (`QueryParser.getRegexpQuery`), and some doc-values fallbacks that constructs new `RegexpQuery` without going through
  `AutomatonQueries`. A pattern that used to fail as too complex now runs.
  - Docs still say Lucene converts every regexp to a determinized automaton.
 - Two QueryStringQueryBuilderTests methods were changed to inject a circuit breaker so they still exercise the ES DFA path: `testToQueryRegExpQueryTooComplex` and `testToQueryRegExpQueryMaxDeterminizedStatesParsing`. They used to call `toQuery(createSearchExecutionContext())`. That context has no breaker, so Lucene 11 never determinizes and the tests stopped throwing. They now wrap the context with `createCircuitBreakerService()` so the ES DFA path still applies the limit.

Stop-gap commits:
  - https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/commit/31e425c55d84f83b56ae7e3c0f9a47ab8b696be3 — drop `determinizeWorkLimit` from `RegexpQuery` construction
  - https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/commit/b11ae1b4bb4a16248b8daa5034348e9aa6d8aae7 — query_string tests inject a breaker so `max_determinized_states` still fails

The goal of this issue is to replace the stop-gap solutions with production ready fixes. The stop-gap compiles and keeps max_determinized_states on DFA / circuit-breaker paths. Lucene `RegexpQuery` paths ignore it. Decide whether to keep that split, always determinize in ES, go NFA everywhere, deprecate the parameter, or use the limit only as a reject check —
    and update the docs to match.

    - [`QueryStringQueryBuilder.java`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/lucene_snapshot_11/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/query/QueryStringQueryBuilder.java)

ESQL: adding a flag to EsqlFlags re-points an existing public constructor's last argument

`EsqlFlags` has a public constructor taking a boolean and four ints. elastic/elasticsearch#148232 left
that parameter list unchanged and changed what the last parameter sets. Before the change,
`git show c3a098ae0846^:x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plugin/EsqlFlags.java`
shows the fifth parameter as `maxBranchCountPerMerge`, assigned directly to that field; after it, the
fifth parameter is `maxFillNullFields`, and the constructor delegates with
`ESQL_MAX_BRANCH_COUNT_PER_MERGE.getDefault(Settings.EMPTY)` in the slot the caller used to control. Any
code written against the old form compiles against the new one. `new EsqlFlags(true, 127, 10, 5, 3)` set
the per-merge branch cap to 3; it now leaves that cap at its registered default of 8 and sends the 3 to
`maxFillNullFields()`. The pattern has already repeated: elastic/elasticsearch#162346 added
`maxCommandCount` on 2026-10-19 as a seventh parameter and left the six-argument form as a delegating
prefix, so the class now exposes constructors of arity 1, 2, 5, 6 and 7 over the same leading types.
There is no query that reproduces this; the defect is in the Java API.

No caller is wrong today, so nothing is currently misconfigured — at main `5b423f7bb0de`,
`git grep -n "new EsqlFlags(" -- '*.java'` finds 45 sites in 29 files outside the class, and every one
passes a single argument except `LogicalOptimizerContextTests.randomFlags`, which passes six. The
equivalent search across `elasticsearch-serverless` returns nothing. The cost is the next edit rather
than this one: the class now carries eleven pairs of same-named entry points where one parameter list is
a prefix of another, counting the constructors and `withMaxBranchLimits(int,int)` against
`withMaxBranchLimits(int,int,int)`. Appending a parameter to any of them silently re-points the shorter
form, and the compiler cannot see it, because the only thing distinguishing the two calls is how many
ints the author happened to write. Both caps this concerns guard memory — one bounds branch expansion,
the other bounds untracked page-block copies in FILLNULL — so a silent swap sets the wrong guard to the
wrong value.

A settings holder with many same-typed fields is being constructed positionally, so the only thing
tying an argument to the field it sets is its index. Every parameter added to such a class makes the
shorter overload a prefix of the longer one, which is a valid call rather than a compile error, and the
named static factories do not escape it because they are overloaded the same way. The class has no
mechanism that makes a caller state which cap it means.

The surviving five-argument form is
`public EsqlFlags(boolean stringLikeOnIndex, int roundToPushdownThreshold, int maxBranchCount, int maxBranchLevel, int maxFillNullFields)`.
Its predecessor had `int maxBranchCountPerMerge` in the fifth position. Both erase to
`(boolean, int, int, int, int)`, so neither the compiler nor a reviewer reading the call site can tell
them apart. The six- and seven-argument forms added since are prefixes of each other by the same
mechanism, and `withMaxBranchLimits` is overloaded as `(int, int)` and `(int, int, int)` where the third
parameter sets `maxBranchCountPerMerge`, which the shared name does not mention.

Construction has to name the field. One public constructor at full arity plus a builder, or named
`with*` factories that are not prefixes of one another, so that adding a cap is a compile error at every
call site that must change rather than a silent re-point at every call site that must not. The named
factories alone are not the fix, since the existing pair demonstrates they carry the identical hazard.

Make the seven-argument constructor the only public one and give `EsqlFlags` a builder, or a factory per
cap that takes a single named value and defaults the rest. The public six-argument form must go with the
five-argument one, because it is itself a prefix of the seven; its callers are
`LogicalOptimizerContextTests.randomFlags`, the in-class `EsqlFlags(boolean, int)`,
`withMaxBranchLimits(int, int, int)` and `withMaxFillNullFields`, all of which can take the builder. Split
`withMaxBranchLimits` into one factory per cap so the two-and-three-argument pair disappears. The
single-argument constructors and `EsqlFlags(ClusterSettings)` are unambiguous and stay.

Add a test asserting that `EsqlFlags` exposes no two public constructors or same-named static factories
where one parameter list is a prefix of the other, by reflection over `EsqlFlags.class.getConstructors()`
and its declared methods. That test fails on main today, naming the eleven pairs, and would have failed
on the commit that introduced the first of them. Keep the existing `LogicalOptimizerContextTests`
coverage green through the migration, and assert that a flags object built naming only the FILLNULL cap
leaves `maxBranchCountPerMerge()` at its registered default of 8 — the value the re-pointed argument
silently changed.

ESQL: FILLNULL silently leaves an unsigned_long column unfilled for values it can apply

FILLNULL accepts the query, returns 200, leaves the column exactly as it was, and warns that the fill
value "could not be applied to the following fields". The same literal `0` fills two numeric column
types and not the third. All three are asserted by committed cases in `fillnull.csv-spec` at main
`2c85bbdf4cc3`:

| Column type | Query | Result | Case that pins it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `long` | `FILLNULL 0 ON a` | fills 0 | `fillNullWithIntegerValueIntoLong` |
| `double` | `FILLNULL 0 ON a` | fills 0.0 | `fillNullWithIntegerValueIntoDouble` |
| `unsigned_long` | `FILLNULL 0 ON *` | stays null, warns | `fillNullIntegerValueForUnsignedLongSkippedForAllFields` |

Two further contradictions inside `unsigned_long` itself. `FILLNULL DEFAULT ON ul` writes 0 into the
column, so the command writes a value it will not accept when asked for it. And
`FILLNULL 18446744073709551615 ON ul` fills, while `FILLNULL 7 ON ul` does not — the accepted values are
exactly those above `Long.MAX_VALUE`, which is the range nobody types. `EVAL ul = COALESCE(ul, 7)` fills
the column, and `Coalesce` is the expression FILLNULL builds for itself, so the warning's claim is false.
Two neighbouring refusals are correct and must stay: `FILLNULL 18446744073709551615 ON l`, where the
value does not fit a `long`, and `FILLNULL "0" ON i`, since ES|QL never implicitly converts a string to
a number. The third case's comment states the rule being contradicted — "An integer value cannot be
applied to an unsigned_long column". Reproduced on a 9.6.0-SNAPSHOT node, `build_hash`
`e18a33c8fe4828f2dedbf871351d5320cdb75c02`; every path exercised is unchanged at `2c85bbdf4cc3`.
FILLNULL is snapshot-only, so the node must be a snapshot one.

```
curl -u elastic-admin:elastic-password -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -XPUT 'localhost:9200/t' \
  -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"ul":{"type":"unsigned_long"}}}}'
curl -u elastic-admin:elastic-password -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -XPOST 'localhost:9200/t/_doc?refresh' -d '{}'
for q in 'FILLNULL DEFAULT ON ul' 'FILLNULL 0 ON ul' 'FILLNULL 7 ON ul' \
         'FILLNULL 18446744073709551615 ON ul' 'EVAL ul = COALESCE(ul, 7)'; do
  curl -s -u elastic-admin:elastic-password -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    'localhost:9200/_query?format=txt' -d "{\"query\":\"FROM t | $q | KEEP ul\"}"
done
```

A user asks for a column to be filled and it is not filled, and the query succeeds. Nothing fails, so
nothing draws attention to it. Everything downstream reads nulls — a `WHERE`, a `STATS`, a dashboard
panel — and the author has no reason to suspect the fill did not happen. The warning makes it worse than
silence, because it states the value could not be applied when it could. On row 2 the accepted range is
the one nobody types, so a user who tries small values concludes the column cannot be filled at all. The
only remedy is to abandon the command and write the `COALESCE` by hand. Scope is explicit fill values
into `unsigned_long` columns on a snapshot build. `DEFAULT` is unaffected, and `long` and `double`
columns take the same literal correctly.

FILLNULL decides which values it can apply before it builds anything, and it asks the wrong question.
`DataType.areCompatible` delegates to `EsqlBinaryComparison.areTypesCompatible`, the predicate for two
operands of a binary comparison. That predicate excludes `unsigned_long` deliberately, because comparing
operands must not silently reinterpret one whose range fits neither a signed long nor a double. Filling a
column is not a comparison. It converts one literal, once, and either the conversion is exact or it is
not. When the predicate says no, FILLNULL drops the column and builds no expression for it, so nothing
downstream can reconsider. The engine already holds the right answer: `Analyzer.ImplicitCasting` promotes
numeric arguments of `Coalesce`, and admits the promotion exactly when the arguments' common type is the
target's type, which for a whole-number literal and an `unsigned_long` column it is. That is why
`COALESCE(ul, 7)` fills what `FILLNULL 7 ON ul` does not. Same expression, same conversion, opposite
outcome, because one path asked whether the types convert and the other asked whether they compare.

`FillNull.buildFields` calls `resolveDefaultValue` per column, and `fillExpression` then builds
`new Coalesce(field.source(), field, List.of(defaultValue))`. Both run during analysis;
`FillNull.surrogate` only wraps the finished aliases in an `Eval` and a `Project`. `resolveDefaultValue`
returns the literal untouched when `fillValue.dataType() == type`. That is why `DEFAULT` works —
`defaultForType` builds its zero already typed `UNSIGNED_LONG` — and why row 2's huge literal works,
since `ExpressionBuilder.visitIntegerValue` types anything above `Long.MAX_VALUE` as `UNSIGNED_LONG`.
Everything else reaches `DataType.areCompatible(fillType, type)`. `areTypesCompatible` admits a numeric
pair only through
`leftType.isNumericOrAmd() && rightType.isNumericOrAmd() && leftType != UNSIGNED_LONG && rightType != UNSIGNED_LONG`,
and admits `unsigned_long` only when both sides are it. So an `INTEGER` or `LONG` literal into an
`unsigned_long` column is refused, `resolveDefaultValue` returns null, the column is left out of
`fields()`, and `WarnUnfillableFillNull` reports it. `FillNull` and `In` are the only consumers of
`DataType.areCompatible`.

FILLNULL should ask whether the literal converts into the column's type exactly, which is the question
the operation poses, and the existing `DataTypeConverter.convert` call plus its exact-round-trip check
already answers it. The cleaner form is to stop deciding at all: build the `Coalesce` and let
`Analyzer.ImplicitCasting` promote the argument as it does for every other `Coalesce`, so one type
policy governs both paths instead of two that disagree. Two consequences need a decision rather than a
patch. The "could not be applied" warning is produced from the columns FILLNULL skipped, so a value
rejected later by a conversion evaluator would surface as a per-row runtime warning and a null instead.
And an `unsigned_long` literal must carry the long encoding every other such literal in the engine
carries, not a `BigInteger`, or the value cannot be turned into a block.

Both routes are open and the choice belongs to whoever owns the command. If the predicate is replaced
rather than removed, the obvious substitution is wrong: requiring the two types' common type to equal the
column's refuses conversions that work today, because it refuses every narrowing conversion. The
common type of a `LONG` literal and an `integer` column is `long`, so the substitution rejects a pair
that works today and that `FillNullTests.testAllFieldsInRangeFillConvertsLiteralToColumnType` pins — it
puts `Literal(7L, LONG)` into an `integer` column and asserts the alias comes out `integer`. Whatever replaces it must keep the `DataTypeConverter.convert` call and the exact-round-trip
check, which is what refuses `FILLNULL 0.5` on a whole-number column. Negatives need no round trip:
`safeToUnsignedLong` throws for a negative value and `resolveDefaultValue` catches it.

`fillnull.csv-spec` asserts the behaviour being changed, so invert
`fillNullIntegerValueForUnsignedLongSkippedForAllFields`: `FILLNULL 7 ON *` fills the `unsigned_long`
column with 7 and emits no warning. Add a case for row 1, `FILLNULL 0` on an `unsigned_long` column,
asserting 0 and no warning. Add cases pinning what must stay refused, each with the unfillable warning:
`FILLNULL -1` and `FILLNULL 0.5` on an `unsigned_long` column, `FILLNULL 18446744073709551615` on a
`long` column, and `FILLNULL "0"` on an `integer` column. Keep `fillNullDefaultForUnsignedLong` and
`fillNullExplicitValueForUnsignedLong` green, since both exercise values that already work. In
`FillNullTests`, assert the resolved fill for a `7` literal into an `unsigned_long` column is a non-null
`UNSIGNED_LONG` literal, and null for `-1`. End to end, add a case to `EsqlActionIT` running
`FILLNULL 7 ON ul | KEEP ul` and asserting 7 with no warning header.

Adapt to ~ operator removal

Lucene 11 removed support for the `~` operator from regexp syntax with [apache/lucene#15750](https://github.com/apache/lucene/pull/15750). It was deprecated in Lucene 10: complement needs a full determinize (can explode), and Lucene 10 no longer determinizes while parsing so regexp can run as an NFA.

The `~` operator is widely used in Elasticsearch. Also, regexp flags are affected as `DEPRECATED_COMPLEMENT` is no longer accepted.
