Highlighting: return the offsets of highlighted fragments and matches Hey team, I'd like to take on #5736, returning where highlighted text sits in the field value. I have the offsets working in a test harness already, so I wanted to agree on the API with you before writing the real implementation Today a client that needs positions, like to underline a match in an editor, strips the tags and searches for each fragment in the value, which breaks on repeated text, with `encoder: html`, and when the value has tag-like text in it. Kibana does exactly this in its field formatters (`findMarkRanges`, elastic/kibana#283345). The unified highlighter already has the offsets, `CustomPassageFormatter` uses them to place the tags and then drops them. #29631 got stuck on this in 2018 over which unit to count in, since each one is natural in some languages and awkward in others, and it closed with a plan to go through highlighter plugins, but a plugin can only return strings. So the idea here is to let the client pick the unit. Shape: ``` GET /my-index/_search { "query": { "match": { "title": "search" } }, "fields": ["title"], "highlight": { "offsets": { "unit": "code_point" }, "fields": { "title": {} } } } ``` For `"title": ["Plain title", "Smile 😀 and search"]`, each hit gets a `highlight_offsets` object next to `highlight`, and `highlight` itself stays exactly as it is: ``` "highlight": { "title": ["Smile 😀 and search"] }, "highlight_offsets": { "title": { "unit": "code_point", "fragments": [ { "value_index": 1, "value_length": 18, [... 7 more lines] ``` How to read it: - `fragments[i]` describes `highlight.title[i]`, and `value_index` says which value it came from, counted the way the `fields` option returns them - offsets, `matches` included, count from the start of that value, so in Python `hit["fields"]["title"][1][12:18]` is `"search"`. The one exception is a fragment that crosses into the next value, see the details - removing the inserted `pre_tags`/`post_tags`, and decoding entities with `encoder: html`, gives exactly the value's text between the offsets, apart from a few rare cases in the details - `value_length` lets a client check it's slicing the right value in the right unit `unit` is required and is one of `utf16`, `code_point` or `utf8`, since languages slice strings differently and the numbers only agree on ASCII. I made it required so a client never gets numbers in a unit it didn't choose: | `unit` | `value_length` | fragment | match | slices natively in | |---|---|---|---|---| | `utf16` | 19 | 0–19 | 13–19 | Java, JavaScript, C#, Kotlin, Dart | | `code_point` | 18 | 0–18 | 12–18 | Python, Ruby, Perl, PHP `mb_*` | | `utf8` | 21 | 0–21 | 15–21 | Go, Rust, PHP `substr`, C | Scope: - the `unified` highlighter on `text`, `match_only_text` and `keyword`, with an error when offsets are explicitly requested anywhere else (a field matched only by a wildcard is skipped quietly, like highlighting does today). `plain` can't support it, since Lucene's `TextFragment` doesn't expose source positions - `fvh`, the `semantic` highlighter and an offsets-only mode (no fragment strings) would each come later in their own PR - one new transport version for the option and the field, so a search that asks for offsets fails with a 400 if an older node is in the cluster. I'd propose shipping it as technical preview One thing to fix first: chunked fetch writes hits at the data node's own transport version and reads them at the coordinating node's, so once offsets are added to `HighlightField`, every highlighted hit changes on the wire, whether or not the search asks for offsets, and chunked fetch would garble them during a rolling upgrade. The version check on the option can't catch that. I fixed a related chunked-fetch bug in #162396, so I'd send this one as a small separate PR first. What I checked: a test-only harness rebuilds every fragment from the value and the proposed offsets, on random analyzers, offset sources, emoji and multi-valued text, and every fragment matched, including ones that cross values. A second test went through nine mappings where `fields` differs from `_source` (nulls in arrays, `ignore_above`, `copy_to`, synthetic source and a few more), and the highlighter saw the same values in the same order as `fields` in all of them. Both are here: https://github.com/yahorbarkouski/elasticsearch/commit/f8a484533b785d52453ae9fdeb0787e230833871 (test-only, not for merging) a few questions: - does this scope look right for the first feature PR? - is it ok to promise that `value_index` follows the `fields` output (or `stored_fields` for a `store: true` field)? - when a fragment crosses into the next value, should its offsets keep counting past `value_length` (for an 18-unit value, the next one starts at 19), or would you prefer an explicit `end_value_index`? - any concerns with a separate `highlight_offsets` object shaped like this? If the direction works for you, the PR would come with a randomized test that rebuilds every fragment from the returned offsets, YAML tests for the examples above, and docs. happy to rework any part of it, and thanks for reading this far :) Details **Edge cases.** - A phrase, span or intervals match can cross into the next value when `position_increment_gap` is 0, or when slop is at least as large as the gap. The fragment then shows both values joined by a space. Its `start_offset` is in value `value_index`, and the offsets keep counting through one separator, so the next value starts at `value_length + 1`. The fragment's `end_offset` and any match in the next value are therefore larger than `value_length`. - A fragment boundary inside a surrogate pair is rounded outward to the whole character, in every unit. - A `\0` character inside a value counts as one unit and shows as a space in the fragment. - Which spans get tagged is up to the highlighter and may change between versions. - On a nested inner hit, `value_index` counts the field's values within that one nested object, as in the inner hit's own `fields` output. **Requests that get an error in the first PR.** - Field types such as `pattern_text`, `annotated_text`, `semantic_text` and `flattened`. - Percolator highlights, and a nested field highlighted on the root hit, until we agree which values `value_index` should count there. - Offsets stored in postings or term vectors, on a `copy_to` target with several source fields or with `matched_fields` whose sources differ. The stored offsets follow the order the values were indexed in, while `value_index` follows the order the highlighter reads them in, and for these mappings the two can differ (#91148). Offsets from re-analysis are computed on the values as read, so they aren't affected. - An analyzer with an `offset_gap` other than 1, because the gap shifts offsets between values. An unsupported field matched only by a wildcard in `highlight.fields` keeps its fragments and gets no `highlight_offsets` entry. These checks need the mapping, so they run on the shards. A single-index search returns a 400. A search across indices with different mappings reports the failing shards in `_shards.failures`, or fails outright if `allow_partial_search_results` is `false`, like other fetch-time highlighting errors. **Prior work.** #49422 tried an approach based on Lucene's Matches API and stalled on nested hits and `inner_hits`. Taking offsets from the highlighter keeps today's highlighting behavior in those cases and for `highlight_query`. **Cost.** On synthetic responses of 10 hits with 2,000-character bodies, offsets added about 15% to the gzipped response. Before opening the PR, I'll use JMH to check that highlighting without `offsets` doesn't get slower.

Gradle toolchain keeps reusing a stale early-access JDK after the GA release

When a build asks for a JDK by major version (for example languageVersion 27) and no explicit runtime JDK is set, Gradle's toolchain reuses any JDK of that major version that is already in `~/.gradle/jdks`. It doesn't check whether the cached JDK is an early-access (EA) build. The toolchain resolvers, including the early-access resolver in `build-tools-internal`, are only used to download a JDK when no matching one is found locally.

How I saw this:
* A JDK 27 early-access build (27-ea+29) was found in `~/.gradle/jdks` and used by a build that had no `RUNTIME_JAVA_HOME` and no `-Druntime.java` set.
 * JDK 27 had already been released at that point, so the build ran on an outdated pre-release JDK without any warning.
 * The EA resolver (`EarlyAccessCatalogJdkToolchainResolver`) is registered last in `settings.gradle`. It downloads the latest EA, RC or GA build from the es-jdk-archive catalog into `~/.gradle/jdks`. Later runs reuse that copy and never check it again.
 * I could not confirm exactly how the EA build got there, because it had been removed by the time I looked. The setup above is the most likely source. ( and I had previously been doing work with EA JDK on this machine, months ago )

Why it matters:
* Test and benchmark results can come from a pre-release JDK with known bugs or different behavior, and nothing flags it.
 * Results are hard to reproduce, because they depend on whatever JDK happens to be cached on each machine.
 * The problem is silent. Nothing fails, and it persists until someone deletes the cached JDK by hand. I only noticed this by accident because I know that 27-ea+35 is the actual GA build.

Possible solutions:
* Add a check after the JDK is resolved. Fail or warn if the runtime version contains "-ea" (or is an RC) when a GA build is expected, or when the bundled JDK version is GA.
* Make the toolchain path less implicit. Require RUNTIME_JAVA_HOME or -Druntime.java for anything that must run on a specific JDK, and document that clearly.
* Stop Gradle from reusing stale JDKs. Turn off auto-detection (org.gradle.java.installations.auto-detect=false) and list JDK paths explicitly.
* Have the EA resolver, or a build step, put EA downloads in a location that GA runs don't pick up, so they can't be mistaken for each other.
* Document that ~/.gradle/jdks should be cleaned when a new JDK version is released.

ES|QL: a `_score` condition ANDed with a search inside an OR doesn't see the search's score

main (9.6.0-SNAPSHOT), reproduced at `b1c8813f4a1b`.

A `_score` predicate ANDed with a search sees that search's score when the AND is at the top level of a `WHERE`, but not when the AND is inside an `OR`. In this case, the score from before the `WHERE` is used, which is 0.0 when nothing has contributed to the score yet. **This means that adding an `OR` branch to a query (which should only ever add rows) can actually remove them.**

Indexed fields and runtime searches behave the same way, for different reasons:
- **Indexed fields:** at the top level, the search is pushed to Lucene, so `_score` already holds its score. Inside an `OR`, the `_score` reference keeps the whole `OR` out of Lucene, so it's evaluated in compute against the score from before the `WHERE`.
- **Runtime searches** (`MATCH`/`MATCH_PHRASE`/`KNN` on an expression or on a federated dataset): a top-level conjunct that reads `_score` is evaluated after the `WHERE`'s other conjuncts have added their scores (#162397). Inside an `OR`, the search and the `_score` predicate are in the same conjunct, so the predicate can't see the search's score.

Using the `books` csv-spec dataset:

```
FROM books METADATA _score
| WHERE match(title, "Rings") AND _score > 0.5
| SORT book_no
| KEEP book_no
```

returns books 2675, 2714, 4023 and 7140. Adding an `OR` branch:

```
FROM books METADATA _score
| WHERE (match(title, "Rings") AND _score > 0.5) OR match(title, "Hobbit")
| SORT book_no
| KEEP book_no
```

returns only 4289, 6405 and 7480, the books whose title matches "Hobbit". The four "Rings" books drop out.

The same queries on a runtime expression, with `| EVAL content = to_text(concat(title, ""))` and `match(content, ...)`, return exactly the same rows.

**Expected:** the second query returns the first query's rows plus the "Hobbit" ones: 2675, 2714, 4023, 4289, 6405, 7140 and 7480.

- #162397: where this came up, in review. Includes `matchAndScoreOrMatchOnRuntimeText` and `matchAndScoreOrMatchOnIndexedField` in `match-function.csv-spec`, which pin the current behavior.
- #162918: in the same kind of query, the `OR` adds the score of a branch that didn't match.
- #160809: `_score` semantics that depend on pushdown.

ES|QL: improve async query creation docs for non-json formats

**Update**

The [automated bug analysis](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/162926#issuecomment-6325336433) mentions `X-Elasticsearch-Async-Id` and `X-Elasticsearch-Async-Is-Running` headers. This actually allows using a non-json format in the initial request, but in practice may not be usable as client libraries not always surface protocol-level information (http headers) in high-level responses.

This deserves a doc update explaining the `"wait_for_completion_timeout": 0` workaround if the client library doesn't expose request headers.

I changed the issue title and changed it from `>bug` to `>docs`.

When creating an async request, the response can be either a response if results have available before the `wait_for_completion_timeout`, or a query creation response.

The `?format` parameter is used for both kinds of responses, which is an issue if different from `json`:
* it is correct when the query result is readily available,
* it produces no usable data for other formats (`csv`, `txt`, `arrow`).

```
POST _query/async?format=csv
{
    "query": "FROM my-index",
    "wait_for_completion_timeout": 0
}
```

Produces two empty lines as a response.

* Force the creation of an async request by using `"wait_for_completion_timeout": 0` with no `format` query parameter to get the query id,
* Use a non-json response format only when fetching results with `GET _query/async/{id}?format=csv`

ES|QL: a disjunction scored outside Lucene adds the score of a branch that didn't match

main (9.6.0-SNAPSHOT), reproduced at b1c8813f4a1b.

When ES|QL scores a disjunction in compute rather than in Lucene, each side's score is added even when that side evaluated to false. Lucene adds a `should` clause's score only when the clause matches. So the same query scores differently depending on whether it was pushed down.

This only matters when a search matches but the branch it's in is false because of another non-search condition in the same branch. For example, `(MATCH(a) AND year > 2000) OR MATCH(b)` on a row matching both matches, where `year <= 2000`.

This affects scoring for all searches on runtime expressions, as well as searches on indexed fields when something in the condition can't be pushed down to Lucene.

`BinaryLogic.BinaryLogicScorer` returns `left + right` for every row, for both AND and OR. It has done that since it was added in #121793. For AND this is harmless, since a row only survives the filter if both sides are true. For OR, a side that evaluated to false still contributes the score of any search inside it that matched.

- #162397: `_score` inside an OR, where this was noticed.
- #160809: `_score` semantics that depend on pushdown.
- #121793: added the scorer.
- #156097: runtime search scoring.

Using the `books` csv-spec dataset. Book 4023, "A Tolkien Compass: … The Lord of the Rings" (1975), matches both "Rings" and "Tolkien" in its title. In every query below, its left branch is false, so it passes on "Tolkien" alone:

| Query | Path | `_score` of book 4023 |
|---|---|---|
| `WHERE match(title, "Tolkien")` | Lucene | 1.46 |
| `WHERE (match(title, "Rings") AND year > 2000) OR match(title, "Tolkien")` | Lucene | **1.46** |
| `WHERE (match(title, "Rings") AND LENGTH(title) < 60) OR match(title, "Tolkien")` | compute | **2.93** |
| `EVAL s = score((match(title, "Rings") AND year > 2000) OR match(title, "Tolkien"))` | compute | **2.93** |
| `EVAL content = to_text(concat(title, ""))` then `WHERE match(content, "Tolkien")` | compute (runtime) | 1.0 |
| `EVAL content = to_text(concat(title, ""))` then `WHERE (match(content, "Rings") AND year > 2000) OR match(content, "Tolkien")` | compute (runtime) | **2.0** |

Each query starts with `FROM books METADATA _score`, and adds `AND book_no == "4023"` to its `WHERE`. "Rings" alone also scores 1.46 on this book, which is why the compute result is exactly double.

**Expected:** the bold rows match the "Tolkien"-only score of their path: 1.46 for indexed and 1.0 for runtime.

Past TSDB index creation fails the whole request when the head's end_time lags behind wall-clock time

With `data_stream.past_tsdb_index_creation_enabled` on, a bulk request can contain a timestamp that no backing index covers and that is not older than the head. This happens when the head's `index.time_series.end_time` has fallen behind wall-clock time. One cause is a master stall that prevents `UpdateTimeSeriesRangeService` from extending it. In that case:

- `TransportBulkAction#isEligibleForPastIndexCreation` only rejects timestamps newer than the request start time. A timestamp in `[head.end_time, requestStartTime]` is therefore queued for past-index creation.
- On the master, `TransportPastTimeSeriesIndexCreationAction.PastTimeSeriesIndexCreationExecutor#executeTask` pops every covered window, because all of them end at or before that timestamp. `nextIndex` is then `null`. The `assert nextIndex != null` fails in tests and a `NullPointerException` is thrown in production.
- The exception fails the whole per-data-stream task. Timestamps in the same request that really are historical, and could have been given a past index, fail as well.

- A timestamp at or after the head's `start_time` that isn't covered (so `>= head.end_time`) is never queued for past-index creation. It falls through to the existing routing error in `BulkOperation`, as it does with the setting off.
- The master rejects such a timestamp with a clear reason instead of throwing, and still processes the other timestamps in the task.

Revise the request circuit breaker limit for small heaps

`indices.breaker.request.limit` defaults to 60% of heap. On small heaps, that leaves little headroom for large fetch responses, so a few big responses can OOM the node before the breaker trips. This came up in #139132.

Redact processor does not apply the Grok watchdog

9.5.4

x-pack / redact

_bundled_

The Redact processor [documentation](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/ingest-processor/redact-processor#grok-watchdog-redact) states that it uses the Grok watchdog and fails when an expression exceeds `ingest.grok.watchdog.max_execution_time`.

However, `RedactProcessor.matchRepeat` [creates and searches](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/581b5cb79bceca48b4d2e79c5be1e0eecc018958/x-pack/plugin/redact/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/redact/RedactProcessor.java#L198) a Joni `Matcher` directly rather than using `Grok.match`. Unlike `Grok.match`, this path does not register the matcher with `MatcherWatchdog`.

As a result, the configured Grok watchdog timeout does not apply to Redact pattern matching. A pathological or expensive Redact pattern can therefore run without the documented execution-time limit.

There is also a related correctness concern: `matchRepeat` treats all negative Joni search results as “no more matches”. This includes `Matcher.INTERRUPTED`, which Grok normally converts into an exception. If interruption were enabled on this matcher without explicit handling, Redact could return a partially redacted value instead of failing.

- `x-pack/plugin/redact/.../RedactProcessor.java`
  - `matchRepeat` calls `grok.getCompiledExpression().matcher(...)`
  - it invokes `matcher.search(...)` without watchdog registration
  - it breaks on `result < 0`
- `libs/grok/.../Grok.java`
  - `match` registers/unregisters its matcher with `MatcherWatchdog`
  - it throws when the result is `Matcher.INTERRUPTED`

Redact processing should honor the watchdog behavior documented for it: expressions exceeding the configured limit should fail the processor rather than continuing without a timeout or returning a partial result.

main, with elastic/elasticsearch#162675 (which adds the warning)

A caller's `SET wildcards_match_views=true` stops at view boundaries: a view returns the same rows whatever the caller's query settings say. When the view body has wildcards that would otherwise have matched views, elastic/elasticsearch#162675 warns the caller and advises the author to "use that setting inside the view definition if you wish to change the view behaviour".

The warning and the advice are the same when the view definition already says `SET wildcards_match_views=false`. There the author has made an explicit choice, and the advice reads as if the definition does not use the setting at all. `ViewQuerySettings` keeps only the resolved values (`wildcardsMatchViews` and `wildcardsMatchDatasets` are plain booleans), and `false` is also the registry default, so `ViewResolver.ViewsScope.forBody` cannot tell an explicit `false` from a definition without `SET`.

`wildcards_match_datasets` goes through the same `ViewQuerySettings` boolean (`ViewResolver` passes `bodySettings.wildcardsMatchDatasets()` to the dataset probe), so an explicit `SET wildcards_match_datasets=false` should get the same warning. This was found by reading the code and has not been reproduced.

Results are unaffected; only the warning is misleading.

Possible fix: record which settings a view definition SETs explicitly (for example, keep the set of explicit setting names alongside the resolved values in `ViewQuerySettings`). Then either skip the warning for a view whose author explicitly opted out, or reword it to name the view's own `SET`.

ES|QL: unmapped_fields view-boundary warning is missing when the view body uses DROP or KEEP *

main, with elastic/elasticsearch#162675 (which adds the warning)

None

bundled

The caller's `SET unmapped_fields="load"` stops at view boundaries: a view returns the same rows whatever the caller's query settings say. When a caller references a field the view does not output, the field is null in the view's rows, and elastic/elasticsearch#162675 adds a warning saying so, but only when the view body would have let the field through had the body been written inline in the caller's query. A body that projects the field away (`KEEP id`) or aggregates it away gets no warning, since the field would be null either way.

The check gets this wrong for `DROP`, and for a `KEEP` whose pattern matches the field, such as `KEEP *`. `KEEP` is an allow-list and `DROP` a deny-list: inline, `FROM probe_idx | KEEP id | KEEP message` hides `message`, but `FROM probe_idx | DROP client_ip | KEEP message` lets it through and loads it. In a view body without its own `SET unmapped_fields`, though, the analyzer resolves `KEEP`, `DROP` and `RENAME` to a plain `Project` of the surviving columns. Over `[id, client_ip, message]`, `KEEP id, message` and `DROP client_ip` both become `Project[id, message]`, and the command kind and patterns are gone. Only under a non-default mode is the result a `ResolvingProject` that keeps them. The warning check (`ResolveUnmapped.viewBodyCanSurfaceLoadedField`, through `Analyzer.ResolveRefs.branchCanSurfaceLoadedField`) cannot tell a deny-list from an allow-list in a plain `Project`, so it treats every plain `Project` as hiding the field, and the warning is missing.

Results are unaffected: the field is null in the view's rows in every case. Only the warning that explains why is missing.

`RENAME` should be affected the same way, but a query over a view whose body uses `RENAME` currently fails before the check runs, which is a separate bug: #162745.

Possible fixes:

1. Keep the command kind and patterns on default-mode `KEEP`, `DROP` and `RENAME` projections, for example by resolving them to `ResolvingProject` in every mode. This touches every query's plan.
2. Record the command kind and patterns of each projection in a view body during analysis, keyed by the node's `Source`, for the warning check alone.

SQL: `Cannot find backing column for ordering aggregation` when ordering by an aggregate

**Description**

A user's ES SQL request failed with an internal `SqlIllegalArgumentException` while the query was executing. The original SQL text isn't available yet. Observed on serverless (`9.6.0`).

```
org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.SqlIllegalArgumentException: Cannot find backing column for ordering aggregation [org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.querydsl.container.AggregateSort@d540f08e]
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.querydsl.container.QueryContainer.sortingColumns(QueryContainer.java:190)
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.execution.search.SourceGenerator.sourceBuilder(SourceGenerator.java:83)
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.execution.search.Querier.query(Querier.java:120)
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.plan.physical.EsQueryExec.execute(EsQueryExec.java:60)
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.plan.physical.LeafExec.execute(LeafExec.java:31)
	at org.elasticsearch.xpack.sql.session.SqlSession.lambda$sql$5(SqlSession.java:192)
	...
```

**What the error means**

- `QueryFolder.FoldOrderBy` turns an `ORDER BY <aggregate function>` into an `AggregateSort`. The sort is keyed by `Expressions.id(aggExpr)`, which is the expression's `hashCode()`.
- `QueryFolder.FoldAggregate` registers each aggregate output column under `Expressions.id(<alias child>)`.
- Aggregate sorts are applied in memory over the result rows. `QueryContainer.sortingColumns()` looks up the output column for each sort key and throws when there isn't one.

So the aggregate in `ORDER BY` didn't structurally match any aggregate in the plan's aggregate list after analysis and optimization.

Normally `Analyzer.ResolveAggsInOrderBy` prevents this. It pushes any `ORDER BY` aggregate missing from the nearest `Aggregate` into that node, then projects the original output on top.

**Hypothesis (not reproduced)**

#159256 (`81c662da1ae6`, "SQL: Fix internal server error on an aggregate over an aggregate alias") added `isRedundantAggregateOverAggregateAlias`. For `F(alias)`, where `F` is SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX/PERCENTILE and `alias` is an alias of another aggregate, `ResolveAggsInOrderBy` now skips that push. An example is `SELECT gender, MIN(salary) AS m ... GROUP BY gender ORDER BY MIN(m)`. The fix relies on alias inlining (`ReplaceReferenceAttributeWithSource`) and then `CollapseAggregateOverAggregate` to turn the `ORDER BY` expression back into exactly the aggregated expression.

If another optimizer rewrite makes the collapsed `ORDER BY` expression structurally different from the one in `Aggregate.aggregates()`, the ids won't match and this exception is thrown. One candidate is the `ReplaceAggsWithStats` / `ExtendedStats` / `Percentiles` `InnerAggregate` replacements, depending on rule ordering. Other query shapes where an `ORDER BY` aggregate never reaches the `Aggregate` could also trigger it, for example when intermediate nodes or sub-selects sit between `OrderBy` and `Aggregate`. This needs to be confirmed.

**Investigation steps**

1. Get the failing SQL text from the user or from request/audit logs, and check whether it uses `ORDER BY AGG(<select alias>)`.
2. Check whether the serverless build that failed includes `81c662da1ae6`.
3. Try to reproduce with:
   - each `SingleValueIdentityAgg` (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, PERCENTILE) wrapped around an aliased aggregate in `ORDER BY`;
   - combinations that trigger the stats rewrites (for example SUM with AVG on the same field, or extended stats);
   - grouped and ungrouped queries.
4. If it reproduces, compare the optimized plan's `OrderBy` expression with `Aggregate.aggregates()` to find which rewrite makes them diverge.

**Expected behavior**

The query returns sorted results, or fails with a clear verification error if the shape isn't supported.

**Workaround**

Order by the `SELECT` alias directly (`ORDER BY m`) instead of wrapping it in an aggregate, or repeat the aggregate exactly as written in `SELECT`.

PromQL: pair selector label matchers with their fields explicitly

A PromQL selector keeps its label matchers and their label fields in two parallel lists, [`Selector.labels` and `Selector.labelMatchers`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a8b386c657172da42441b77d070af75e7f42c783/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plan/logical/promql/selector/Selector.java#L45-L46). [`LabelMatchers.predicate`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a8b386c657172da42441b77d070af75e7f42c783/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plan/logical/promql/selector/LabelMatchers.java#L87) rebuilds which field belongs to which matcher from positions and list sizes.

The two lists don't line up for every spelling of the metric name. `tx{...}` [adds a `__name__` matcher without a field](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a8b386c657172da42441b77d070af75e7f42c783/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/parser/promql/PromqlLogicalPlanBuilder.java#L248), while `{__name__="tx",...}` and `{"tx",...}` [add both](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a8b386c657172da42441b77d070af75e7f42c783/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/parser/promql/PromqlLogicalPlanBuilder.java#L276-L277). This difference caused the bug fixed in #161113, where matchers after a braced `__name__` filtered the wrong label. The fix compensates with an offset of `matchers.size() - fields.size()` and an assertion. That works, but it keeps details of the query syntax relevant at translation time, and any new way of building a selector has to preserve the implicit alignment.

Pair each label matcher with its field explicitly when the selector is built, so that consumers never rely on positions, and so that metric-name matchers are handled the same way whichever way the name is written. Repeated matchers on one label (`{host=~"a|b",host!="b"}`) can stay as separate entries; grouping them by label name isn't required.

The label fields are `UnresolvedAttribute`s that the analyzer resolves through generic expression traversal ([`QueryPlan.doTransformExpression`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/a8b386c657172da42441b77d070af75e7f42c783/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plan/QueryPlan.java#L144)). That traversal only reaches expressions and lists of expressions. A plain (matcher, field) pair object would therefore never get its field resolved; the pairing has to be an expression node itself, or resolution has to handle it explicitly.

Expected touch points:
- `Selector` and its subclasses `InstantSelector`, `RangeSelector` and `LiteralSelector`, including their node info and equality.
- `PromqlLogicalPlanBuilder.visitSelector`.
- `ResolvePromqlFunctions`, which rebuilds a `RangeSelector` from an `InstantSelector`.
- `LabelMatchers.predicate`, and the `nameLabel()` checks in the `PromqlCommand` verifier.
- The test helper `PromqlFakeResolver`, which collects label names from `Selector.labels`.

ESQL: ViewResolver async traversal resets its stack-depth budget on every nested replaceViews call

Async `Node.transformDown(rule, executor, listener)` limits stack growth by handing the recursion to the executor every `ASYNC_TRANSFORM_STACK_DEPTH_LIMIT` (100) levels. The depth counter belongs to a single `transformDown` call, though. `ViewResolver.replaceViews` starts a new `plan.transformDown` at depth 0 for each nested traversal: a view body in `replaceViewsUnresolvedRelation`, an IN subquery rewritten into a semi/anti/mark join in the `Filter` / `Eval` / `Aggregate` cases, and the left and right sides in `replaceViewsSubqueryJoin`. Whenever these nested calls continue on the same thread, their stretches add up on one stack. The 100-level limit then bounds each stretch but not the thread's total depth.

#162598 shows what happens when the total gets too deep. A test double that completed `EsqlResolveViewAction` inline stacked about 300 plan levels (about 4,800 frames) on one search thread, and hit a `StackOverflowError` under a 1 MB stack with cold-JIT frames. Because it is an `Error`, `delegateFailureAndWrap` and `AbstractRunnable` don't catch it, so the request listener is never completed. In a real node, `ElasticsearchUncaughtExceptionHandler` treats an uncaught `StackOverflowError` as fatal and halts with exit code 126. Production `ViewResolver.doEsqlResolveViewsRequest` forks each view response with `ThreadedActionListener`, which resets the stack at every view expansion. I couldn't overflow it with nested IN subqueries alone: five levels of about 95 pipes each passed under `-Xss1m -Xint`. So there is no known production repro. The safety still depends on that fork, and on the node limit keeping nested IN/FROM subquery chains short, not on the traversal itself.

A sturdier version would bound the depth per thread, not per call. One option is to pass the current depth into nested `replaceViews` calls, so the bounce counter keeps counting across nested traversals. Another is to always bounce when a nested traversal starts. A unit test that runs deeply nested IN subqueries and views through `ViewResolver` with a counting executor, and asserts the maximum recursion depth per thread, would catch regressions deterministically instead of depending on stack size and JIT state.

Follow-up from #162598 / #162621.

Better ES|QL partial resolution failures

ESQL query could be executed against multiple patterns in a single from statement (`FROM index-1,index-2`). Such query fails with partial resolution failure if at least one of the concrete patterns did not resolve indices:

https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/ae3de4388711629c20b91b5f1d9d9273a79d6eec/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/internalClusterTest/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/plugin/IndexResolutionIT.java#L348-L389

Validate icu_tokenizer rule_files against ICU dictionary break engines

A custom `icu_tokenizer` `rule_files` rule set can put a character in a dictionary character class that the matching ICU4J break engine doesn't handle. If that happens, analyzing a single matching character makes ICU4J allocate break engines without limit until the node runs out of memory. The leaked memory is static ICU state that the circuit breakers don't track, so the breakers never trip, a full GC can't reclaim it, and only restarting the node clears it.

We saw this on 9.5.4 (ICU4J 77.1). A rule file widened `$HangulSyllable`/`$dictionary` to include Hangul Jamo (`\u1100-\u11FF`, `\uA960-\uA97F`, `\uD7B0-\uD7FF`). A single `_analyze` call on NFD Korean text was enough to OOM the node.

`RuleBasedBreakIterator.getLanguageBreakEngine(c)` picks an engine by the character's Unicode script, builds it, and appends it to the static `gAllBreakEngines` list without checking `eng.handles(c)`. `populateDictionary` then makes no progress and asks again, which creates another engine, around 2 MB each for CJK. Characters that can trigger this when they're placed in a dictionary class:

- Hangul: anything outside `\uAC00-\uD7A3`, such as Jamo, compatibility Jamo, halfwidth and enclosed Hangul
- Thai/Lao/Khmer/Myanmar: anything outside `[[:Script:]&[:LineBreak=SA:]]`, such as digits and punctuation

The real fix belongs upstream. ICU should fall back to `UnhandledBreakEngine` when a newly built engine doesn't handle the character. We should file that with ICU separately.

Harden `IcuTokenizerFactory` so a rule file like this is rejected with a clear error when the tokenizer is created, instead of OOMing at analysis time:

1. In `parseRules()`, after compiling the `RuleBasedBreakIterator`, scan every code point whose category is `>= fRData.fFTable.fDictCategoriesStart` (via `fRData.fTrie`).
2. For each one, resolve the script to the engine ICU would choose and check that the engine handles the character.
3. If any characters fail, throw `IllegalArgumentException` naming the rule file and the unhandled ranges.

- `fRData`/`RBBIDataWrapper` are public but `@internal` in ICU4J, so we'd want a test that fails loudly on ICU upgrades.
- Should we copy the engines' `UnicodeSet` patterns, or build each engine once and call `handles(c)`?
- Should validation apply only to new indices? Existing indices with bad rule files would otherwise fail to open after an upgrade.

ML datafeed on API-key remote cluster stops: delayed data check runs as internal _xpack user

A real-time anomaly detection datafeed whose indices are on a remote cluster connected via **API-key based (RCS2) cross-cluster access** stops with:

```
java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Internal user [_xpack] should not be used for cross cluster requests
  at ...CrossClusterAccessTransportInterceptor$1.sendWithCrossClusterAccessHeaders(CrossClusterAccessTransportInterceptor.java:214)
  ...
  at ...TransportSearchAction.ccsRemoteReduce(TransportSearchAction.java:1011)
  ...
  at ...SecurityContext.executeAsInternalUser(SecurityContext.java:174)
  at ...AuthorizationUtils.switchUserBasedOnActionOriginAndExecute(AuthorizationUtils.java:178)
  ...
  at ...DatafeedDelayedDataDetector.checkCurrentBucketEventCount(DatafeedDelayedDataDetector.java:141)
  at ...DatafeedDelayedDataDetector.detectMissingData(DatafeedDelayedDataDetector.java:101)
[... 3 more lines]
```

Reported on 9.5.3 (internal report in Slack: the datafeed used `indices: ["<remote>:logs-*"]`, the user was authenticated via SAML, and the datafeed always stopped after a few minutes). Reproduced on a build of `7cd249ba6418` (9.6.0-SNAPSHOT).

**1. The delayed data check runs as the internal `_xpack` user.**
`DatafeedDelayedDataDetector.checkCurrentBucketEventCount` (and `checkBucketEvents`) use `client.threadPool().getThreadContext().stashWithOrigin(ML_ORIGIN)` and do not apply the datafeed's stored security headers. The regular extractors use `ClientHelper.executeWithHeaders(...)` (see `ScrollDataExtractor`, `AbstractAggregationDataExtractor`), which is why normal extraction works. With remote indices, the delayed data check's search is sent cross-cluster as `_xpack`, which `CrossClusterAccessTransportInterceptor` rejects.

The check only runs after `xpack.ml.delayed_data_check_freq` (default 15m) has elapsed, and only in a real-time cycle that found at least one record (`DatafeedJob.run` throws `EmptyDataCountException` before `checkForMissingDataIfNecessary` when the record count is 0).

**2. The failure is not surfaced in the job messages (from code reading; not observed in a test).**
An unexpected exception in the real-time loop goes to the generic `catch (Exception e)` in `DatafeedRunner.doDatafeedRealtime`, which logs to the server log and calls `holder.stop("general_realtime_error", ...)`. `Holder.stop` writes only `auditor.info(jobId, "Datafeed stopped")`. The `ProblemTracker` (the component that writes warning/error audit messages) is only reached for `ExtractionProblemException`/`AnalysisProblemException`, so the cause is never audited. A real-time datafeed does not auto-close the job, so the job stays `opened` and Job Messages show only an info "Datafeed stopped".

Added to `RemoteClusterSecurityMlIT` (`x-pack/plugin/security/qa/multi-cluster`), which already sets up an RCS2 remote cluster with `ml_jobs_shared_airline_data`:

1. `configureRemoteCluster()`; set `xpack.ml.delayed_data_check_freq` to `1s`.
2. Index a couple of documents into `shared-airline-data` on the fulfilling cluster.
3. Create and open a job with `datafeed_config.indexes: ["my_remote_cluster:shared-airline-data"]`, `frequency: 1m`, `query_delay: 1s`, default `delayed_data_check_config` (enabled); start the datafeed (real-time).
4. Keep indexing a document with a current timestamp every few seconds.

At the first real-time cycle that processes records, the delayed data check fails at `CrossClusterAccessTransportInterceptor.java:213` with "Internal user [_xpack] should not be used for cross cluster requests". (In the test cluster, assertions are enabled, so `assert false : message` throws an `AssertionError` before the `IllegalArgumentException`; being an `Error`, it escapes the datafeed's `catch (Exception)` and kills the node. In production the `IllegalArgumentException` is thrown, as in the trace above.) The same test with `delayed_data_check_config.enabled: false` does not fail.

Stop the datafeed, disable the delayed data check, restart:

```
POST _ml/datafeeds/<datafeed_id>/_update
{ "delayed_data_check_config": { "enabled": false } }
```

- Run the delayed data check's search with the datafeed's stored headers (as the extractors do) instead of `stashWithOrigin(ML_ORIGIN)` alone, or skip/degrade the check for remote indices.
- Audit unexpected real-time failures at warning/error level with the cause, so they appear in Job Messages.

ES|QL: one-element lists break CIDR_MATCH pushdown and STARTS_WITH

A one-element list should behave like its single value (as fixed for `CASE` in #157956). `CIDR_MATCH` and `STARTS_WITH` don't, and silently return no rows.

Kibana ES|QL multi-select controls hit this: they send an array param even when one option is selected.

Verified on 9.5.1 and on a recent `main` snapshot.

```
PUT test
{"mappings": {"properties": {"ip": {"type": "ip"}, "host": {"type": "keyword"}}}}

POST test/_doc?refresh
{"ip": "192.168.1.1", "host": "web-01"}
```

```
FROM test | WHERE CIDR_MATCH(ip, ["192.168.0.0/16"])  // 0 rows, is_partial: true. Expected 1
FROM test | WHERE STARTS_WITH(host, ["web"])           // 0 rows. Expected 1
```

- `CIDR_MATCH`: the shard fails with `'[[31 39 32 ...]]' is not an IP string literal`. Only the pushdown fails: `EVAL m = CIDR_MATCH(ip, ["192.168.0.0/16"])` is `true`.
- `STARTS_WITH`: also wrong when evaluated (`false`).
- Same with a param: `"params": [{"p": ["web"]}]`.
- The scalar forms work, and so does `host == ["web-01"]`.

`CIDRMatch.asQuery` and `StartsWith` use the folded value as a scalar, so the one-element `List` becomes the text `"[...]"`.

Inconsistent unit-length vectors when using semantic_text with some inference providers

9.4.x

_bundled_

We have observed that, in rare cases, some inference providers that use dot product similarity return unit vectors that violate our [magnitude epsilon](https://github.com/Mikep86/elasticsearch/blob/ad192c51f4b59fb8407b8d65e9d046607bd7311c/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/index/codec/vectors/BQVectorUtils.java#L29-L29).

In the past, [we increased epsilon to account for this](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/110240), and thought the issue was addressed. However, we have received recent reports of this issue happening again. We think it is due to a combination of two factors:

- Models using more dimensions, allowing for more accumulated magnitude error
- [`semantic_text` defaulting to `bfloat16` in ES 9.4.x](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/144236), which decreases the precision of each dimension

Users can work around this issue in one of two ways, not mutually exclusive:

- If using `semantic_text` and an inference endpoint that uses `float` element type, configure it to use `float` instead of `bfloat16`:

```
PUT my-index
{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "my_semantic_field": {
        "type": "semantic_text",
        "inference_id": "my-inference-endpoint",
        "index_options": {
          "dense_vector": {
            "element_type": "float"
[... 6 more lines]
```

- Use an inference endpoint configured to use `cosine` similarity. Vector magnitude checks are not run when using `cosine` similarity.

```
PUT _inference/text_embedding/openai-cosine-embeddings
{
  "service": "openai",
  "service_settings": {
    "api_key": "<api_key>",
    "model_id": "text-embedding-3-small",
    "similarity": "cosine"
  }
}
```

1. Create an index with a `semantic_text` field that uses an inference service with `float` element type and `dot_product` similarity
2. Index values that produce embeddings with magnitude close to or exceeding Elasticsearch's unit vector epsilon (it can be difficult to find such values)

Share analyzers across indices on a node

`AnalysisRegistry#build` runs once per index, so two indices with the same analysis recipe each build and hold their own `NamedAnalyzer` — and everything it carries (e.g. a synonyms chain's MB-scale `SynonymMap`, plus the per-analyzer `CloseableThreadLocal` graph). With data streams and templated indices pushing one recipe onto hundreds of indices per node, that recipe is built and held hundreds of times.

This makes the **analyzer the unit of sharing**: indices that resolve to a byte-identical recipe share one reference-counted `NamedAnalyzer`, built once per node and keyed on recipe structure. Each factory exposes a `sharingKey()` — identity by default (never shared; safe), overridden to opt in. Built once (single-flight), reloaded once per request, closed on last release. Gated by the `shared_analyzers` feature flag (off in release). Synonyms motivate it, but it also de-duplicates the default / language / custom analyzers.

Originally implemented end-to-end in #150797; splitting into smaller, focused PRs to ease review. Enabling the flag in release is a separate, macro-benchmark-gated follow-up.

  - A refresh=false update isn't seen by an index that joins an analyzer already loaded on that node. It applies on the next reload or node restart. Use separate synonym sets for staged rollouts.
  - Reloading any index reloads every index sharing the analyzer.

On closer inspection this was because of the total size of _responses_ which today are untracked (and in this case contained a lot of `IndexNotFoundException` instances each of which takes over 1kiB of heap):

```
Class Name                                                                                                                              | Shallow Heap | Retained Heap
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.IncrementalBulkService$Handler @ 0xc1ad41c8                                                               |           64 |    29,315,504
'- responses java.util.ArrayList @ 0xc1ad43c8                                                                                           |           24 |    29,313,384
   '- elementData java.lang.Object[13] @ 0xe141ff58                                                                                     |           72 |    29,313,360
      '- [12] org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.BulkResponse @ 0xf5fdb728                                                                   |           40 |     6,149,096
         '- responses org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.BulkItemResponse[4166] @ 0xf5fdb750                                                 |       16,680 |     6,149,032
            |- [500] org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.BulkItemResponse @ 0xf0a7bd60                                                        |           32 |         1,472
            |- [501] org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.BulkItemResponse @ 0xf0a7c320                                                        |           32 |         1,472
            |- [502] org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.BulkItemResponse @ 0xf0a7c8e0                                                        |           32 |         1,472
[... 24 more lines]
```

We pretty much only accumulate these things so we can combine them together at the end via `BulkResponse#combine`, computing a few simple stats and then streaming them out as `XContent`. I think we should accumulate them as bytes rather than in an unbounded list like this: a bytes-based representation is going to be denser than all these heap objects, even if uncompressed, and if we use bytes then we can keep track of how large these things are, feed that into the indexing pressure, and ultimately fail these requests before they hurt the node.

We could even perhaps render them straight to the final `XContent` output and accumulate that.

[Inference API] Potentially sensitive URL information may be logged when URISyntaxException is thrown constructing inference endpoint URI

The `RequestUtils.buildUri()` method contains a comment indicating that we do not want to log URL details if an exception is encountered when building the URI:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/f716931ef78c89428a3ea443c08624b24e0a9646/x-pack/plugin/inference/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/inference/external/request/RequestUtils.java#L32-L39
Using a 400 status error prevents the exception from being logged by the `rest.suppressed` logger in `RestResponse`, but it still may be logged in other places in the inference module. For example, using an invalid URL component when creating an Alibaba Cloud Search endpoint results in the following, which contains the full URL in the "Caused by" exception:

[ML][Inference API] Tag trained model deployments created by the Inference API

The `elasticsearch` inference service deploys models on ML nodes, these deployments appear in ML Trained Models UI even though they are managed by the inference service. It is easy to confuse models managed by Trained Models and those managed by the `elasticsearch` inference service.

The inference service should _tag_ deployments it creates with the inference ID so that the UI has an easy way to distinguish ownership. Once this is implemented it may be desirable to limit actions in the Trained Models UI/API if the deployment was created by inference.

[ML] Update Inference Settings cannot clear settings

Unsetting or explicitly setting a value to `null` does not clear the setting:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/inference/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/inference/services/cohere/embeddings/CohereEmbeddingsTaskSettings.java#L116

All of our [updatedTaskSettings](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/x-pack/plugin/inference/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/inference/services/cohere/embeddings/CohereEmbeddingsTaskSettings.java#L197) should check if a user is explicitly setting a field to `null` and, if so, clearing the field.

If a user creates an endpoint with `input_type` set:
```
    "task_settings": {
        "input_type": "search"
    }
```

An update like this should clear the `input_type` setting:
```
    "task_settings": {
        "input_type": null
    }
```

Whereas an update like this should not:
```
    "task_settings": {
    }
```

Workaround is to delete and recreate the endpoint with the desired `task_settings`

ESQL: Make PhysicalPlan.output() include all physically emitted columns/attributes

For `PhysicalPlan` inheritors that represent commands that add columns, like
- EvalExec
- DissectExec
- GrokExec
- EnrichExec
- LookupJoinExec

the `.output()` method returns the _logical_ output, which in case of name conflicts does not include conflicting attributes from the upstream plan.

E.g. for an index with 1 field `idx_field` the plan for `FROM idx | EVAL idx_field = to_upper(idx_field)` will have an `EvalExec` whose `.output()` method will include only the newly evaluated `idx_field`, not the original field from the index. This is facilitated by the helper method [mergeOutputAttributes](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/bb67a7c4abad248e28661d3d03bec4e8e51948c2/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/NamedExpressions.java#L26).

However, the corresponding, actual physical `EvalOperator` does not implement any handling of name conflicts; it simply [appends blocks to incoming pages](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/92d1d31eea496a014bd400dea727fe572f74a521/x-pack/plugin/esql/compute/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/compute/operator/EvalOperator.java#L46). The same is true for the physical operators corresponding to the other `...Exec` classes from above.

The fact that name conflict logic spills into physical plans leads to complications. For instance, physical plans with remote `ENRICH`s sometimes require the presence of two columns with the same name: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/118531

It also makes PhysicalPlans harder to reason about and doesn't correctly represent actual physical operations.

To have more simplicity in our query plans, we should change the contract for `PhysicalPlan.output()` to not return the _logical_ output of the physical plan, but the actual physical output. Then https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/118531 will be solved, too.

This is also required if we later want to go one step further and remove name conflict handling from `LogicalPlan`s (however that might look). Name conflicts only strictly need to be handled in the Analyzer, to resolve what each name in a query refers to.

ESQL: Conflict between real and synthetic attribute names

In several optimizer/analyzer rules, ESQL creates new attribute names in a way that is meant not to conflict with existing attributes. (The names are created by `SubstituteSurrogates.rawTemporaryName`.)

There is no mechanism in place that ensures these actually never conflict with real column names.

Conflicts can occur, as seen in this union types example:

```
curl -u elastic:password -H "Content-Type: application/json" "127.0.0.1:9200/testidx?pretty" -XPUT -d '
{"mappings": {"properties": {"client_ip": {"type":"ip"}}}}'

curl -u elastic:password -H "Content-Type: application/json" "127.0.0.1:9200/testidx2?pretty" -XPUT -d '
{"mappings": {"properties": {"client_ip": {"type":"keyword"}}}}'

from testidx* | eval `$$client_ip$converted_to$ip` = \"1.1.1.1\"::ip | eval x = client_ip::ip | eval y = `$$client_ip$converted_to$ip`

->
"illegal_state_exception","reason":"Found 1 problem\nline 1:70: Plan [Project[[client_ip{f}#80, $$client_ip$converted_to$ip{f}#81 AS x, $$client_ip$converted_to$ip{r}#73 AS y]]] optimized incorrectly due to missing references [$$client_ip$converted_to$ip{f}#81]"}]
[... 9 more lines]
```

I see two options to fix this:
1. Disallow using a specific identifier pattern that is reserved for internal use only (e.g. `\$\$.*\$.*\$.*` which we use right now); **technically a breaking change**
2. Append a unique counter or id (uuid?) to generated names.
3. Stop relying on names in logical plans and instead rely on attributes' name ids. (Bigger change overall)

ES|QL: Make date_range groupable

`date_range` supports `==` and is not groupable. Its sibling `double_range` has been groupable since 9.6.

`BlockHash.newForElementType` rejects `ElementType.LONG_RANGE`, so a `date_range` grouping key has no hash yet. #166846 keeps `date_range` non-groupable and pins it as a type that has `==` but cannot group. This issue is the follow-up to mirror the `double_range` grouping support.

ES|QL: Revisit Join.UNSUPPORTED_TYPES against groupable types

`Join.UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` is still a separate list from `DataType.isGroupable()`. It rejects some types that are groupable (`text`, `version`, `unsigned_long`, the spatial and grid types, `flattened`, `histogram`, `dense_vector`, `double_range`, `_source`, `_tsid`, and others) for join-specific reasons, such as the missing `VERSION` term query noted in `Join.postAnalysisVerification`.

#166819 was the only issue tracking that list. #166846 makes grouping eligibility a property of the data type and leaves `Join.UNSUPPORTED_TYPES` unchanged. This issue is the follow-up: decide which of those rejections are still required, and which groupable types a join should accept.

Search phases drop the cancellation reason from TaskCancelledException

In most places where search code throws `TaskCancelledException`, the task's cancellation reason is available but dropped, and a generic message is thrown instead.
For example:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/b9891857a49d/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/search/aggregations/bucket/BucketsAggregator.java#L167-L169

Without the reason, a client can't tell whether its own request was cancelled or it inherited another client's cancellation, as in #157302 (#157457 fixed that path, but the reason is still lost everywhere else).

`DfsPhase` already throws `getTaskCancelledException()` (since #155800).
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/b9891857a49d/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/search/dfs/DfsPhase.java#L88-L90
The proposed change applies the same pattern to the other phases.

About 14 call sites need the fix, in three areas:

- Fetch and rank-feature phases
- Shard-side aggregations
- Reduce side

@mitar asked for this in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157302#issuecomment-5361019099

I'd like to work on this. If the approach sounds right, I'll start with the fetch and rank-feature phases and do the other two areas in follow-up PRs, or do it as a single PR if the team prefers.

ESQL: a field's other types are lost when one of its types is unsupported

When a field has an unsupported type (such as `rank_feature`) in at least one of the queried indices, ES|QL reports it as unsupported with a single original type, and loses the rest:

- If the other indices map it to **another unsupported type** (`rank_features`), only one of the two types is reported, in `original_types` and in error messages. Which one depends on the order of the indices in `FROM`.
- If the other indices map it to a **supported type** (`long`), the supported type isn't reported at all. The field looks like a plain `rank_feature` field, its values are `null` even in the `long` index, and the error says nothing about the `long` mapping.

For comparison, a conflict between two supported types reports both types, with the indices for each.

Reproduced on 9.5.7; the code is the same on `main`.

```
PUT origtypes_rank_feature
{"mappings": {"properties": {"id": {"type": "keyword"}, "f": {"type": "rank_feature"}}}}

PUT origtypes_rank_features
{"mappings": {"properties": {"id": {"type": "keyword"}, "f": {"type": "rank_features"}}}}

PUT origtypes_long
{"mappings": {"properties": {"id": {"type": "keyword"}, "f": {"type": "long"}}}}

PUT origtypes_keyword
[... 11 more lines]
```

**Two unsupported types: only one is reported, and which one depends on the index order**

| Query | `f` column | Error |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM origtypes_rank_feature,origtypes_rank_features \| KEEP id, f` | `"type": "unsupported", "original_types": ["rank_features"]` | |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_features,origtypes_rank_feature \| KEEP id, f` | `"type": "unsupported", "original_types": ["rank_feature"]` | |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_feature,origtypes_rank_features \| EVAL x = f::keyword` | | `Cannot use field [f] with unsupported type [rank_features]` |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_features,origtypes_rank_feature \| EVAL x = f::keyword` | | `Cannot use field [f] with unsupported type [rank_feature]` |

**A supported and an unsupported type: the supported one disappears**

| Query | `f` column | Values / error |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM origtypes_long \| KEEP id, f` | `"type": "long"` | `["long_doc", 42]` |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_feature,origtypes_long \| KEEP id, f \| SORT id` | `"type": "unsupported", "original_types": ["rank_feature"]` | `["long_doc", null]`, `["rank_feature_doc", null]` |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_feature,origtypes_long \| EVAL x = f::long` | | `Cannot use field [f] with unsupported type [rank_feature]` |
| `FROM origtypes_rank_feature,origtypes_long \| WHERE f > 1` | | `Cannot use field [f] with unsupported type [rank_feature]` |

**For comparison, two supported types: both are reported**

| Query | `f` column | Error |
|---|---|---|
| `FROM origtypes_long,origtypes_keyword \| KEEP id, f` | `"type": "unsupported", "original_types": ["keyword", "long"], "suggested_cast": "keyword"` | |
| `FROM origtypes_long,origtypes_keyword \| WHERE f == "hello"` | | `Cannot use field [f] due to ambiguities being mapped as [2] incompatible types: [keyword] in [origtypes_keyword], [long] in [origtypes_long]` |

- `original_types` lists every type the field has, for example `["rank_feature", "rank_features"]` or `["long", "rank_feature"]`, regardless of the order of the indices.
- Error messages name all of them, ideally with their indices, as type conflicts already do.

Open question: when a supported type is listed next to an unsupported one, `suggested_cast` should probably still be omitted. No cast can read the unsupported indices today, and `DataType.suggestedCast` ignores names that aren't ES|QL types, so `["long", "rank_feature"]` would suggest `keyword`.

`IndexResolver` stops looking at a field's types as soon as it sees an unsupported one:

- `createField` compares ES|QL types ([`IndexResolver.java:911-915`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3434068257bc94aa9282ddae5476a2899162ae76/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/session/IndexResolver.java#L911-L915)). `rank_feature` and `rank_features` are both `UNSUPPORTED`, so it detects no conflict and builds the field from a single index's capabilities.
- `conflictingTypes` returns `unsupported(name, fc)` at the first index with an unsupported type ([`IndexResolver.java:1103-1106`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3434068257bc94aa9282ddae5476a2899162ae76/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/session/IndexResolver.java#L1103-L1106)). The other indices' types, including supported ones, are dropped.

- **DEDUP:** #164589 (DEDUP rejects union-type columns) treats a column as a type conflict when `originalTypes().size() > 1`, and ignores single-type unsupported columns because they're always `null`. With this fixed, a `rank_feature` + `rank_features` column would have two original types while still being always `null`, so DEDUP's rule should become "ignore the column when all its types are unsupported", whatever the count.
- **Lenient casts:** the lenient casts work for #144400 keeps the per-index types internally, so casts over a `long` + `rank_feature` field convert the `long` indices. It doesn't change `original_types`, and for a field whose only types are different unsupported ones, its cast warning names only the reported type.
- **Related:** #145916 (sub-fields of unsupported fields), #146790 (column metadata in the response).

Change mutateInstance overrides that replace the whole instance

`mutateInstance` exists so a serialisation test can prove `equals` and `hashCode` notice a change. A correct implementation copies the object and changes only one field. Each run picks a different field, so over many test runs every field is checked. If equals or hashCode ignores a field, that run fails, and you can see which field was missed.

Two shortcuts hide that bug. Building a brand new random object, or calling `randomValueOtherThan` to get any other object, only proves that two different objects are not equal. They can differ in several fields at once, so a field that equals ignores never gets caught.

This ticket is to fix existing tests that break this convention

`completion` field expands dotted keys depending on `subobjects`

The `completion` field's object format has a nested `contexts` object (`{"input": ..., "weight": ..., "contexts": {...}}`). `CompletionFieldMapper` doesn't call `context.path().setWithinLeafObject(true)` while parsing its value. So whether `DotExpandingXContentParser` expands dotted keys inside the value depends on where the field is mapped, not on the field itself:

- **Subobjects enabled (default):** dotted keys are expanded into objects.
- **Subobjects disabled** (an object with `subobjects: false`, a `passthrough` object, or a strict columnar index mode): dotted keys reach the parser verbatim.

This has two visible effects:

1. `"contexts.place_type": "cafe"` is silently accepted as `"contexts": {"place_type": "cafe"}` with subobjects enabled, but rejected with subobjects disabled.
2. A context whose name contains a dot, e.g. `place.kind`, can't be used with subobjects enabled: `"contexts": {"place.kind": "cafe"}` is expanded to `place: {kind: "cafe"}` and rejected, while the same document is accepted with subobjects disabled.

This is the same bug as #167495 for `exponential_histogram`.

```
PUT test
{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "suggest": {
        "type": "completion",
        "contexts": [
          { "name": "place_type", "type": "category" },
          { "name": "place.kind", "type": "category" }
        ]
[... 33 more lines]
```

Dotted keys inside a `completion` value are kept verbatim regardless of `subobjects`: documents 1 and 2 are rejected, documents 3 and 4 are accepted. The fix is to set `withinLeafObject` while parsing the value, as `flattened`, `sparse_vector`, `rank_features` and (with #167495) `exponential_histogram` do.

[ML] ES|QL datafeeds: an outer LIMIT below 10000 silently caps every extraction chunk

ES|QL datafeeds treat the query as a black box: ML appends `| SORT <time> ASC | LIMIT 10000` to every extraction query and parses nothing. An outer `LIMIT` in the user query that is smaller than 10000 therefore comes first in the pipeline and silently caps every extraction chunk.

For `FROM logs | LIMIT 20`:

- Every chunk returns at most 20 rows. The rows are arbitrary, because the cap applies before the `SORT`.
- The row count stays below 10000, so the truncation check never fires. There is no chunk shrink, no incomplete interval and no audit message.
- The lookback summary counts at most 20 output rows, so the chunk span is sized too large.
- The delayed data check is capped the same way.
- The same applies to a manual `chunking_config.time_span` with `SORT ... | LIMIT 1`: one row per window instead of one per chunk.
- With `SORT @timestamp DESC | LIMIT 1`, the lookback summary sees only the newest row, so the chunker starts at that row and never queries earlier chunks.

PUT used to warn about an outer `LIMIT`. That warning was removed in #167093 because it needs a scan of the query text, which the black-box approach avoids.

Options: detect a trailing `LIMIT` through the ES|QL planner, for example with a `DESCRIBE` attribute, and reject it or warn at PUT. Or document that an outer `LIMIT` is not supported in an ES|QL datafeed query.

Evaluate enabling `_id` bloom filter by default on stateful data streams

Follow-up to #167480, which exposes the `_id` bloom filter on stateful data streams as an opt-in. This issue decides whether to turn it on by default.

1. Benchmark a stateful logging workload with explicit and auto-generated IDs, covering random IDs (fingerprint hashes) and sequential ones (Kafka offsets).
2. Set the default from the results. Serverless already has the filter on ([#164678](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/164678)), so a different stateful default needs a reason.

An index can mix explicit and auto-generated IDs, and index metadata doesn't record which an index uses, so the default can't be chosen per workload.

Allow `_id` bloom filter opt-in on stateful data streams

[#164678](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/164678) enabled the `_id` bloom filter for data streams on stateless. Stateful data streams can't enable it. Expose it on stateful as a per-index opt-in. Whether to turn it on by default is tracked separately in #167482.

Indexing with an explicit `_id` does a version lookup in every segment. The `_id` bloom filter is on by default for regular indices (8.5, [#88409](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/88409)) and time series data streams (8.7, [#92115](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/92115)), but not for standard or LogsDB data streams, which are assumed to use auto-generated IDs. Not all do:

- Pipelines that supply deterministic IDs for idempotent retries, such as Kafka Connect's topic/partition/offset IDs. Moving one of these workloads (several TB/day) from alias-backed indices to a standard data stream has been reported to roughly double indexing CPU and latency.
- 311 of 1,340 data streams in elastic/integrations set `_id` with the `fingerprint` processor. None are TSDB, so on stateful none of them get the filter.

Expose the existing setting on stateful so users can enable the `_id` bloom filter on data stream backing indices through index templates. The default stays off.

9.6 if feasible, otherwise 9.7.

ES integration tests silently ignore Elasticsearch-specific formats

By default, `ESIntegTestCase` uses [`lucene_default` codecs](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/test/framework/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/test/ESIntegTestCase.java#L485) - this means it uses codecs from lucene, and not from Elasticsearch.

This is a trip hazard - if ES has a custom format for something, you need to remember to add `SuppressCodecs("*")` to the test class to actually test ES-specific codecs, or override the codec some other way. Integration tests are not actually testing what they should be testing.
