ESQL: INTO planning-time checks run before authorization

Part of #167141.

`INTO` writes with the caller's privileges, and a caller who may not write must learn nothing about the destination. That does not hold for the planning-time checks.

Authorization for the destination only happens at runtime, when the first bulk is sent with the caller's privileges. Everything `INTO` checks before that reads the cluster-state snapshot directly (`AnalyzerContext.projectMetadata()`), which security does not filter. A `ROW` source needs no index privilege, so any caller who can run `_query` can probe any destination name with `ROW ... | INTO <name>`.

**Already on `main`.** `IntoPageWriter.Factory.requireBatchDestination` reports destination-specific errors ("does not support ingest pipelines", "does not support indices that route from _source") before any authorization. It already carries a TODO for this. `EsqlSession` also rejects a destination that the query itself reads, and says whether it exists, before authorization.

**Planned planning-time mapping check** (sub-issue "ESQL: INTO mapping checks") would resolve the destination (index, alias write index, data stream, or the matching V2/V1 template when the index does not exist) and report whether the name exists and is a data stream, its field names and types, its `dynamic` and `_source` settings, and the merged mappings of a matching template. By varying the columns of a `ROW`, a caller could binary-search the full mapping.

**Required ordering.** The caller's write access to the destination has to be authorized before `requireBatchDestination` and the mapping check run. An unauthorized caller must get the same generic denial the bulk would return, indistinguishable from a missing destination. Neither check may report anything destination-specific until then.

**Exposure.** `INTO` is snapshot-only (`INTO_COMMAND` is `Build.current().isSnapshot()`), so nothing leaks in released builds today. This needs to be resolved before technical preview.

Add a ColumNAR format version that does not write null slots

The ColumNAR string column records null array elements. #165909 drops them at indexing and #167450 enforces that in the mappers, so after both the codec receives no null for an index on the new `IndexVersion`. The representation of a null then only costs bytes, code and test surface in the new write format.

ColumNAR ships in 9.6 and is enabled by default for `keyword`, `text` and `match_only_text` in `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar`. Indices created with it can hold null slots, so the representation is a persisted format. This issue adds a format version that does not write it. It depends on #167450. Part of #166867.

- **Payload:** a null slot is `[vint 0]` and a real length is stored plus one, so `0` can mean null. This keeps `[null]` distinct from an absent field (`StringBinaryPayload`).
- **Metadata:** the column stores `numNullSlots` for every layout (`StringColumnMetadata`).
- **Layouts:** the dictionary layout reserves ordinal `0` as `NULL_ORDINAL`. The plain layout keeps a null table.
- **Write and merge:** `StringColumnWriter` counts and writes null slots. `ColumNARDocValuesConsumer` sums `numNullSlots` of its inputs into the totals and carries the counts through `StringColumnValues`.
- **Read:** `PlainStringColumnReader`, `DictionaryStringColumnReader` and `ColumnarStringBinaryDocValues` test each slot with `isNullSlot` and skip or count it.

Numeric null positions are outside this issue. They belong to the mapper policy of #167450 and the numeric workstream (#164320).

- A new `FormatVersion` constant becomes `CURRENT`. `ColumnarCodecUtil#checkHeader` accepts files in `[BASELINE, CURRENT]`, so an older reader rejects the new files with a typed exception instead of misreading them.
- A segment written in the new version has no null slot encoding, no null count in the metadata, no `NULL_ORDINAL` and no null table.
- A document with no remaining value has no doc-values entry.

The `IndexVersion` that activates null dropping in the mappers (#167450) also activates the new write format, so the mapper and the codec agree on whether a null reaches the codec. No ColumNAR-specific activation mechanism is added. The constant is added with the implementation.

- `ColumnarDocValuesFormatSelector#writeVersion` maps the index creation version to a write version, and `select` builds the format of an index with it. A flush and a merge of the same index therefore write the same version. `writeVersion` gains a branch for the new `IndexVersion`.
- An index created before the new `IndexVersion` keeps writing the legacy format, null slots included, through flushes and merges and after a cluster upgrade. A data stream moves to the new format on rollover. Shrink, split and clone keep the creation version of the source index.
- `MetadataCreateIndexService` gives a new index the lower of the current index version and the highest one that every data node supports, so no index uses the new format before all data nodes can read it.
- A temporary feature flag gates the development until the `IndexVersion` exists. The `IndexVersion` gate is permanent.

- Readers keep decoding every older version, including segments with null slots. Legacy decoding is not removed.
- The format version of the target writer decides a merge. A merge into an older version preserves null slots. A merge into the new version never writes one. It discards legacy null slots and keeps the relative order and multiplicity of the remaining values. A legacy document that holds only nulls has no remaining value, so the merge cursor skips it and it has no doc-values entry. The totals of such a merge are computed from the filtered cursor, because the shortcut in `stringMergeCursor` sums the `numNullSlots` recorded by each input.
- Because the write version follows the creation version, an index writes one format for all its new segments, and the paths above keep the creation version. No production path that merges legacy segments into the new format has been found. Not verified: snapshot restore, CCR followers and an explicit `index.version.created`. The merge rule is therefore exercised in library tests with inputs built directly, and it is a safeguard for any path found later.

ColumNAR library tests, which need no Elasticsearch or Lucene structures:
- BASELINE and `VERSION_SKIP_INDEX_PLAIN` fixtures, and fixtures of the new version, in the BWC fixture test that the `FormatVersion` Javadoc requires before a bump merges.
- The new reader reads legacy segments with null slots and returns the same values as before.
- The new version writes no null slot encoding.
- Empty strings stay distinct from missing values, and a column that mixes null, empty and non-empty values round-trips, in both the plain and the dictionary layout.
- Merges of legacy into legacy, new into new and legacy into new inputs, including a legacy column that holds only nulls.
- A merge into the older version keeps null slots. A merge into the new version drops them, keeps order and multiplicity, filters out documents with no remaining value so that they have no doc-values entry, and computes correct column metadata. It covers mixed-version inputs and inputs with deletions.

Elasticsearch tests:
- `writeVersion` returns the legacy version for an index created before the new `IndexVersion` and the new one at or after it.
- On an index at the new `IndexVersion`, a document with no remaining value leaves no field-presence structure behind: no doc values, norm, term or point.

BWC tests:
- An index created before the new `IndexVersion` keeps the legacy format and null semantics after a rolling upgrade and after a full cluster restart.
- An index created after the upgrade, and a data stream after rollover, use the new format and semantics.

- No null slot encoding is written by the new format version.
- The requirements above pass.
- The library merge tests remain as a safeguard whether or not a production path merges legacy segments into the new format. If the investigation below finds such a path, the Elasticsearch tests also cover the norms, terms and points of a merged legacy null-only document, and any structure that still makes the field present is fixed. If no such path exists, no rewriting of norms, postings or points is required for it.

- Whether snapshot restore, CCR followers or an explicit `index.version.created` can place legacy segments in an index at the new `IndexVersion`.
- If such a path exists, what a merge into the new format leaves in norms, terms and points for a legacy null-only `text` document.

Enforce null dropping in the mappers for strict columnar index modes

#165909 defines the null semantics of the strict columnar index modes: null array elements are dropped after `null_value`. Today the null decision is spread over the mappers, the batch path and the codec, and the codec side keeps the null positions. The regular and the batch indexing path give different results for the same document, as in #166893, where `text` with `[null]` matches `exists` on the regular path and not on the batch path.

This issue implements #165909 in the mappers. #167451 is the follow-up in the codec and depends on this issue. Part of #166867.

The mappers own the logical null policy and the codecs own the physical representation. A null that remains after `null_value` is dropped before the values and the reconstruction metadata reach the codec. Every codec then receives the same logical values:
- `ES819` `.offsets` keeps what is needed to rebuild order and duplicates and, on an index at or after the new `IndexVersion`, no longer records null positions.
- ColumNAR receives the same values and stores them in its own representation.

One index holds both codecs, and the `_source` must not depend on which one a field uses.

The `null_value` handling does not change. A field with `null_value` still indexes the configured value in place of a null, and only the nulls that remain after that are dropped.

Regular indexing, batch indexing and the fallback from batch to regular apply one policy. A bulk request is mapped by batch only when every field and document supports it, so one unsupported field sends the whole bulk to the regular path. Today a null element of a leaf array that the batch path writes through `ColumnarOffsetsBuilder` turns the element column into a union, and the batch falls back to the row path. The policy must give the same result whether or not that fallback stays.

The policy applies to strict columnar indices created at or after the new `IndexVersion` planned for 9.7 (see #166867). An index created before it keeps the legacy policy and keeps recording null positions. The same `IndexVersion` activates the new ColumNAR write format (#167451). The mapper reads the version from `DocumentParserContext#indexSettings`, as other mappers do for earlier gates. A temporary feature flag gates the development until the `IndexVersion` exists.

- `MultiValuedBinaryDocValuesField#keepsNullSlot` is the shared predicate. For a strict mode it returns true when the null is an element of the field's own array, so the null keeps a slot. The policy of this issue makes it return false for a strict mode index at or after the new `IndexVersion`. It keeps returning what it returns today for earlier indices and for every other index mode.
- `FieldArrayContext#recordNull` and the `.offsets` encoding. The `_ignored_source` fallback of an oversized offsets array writes explicit nulls for null slots. It stops doing so on an index at or after the new `IndexVersion`, and keeps doing so on earlier indices.
- `ColumnarBinaryDocValuesField#recordNull` and `MultiValuedBinaryDocValuesField.ArrayOrderInlineNull#recordNull`.
- The mappers that record nulls: `KeywordFieldMapper`, `TextFieldMapper`, `NumberFieldMapper`, `DateFieldMapper`, `BooleanFieldMapper`, `IpFieldMapper`.
- `FlattenedFieldParser`, for null keys and elements.
- The batch path in `org.elasticsearch.escf`: `ColumnarOffsetsBuilder` and `NumberColumnTransform`.
- `ColumnarPayloadBinaryDocValuesSyntheticFieldLoaderLayer`, which reads the null slot count when it rebuilds `_source`.

On an index at or after the new `IndexVersion`, a document whose values are all dropped has no value for the field. It writes no doc values, no norm, no terms, no point and no `.offsets` entry, so `exists` and every other consumer treat the field as absent.

- **Norms:** on the regular path `text` with `[null]` gets a norm of 0, and on the batch path no norm (#166893). Neither path writes one on the new `IndexVersion`.
- **Points:** a document with doc values but no point for a point-indexed field is rejected by Lucene. A dropped null writes neither, so the conflict that #165514 worked around does not arise for it.
- **Ignored values:** a value dropped by `ignore_above` or `ignore_malformed` occupies no offsets slot and is recorded relative to the next slot. On the new `IndexVersion` slots count only values that remain.

- The cases of #165791 muted for #165909 and #166893 are unmuted and pass on an index at the new `IndexVersion`, on both indexing paths.
- On an index created before the new `IndexVersion`, each indexing path keeps its existing behavior for a null array element, including after a flush and a merge.
- An oversized `.offsets` array that moves to `_ignored_source` reconstructs correctly on both versions.
- On an index at or after the new `IndexVersion`, regular indexing, batch indexing and the batch fallback produce equivalent results. An index created before it keeps its existing behavior, including any difference between the indexing paths. This issue does not fix legacy path differences.
- One contract test runs against both paths without duplicating its expectations.
- `ES819` and ColumNAR fields in one index return the same `_source` and the same `exists` result.
- A document with only nulls on a point-indexed field is accepted and does not match `exists`.
- Arrays that mix nulls, `null_value`, and values ignored by `ignore_above` or `ignore_malformed` reconstruct in order.
- A rolling-upgrade test shows that an index created before the new `IndexVersion` keeps the legacy semantics after the upgrade, and that an index created after it uses the new ones.

Compound retrievers ignore the request _slice when filling their rank window

An agent alerted me to this while looking at removing the support for `_all` slice queries. Here is the generated summary of the issue:

>
> ### Elasticsearch Version
> main (observed at 48af2d7c5ba1)
>
> ### Description
>
> A search that names a slice on a slice-enabled index applies the slice filter to its own query, but a compound retriever (`rrf`, `linear`) runs its inner retrievers as separate searches over the point in time it opens, and those inner searches carry no slice. Each inner retriever therefore ranks documents from every slice, and documents of other slices take the places in `rank_window_size`.
>
> The final `RankDocsQuery` runs under the request's slice filter, so the other slices' documents are dropped from the response. The documents of the requested slice that lost their place in the window are not lost, because the rank docs query also matches them through its tail clause, but they come back with a score of `0` and in tail order instead of their fused rank. With a window of `n` and more than `n` better-scoring documents in other slices, the requested slice gets no fused ranking at all.
>
> ### Steps to Reproduce
>
> ```
>   - do:
>       indices.create:
>         index: sliced
>         body:
>           settings:
>             index.slice.enabled: true
>             number_of_shards: 1
>           mappings:
>             properties:
>               text:

```

ES|QL: TBUCKET accepts an unsigned_long bucket count and reads its encoded value (2^63 + 6 acts as 6)

9.5.7 (build d16690c781d994379d7d7be885c266543c2f6991); also 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT from `main` (build 7bad05334106adbc8df326c8bfd0c4eda90325b7, 2026-11-24)

none (official docker image)

bundled JDK (`openjdk version "27.0.1.1" 2026-11-17`)

`TBUCKET(buckets, from, to)` documents `buckets` as `integer` (or `date_period` / `time_duration`), and a `double` is
rejected with `must be [integer, date_period or time_duration]`. An `unsigned_long` count is accepted, and the count
that is used is the value's internal encoding (the top bit flipped), not the value:

| buckets | buckets returned for one hour of per-minute data |
|---|---|
| `6` | 6 (10-minute buckets) |
| `9223372036854775807` (long) | 60 (1-minute buckets) |
| `9223372036854775814` (unsigned_long, 2^63 + 6) | 6, as for `6` |
| `9223372036854775808` (2^63) | 1 bucket, `2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` (yearly rounding) |
| `6::unsigned_long` | 1 bucket, `2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z` |
| `6.0` | type error |

Expected: a type error for `unsigned_long`, as for `double` (or the count read as its `unsigned_long` value).

`TBucket.resolveType()` checks the count with `dt.isWholeNumber() || DataType.isTemporalAmount(dt)`
([TBucket.java#L278-L286](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3385fe99e450dc4ca87cc6954db842b802a3a978/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/grouping/TBucket.java#L278-L286)),
which is true for `unsigned_long`. The function is then rewritten to `BUCKET`, whose `getDateRounding()` folds the count
with `((Number) buckets.fold(foldContext)).longValue()`
([Bucket.java#L849](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3385fe99e450dc4ca87cc6954db842b802a3a978/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/expression/function/grouping/Bucket.java#L849)),
and an `unsigned_long` literal folds to its sortable `long` encoding.

This is the `TBUCKET` counterpart of what #162881 fixes for `BUCKET` ("`unsigned_long` is rejected as the buckets
count/span"). That PR changes `Bucket.resolveType()` only; `TBucket` has its own `resolveType()`, which the PR does not
touch.

```
PUT tb_test
{"mappings": {"properties": {"@timestamp": {"type": "date"}}}}

POST tb_test/_bulk?refresh=true
{"index":{}}
{"@timestamp":"2024-05-01T10:00:00Z"}
{"index":{}}
{"@timestamp":"2024-05-01T10:01:00Z"}
... (one document per minute up to 2024-05-01T10:59:00Z)

[... 8 more lines]
```

Results (9.5.7 and 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT):

```
buckets = 6, lo = 2024-05-01T10:00:00.000Z
buckets = 6, lo = 2024-05-01T10:00:00.000Z
buckets = 1, lo = 2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
```

The same happens with only a few documents; the per-minute data only makes the bucket widths visible.

ES|QL: TO_INTEGER(unsigned_long) returns a negative integer for values >= 2^64 - 2^31 instead of null

9.5.7 (build d16690c781d994379d7d7be885c266543c2f6991); also 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT from `main` (build 7bad05334106adbc8df326c8bfd0c4eda90325b7, 2026-11-24)

bundled JDK (`openjdk version "27.0.1.1" 2026-11-17`)

`TO_INTEGER` (and the `::integer` cast) of an `unsigned_long` value rejects values from 2^31 up to 2^64 - 2^31 - 1
with the warning "out of [integer] range" and a null result, but for the top 2^31 values, 2^64 - 2^31 to 2^64 - 1,
it returns a negative integer (the value minus 2^64) with no warning:

| query | result |
|---|---|
| `ROW x = TO_INTEGER(2147483648)` | null, warning `[2147483648] out of [integer] range` |
| `ROW x = TO_INTEGER(18446744071562067967)` | null, warning `[18446744071562067967] out of [integer] range` |
| `ROW x = TO_INTEGER(18446744071562067968)` | `-2147483648` |
| `ROW x = TO_INTEGER(18446744073709551614)` | `-2` |
| `ROW x = TO_INTEGER(18446744073709551615)` | `-1` |
| `ROW x = 18446744073709551615::integer` | `-1` |
| `ROW x = TO_LONG(18446744073709551615)` | null, warning `out of [long] range` |

The same happens for an `unsigned_long` field (see the steps below), and inside expressions such as
`MEDIAN_ABSOLUTE_DEVIATION([0, 18446744073709551614, 5, 6]::integer)`, which returns `3.0`, the answer for
`[0, -2, 5, 6]`.

Expected: null and the "out of [integer] range" warning for every `unsigned_long` value above 2147483647.

The cause is `EsqlDataTypeConverter.unsignedLongToInt`
([source](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/3385fe99e450dc4ca87cc6954db842b802a3a978/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/type/EsqlDataTypeConverter.java#L980-L987)):

```
    public static int unsignedLongToInt(long number) {
        Number n = NumericUtils.unsignedLongAsNumber(number);
        int i = n.intValue();
        if (i != n.longValue()) {
            throw new InvalidArgumentException("[{}] out of [integer] range", n);
        }
        return i;
    }
```

For values >= 2^63 `unsignedLongAsNumber` returns a `BigInteger`, whose `longValue()` and `intValue()` both keep only
the low-order bits. For 2^64 - k with k <= 2^31 both are -k, so the check passes. `unsignedLongToLong` uses
`DataTypeConverter.safeToLong(Number)`, which handles the `BigInteger` case; `unsignedLongToInt` could do the same
(for example `safeToInt(safeToLong(n))`).

```
PUT ul_test
{"mappings": {"properties": {"u": {"type": "unsigned_long"}}}}

POST ul_test/_bulk?refresh=true
{"index":{}}
{"u": 1}
{"index":{}}
{"u": 2147483648}
{"index":{}}
{"u": 18446744071562067968}
[... 8 more lines]
```

Result of the first query (9.5.7 and 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT):

```
         u          |       i
--------------------+---------------
1                   |1
2147483648          |null
18446744071562067968|-2147483648
18446744073709551615|-1
```

with the warning `evaluation of [TO_INTEGER(u)] failed, treating result as null` / `[2147483648] out of [integer]
range` for the second row only. The second query returns `a = null` (with the warning), `b = -2147483648`, `c = -1`,
`d = -1`.

Update-by-query scripted deletes drop the seq_no/primary_term concurrency check

During code review for a slice PR, the Libra AI tool identified a pre-existing bug in the script reindexing logic: https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167212/changes#r4688040237. I had 🤖 analyze it too and create the below description.

> ### Description
>
> When an update-by-query script sets `ctx.op = "delete"`, `AbstractAsyncBulkByPaginatedSearchAction.ScriptApplier#requestFromOp` converts the prepared `IndexRequest` into a `DeleteRequest`. Update-by-query prepares the index request with `ifSeqNo`/`ifPrimaryTerm` from the search hit (`TransportUpdateByQueryAction#buildRequest`), but the conversion only copies `version`, which update-by-query does not set. The delete therefore runs with no concurrency check: if the document changed between the search and the bulk, the newer revision is deleted instead of a version conflict being reported.
>
> This is independent of slices and predates them; the conversion has looked like this for a long time. It was noticed in the review of #167212 (https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167212#discussion_r4688040237), which fixes a different field dropped by the same conversion.
>
> ### Fix
>
> Expose `ifSeqNo`/`ifPrimaryTerm` on `RequestWrapper` and copy them in the delete branch of `requestFromOp`. Reindex does not set them, so `UNASSIGNED_SEQ_NO`/`UNASSIGNED_PRIMARY_TERM` pass through unchanged there.
>
> ### Coverage
>
> A unit test on the conversion, and an update-by-query test that modifies a document after the search phase has read it (`conflicts: abort` default) and asserts a version conflict rather than a delete.
>

Batch indexing accepts unmapped empty object under dynamic: strict

In strict-columnar index modes, the batch indexing path accepts a document that the sequential (row) path rejects: an unmapped empty object under `dynamic: strict`.

With root `dynamic: strict`, indexing `{"host": "srv", "sibling": {}}` (where `sibling` is unmapped):

- **Row path**: `DocumentParser.parseObjectDynamic` calls `ensureNotStrict` before anything else and throws `StrictDynamicMappingException`.
- **Batch path**: `ShardBatchMapper.resolveMappers` skips every unmapped column whose present rows are all `{}` in strict-columnar modes, whatever the `dynamic` setting is, so the document is indexed.

The skip was added in #159069. Its comment says the sequential path produces nothing for an empty object "regardless of dynamic setting". That holds for `true` (strict-columnar flattens object mappers away) and `runtime` (no-op object mapper), but not for `strict`.

1. Create an index with `index.mode: columnar` and a mapping with root `"dynamic": "strict"` and one mapped field, e.g. `host: keyword`.
2. Bulk index `{"host": "srv", "sibling": {}}` through the batch path.
3. The document is accepted. Indexing the same document through the row path fails with `strict_dynamic_mapping_exception`.

Unit-level repro: `ShardBatchMapper.resolveMappers` on an `EscfBatch` of that document returns a non-null resolution, while `documentMapper().parse(...)` of the same source throws `StrictDynamicMappingException`.

This was found by a covering-array differential test between the two paths. It was initially masked because the rejected shapes shared one batch, so another rejected document made the batch path fall back for the whole batch. Sending one batch per rejected shape exposes it.

Exclude `dynamic: strict` from the empty-object skip so the batch falls back and the row path raises the error per document, matching how the `routing_path` case already falls back.

ES|QL: concurrent wide LOAD_ALL queries keep a minimal serverless search node out of the cluster for about two minutes

On a minimal serverless project (1 search pod, 1 vCPU and 2GB), 24 concurrent clients each running `SET unmapped_fields="LOAD_ALL"; FROM idx | LIMIT 5000` over 5,000 documents of 1,000 unmapped leaves (about 110MB of rows per query) make the search node lose its master. It stays out for 126 to 171 seconds. `FROM idx METADATA _source | LIMIT 5000` with the same shape loses the master too, but rejoins in 7 to 9 seconds.

**Evidence (QA, serverless `main` `2ddf7d0a`, two projects)**
- Node log: `[3] consecutive checks of the master node ... failed`, `master node changed`, `readiness change: masterElected=false`. The pod name and node id do not change, so it is a disconnection, not a restart.
- Clients get a proxy 429 "The requested resource is currently unavailable" or a 503 `no_shard_available_action_exception`, for all queries that start during the outage.
- The node rejoins within a second of the queries finishing.
- The request breaker works throughout: 429 `circuit_breaking_exception` at 614MB, no OOM.
- A single `LOAD_ALL` query takes about 20 s against 10 to 12 s, and a round of 24 takes about 229 s against about 59 s.
- The default `LIMIT` of 1,000 rows with 24 clients is fine.

**Not known:** why the node cannot answer the master's checks, and whether it happens on a bigger node. CPU saturation is a guess.

**Reproduce:** index 5,000 documents of `{"id": "<n>", "f<k>": 1, ...}` with 1,000 distinct names each into an index with `dynamic: false` and a mapped `id`, then run the query above from 24 threads at once.

Preserve slice routing when bulk-by-search scripts delete documents

Found a bug while working on https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167212. Fix should be fairly simple. Below is the :robot: description.

When a reindex or update-by-query script sets `ctx.op = "delete"`, `AbstractAsyncBulkByPaginatedSearchAction.ScriptApplier#requestFromOp` converts the prepared request into a `DeleteRequest`. The conversion copies the routing value but does not copy `routingFromSlice`.

For a slice-enabled target, the resulting delete is therefore treated as ordinary routing and rejected even though the request was correctly prepared with a slice.

This is a latent gap from adding slice provenance to bulk-by-search requests; it is not specific to the recent reindex script metadata changes.

The converted `DeleteRequest` should preserve both routing and its provenance:

```
delete.setRouting(request.getRouting());
delete.setRoutingFromSlice(request.isRoutingFromSlice());
```

- Unit test that `ctx.op = "delete"` preserves `routingFromSlice`.
- Integration coverage for a scripted delete against a slice-enabled index, covering reindex or update-by-query.

- [`runPolicyAfterStateChange`, line 417](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/02d170aef8f3d271a29994eae12055e2ef9c8921/x-pack/plugin/ilm/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/ilm/IndexLifecycleRunner.java#L417)

`IndexLifecycleService.triggerPolicies(state, true)` calls `runPolicyAfterStateChange` for every managed index each time the master processes a cluster state update. So every skipped index logs one INFO line per cluster state update, and the remaining path is the one that matters most.

Separately, these look like leftover clones that ILM will never process. If so, [elastic/elasticsearch#154690](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/154690) (orphaned fm-clone cleanup) would remove the source of the messages, but the log level should be fixed regardless.

TaskCancelledException in fetch, aggregation and reduce code says only "cancelled", without the reason

In most places where search code throws `TaskCancelledException`, the task's cancellation reason is available but dropped, and a generic message is thrown instead.
For example:
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/b9891857a49d/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/search/aggregations/bucket/BucketsAggregator.java#L167-L169

Without the reason, a client can't tell whether its own request was cancelled or it inherited another client's cancellation, as in #157302 (#157457 fixed that path, but the reason is still lost everywhere else).

`DfsPhase` already throws `getTaskCancelledException()` (since #155800).
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/b9891857a49d/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/search/dfs/DfsPhase.java#L88-L90
The proposed change applies the same pattern to the other phases.

About 14 call sites need the fix, in three areas:

- Fetch and rank-feature phases
- Shard-side aggregations
- Reduce side

@mitar asked for this in https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/157302#issuecomment-5361019099

I'd like to work on this. If the approach sounds right, I'll start with the fetch and rank-feature phases and do the other two areas in follow-up PRs, or do it as a single PR if the team prefers.

Preserve ingest pipeline behavior when OTLP metrics uses ESCF

An OTLP metrics export should continue to run the destination’s configured ingest pipelines when ESCF batch indexing is enabled. Enabling ESCF should preserve the indexed result, including any field changes or rerouting performed by the pipeline.

Today, an otherwise eligible export can build an ESCF batch before bulk resolves the default or final pipeline. If either pipeline applies, bulk rejects the entire export before any processors run with `bulk with pre-built source batches cannot run ingest pipelines`. The same export can succeed through the existing document path.

Before enabling ESCF by default for OTLP metrics in 9.7, verify that exports succeed and pipeline effects are visible with `index.default_pipeline` and `index.final_pipeline` configured independently.

Add initial batch indexing support for nested field type in indices with strict columnar index modes

`ShardBatchMapper#resolveMappers` sends a whole batch to the sequential path when the mapping has any `nested` mapper, even if no document in the batch uses it. Nested is legal in all strict-columnar modes (`columnar`, `logsdb_columnar`, `vectordb_columnar`), so these indices currently get no batch indexing at all. We want to add nested support for strict-columnar modes only, and we keep the existing columnar limits (no `copy_to`, no dynamic mapping on the batch path, and so on). Note that `include_in_parent` / `include_in_root` are out of scope, because strict columnar will reject them (elastic/elasticsearch#166393).

The detailed plan (design, files, verification) is in the first comment on this issue. It is the source of truth if the two differ.

The ESCF encoder runs on the coordinator and does not use the mapping. So an array of nested objects reaches the shard as one opaque `UNION` column of `KEY_VALUE` blobs, and the object spelling (`{"n":{"b":1}}`) reaches it as ordinary leaves under `n`. We shred on the shard first. Shredding on the coordinator needs a wire-format change and a transport version, the coordinator's mapping can lag behind the shard's, and one encoded batch serves every shard. A Phase 1 investigation decides whether the coordinator-side change is required.

For each nested path that a chunk uses, we build a **child batch**: a real `EscfBatch` whose rows are nested elements, not operations. We also build `parentOffsets`, which gives each operation its contiguous range of child rows in source order. The existing `resolveMappers` / `FieldMapper#mapColumnBatch` machinery then runs over the child batch without changes, so child fields stay column-major. Strict columnar keeps this simple: every nested mapper is a direct child of the root, nested inside nested is rejected, and a dotted sibling cannot alias a nested path.

Child documents carry the same metadata as on the row path, through a new `MetadataFieldMapper#postColumnarParseNested` hook:
- `_id`: the indexed identity term, plus binary doc values in columnar `_id` mode;
- `_nested_path`;
- `_seq_no` and `_version`, but no `_primary_term`;
- `_field_names`.

`_ignored` from child fields goes to the root document. Required fields are enforced per child document, and `columnar_stored` gets the children and the root as linked documents for its source blob.

Some shapes typically stay on the sequential path in v1. Each of them falls back for the whole chunk, so we never diverge silently:
- an object inside a nested element, which makes an extra level of Lucene documents under `subobjects: false`;
- a dotted key that crosses the nested boundary;
- null or scalar elements;
- unmapped child fields;
- numbers in blobs that a string-typed child field receives;
- more children than `index.mapping.nested_objects.limit`.

Lucene's `addBatch(ColumnBatch)` currently cannot write document blocks: it has no block boundaries, it does not call `setHasBlocks`, and every doc is its own parent. The engine's per-row write (`writeLuceneDocuments` → `addDocuments`) already handles blocks. So we split the work:
- **Phase 1** maps nested columnar and writes each operation as children-then-root through `addDocuments`. It needs no Lucene change. Sub-batches without nested values keep `addBatch`.
- **Phase 2** adds block boundaries to `ColumnBatch` in Lucene (`main`, backported to `branch_11x`, released in 11.0). Then ES maps the root and child columns into one physical document space, so that appends with nested use `addBatch` too.

Is Phase 1 faster? Partly. It removes per-document `DocumentParser` work on primaries and replicas, but the Lucene side stays per-document, and shredding adds a copy. We measure the column-mapping-plus-row-write pairing on the flat benchmark shapes before we enable Phase 1 for sub-batches with children.

Phase 0 changes no production code. The parity scenarios cannot pass before Phase 1, because the oracle fails when `resolveMappers` refuses a mapping. So we write them in Phase 0 but keep them disabled, and Phase 1 enables them.

- The order of child documents across different nested paths in one block: we use mapping order, and the row path uses JSON key order. We think nothing observable depends on it.
- ~~What does the sequential path do for a root dotted key that crosses the nested boundary, and for null elements?~~ Answered in #167226. A dotted key across the boundary trips an assertion in `DocumentParser#getLeafMapper`, the dotted value spelling indexes like the object spelling, a null element is skipped and a scalar element is rejected. The batch path falls back for all of them.
- Does the shredding cost eat the mapping gain? The Phase 1 investigation decides whether shredding on the coordinator (a wire-format change) is required, or a follow-up.
- ~~Is the rejection of `include_in_parent`/`include_in_root` gated by index version?~~ Answered in #167226 (via #167177). Yes, by `IndexVersions.COLUMNAR_REJECTS_NESTED_INCLUDE_IN_PARENT`. Older indices still accept the parameters, so the batch path keeps a fallback for them.

Preserve order and duplicates of multivalued fields in strict columnar index modes

In `columnar`, `logsdb_columnar` and `vectordb_columnar`, the reconstructed `_source` of a multivalued field keeps the relative order of its values and every occurrence of a repeated value (#166867). Both carry information that a reader of `_source` cannot recover: the points of a path, repeated measurements, a sequence of events. The strict modes do not accept `synthetic_source_keep`, so a user cannot choose to keep them.

The examples are in the contract of #166867.

This issue guarantees the sequence of the mapped values, not the exact original JSON representation. A documented normalization of a value stays: `geo_point` is returned with reduced precision and a date in its formatted form, and the expected value is the normalized one.

The issue is a parallel track. It does not depend on #167450 and #167451, and it interacts with null dropping only in inputs that mix nulls and repeated values, such as `["b", null, "a", "b"]`.

Confirmed on `main` (`00482515b8c0`) in the three modes, and in `columnar_stored` for `version`. The probe was not repeated since. The history of the `version` and `geo_point` mappers and of the multivalued doc values code shows no change to their ordering logic since that build.

- `version` returns the values sorted and deduplicated. `["2.0.0", "1.0.0", "2.0.0"]` is returned as `["1.0.0", "2.0.0"]`.
- `geo_point` returns the values sorted by their stored value and keeps the duplicates. `["40.0,50.0", "1.0,2.0", "40.0,50.0"]` is returned as `1.0,2.0`, `40.0,50.0`, `40.0,50.0`.

An ordinary index does the same for `version` with the default `synthetic_source_keep: none`, and for `geo_point` in every mode. Both fail the contract of this issue, not an earlier guarantee. `keyword` and `long` keep their input in the three modes.

```
PUT test
{
  "settings": { "index.mode": "columnar" },
  "mappings": { "properties": { "ver": { "type": "version" }, "geo": { "type": "geo_point" } } }
}

PUT test/_doc/1?refresh=true
{ "ver": [ "2.0.0", "1.0.0", "2.0.0" ], "geo": [ "40.0,50.0", "1.0,2.0", "40.0,50.0" ] }

GET test/_doc/1
```

A fix moves into its own issue if it needs a design or a compatibility gate (see Compatibility).

- Every field type that a strict mode accepts and that can hold several values, in all three modes.
- Synthetic source and `columnar_stored`.
- One run per codec setting of a field type.
- Both indexing paths. A YAML test cannot choose the path, so it uses the default and `index.batch_indexing: false`. Java tests use `IndexWriter#addDocument` and `#addBatch`.
- Shapes: sorted, reversed, unsorted, adjacent and non-adjacent duplicates, all equal, one element, a scalar, 300 elements, duplicates with nulls.
- Each case read before and after a force merge, and across segments.
- Expected values computed from the input, not from another read of the same index.
- Cases that contain nulls take their expectation from the null semantics of the index version, not from whether an ordering fix is enabled.

The fixes are independent of the null-removal `IndexVersion` of #167450. Two questions stay separate, and each implementation issue answers both for its fix:

- **Persisted format:** whether the fix changes what is stored. The confirmed failures lose the order because the stored values are sorted, and `version` also deduplicates, so a fix probably adds persisted data. A fix that only changes reconstruction may not need a new persisted-format version.
- **Observable semantics:** whether the `_source` of an existing index may change. This follows the compatibility policy that applies to the fix. If a gate is needed, it follows the creation-version model: an index created earlier keeps its behavior, and readers keep handling an index that has no order data.

- Complex and less common types: `text`, `match_only_text`, `flattened`, `binary`, `counted_keyword`, the range types, the other geo types and the histogram family. The order of their mapped values is not verified.
- Arrays that mix indexed values with values dropped by `ignore_above` or `ignore_malformed`. The ignored values are recorded relative to the slot of the next indexed value, so their position should survive. No test covers it.
- The flagged numeric codec (`index.binary_numeric_doc_values.enabled`), and the batch path against the document path.

- The tests above run in CI.
- Every failing case is muted with `awaits_fix` and links this issue, or the implementation issue once its fix has one.
- This issue closes when no case is muted and all pass.

Multivalued field semantics in strict columnar index modes

Give the strict columnar index modes (`columnar`, `logsdb_columnar`, `vectordb_columnar`) one codec-independent contract for the reconstructed `_source` of multivalued fields. Today the same field gives different answers depending on the reader, the field type and the indexing path:

- A `keyword` field holding `[null]` matches `exists`, but the `missing` aggregation counts it as missing and `value_count` counts no value (#165909).
- `version` returns its values sorted and deduplicated in the reconstructed `_source`, and `geo_point` returns them sorted (#166868).
- `text` holding `[null]` matches `exists` when indexed one document at a time and does not when indexed by batch (#166893).

**Contract.** These are the target semantics of the reconstructed `_source` of a multivalued field. Each sub-issue states its own compatibility gate. Null dropping is gated by the new `IndexVersion` planned for 9.7. The fixes for order and duplicates may have independent gates (#166868).

- Null elements are dropped after `null_value` is applied.
- A field with no remaining value is absent.
- The remaining values keep their relative order.
- Every occurrence of a repeated value is kept.
- A single remaining value is returned as a scalar.

| Input | `_source` |
|---|---|
| `["b", null, "a", "b"]` | `["b", "a", "b"]` |
| `[null, "a"]` | `"a"` |
| `["c", "a", "b"]` | `["c", "a", "b"]` |
| `["a", "a", "a"]` | `["a", "a", "a"]` |
| `[null]`, `[null, null]`, `[]` | absent |

Dropping nulls does not change how values kept by `ignore_malformed`, `ignore_above` or a similar mechanism are reconstructed. With `ignore_malformed`, `[null, "malformed"]` drops the null and still returns the ignored value. A documented normalization of a value stays, for example the reduced precision of `geo_point`.

The contract holds in the three modes, for all supported field types, for regular indexing, batch indexing and the fallback from batch to regular, for synthetic source and `columnar_stored`, and for every codec. Mappers own the logical null semantics and codecs own the physical representation, so the result does not depend on the codec. It is the same after a flush, a merge and across segments.

It can be stronger than the synthetic `_source` of an ordinary index, which sorts or deduplicates some field types by default. The strict modes do not accept `synthetic_source_keep`. A failure against the contract is a gap, not necessarily a regression.

**Out of scope.**
- `dense_vector` and `sparse_vector`, whose array is one atomic value, and `constant_keyword`, which rejects nulls.
- Order and multiplicity of query, aggregation and ES|QL results. The contract is about reconstructed `_source`.
- Other index modes, and any other change to mapping or source reconstruction.

**Compatibility.** The new null semantics and the new ColumNAR string format version are planned for 9.7. One new `IndexVersion` gates both, and the index creation version decides.

- An index created before it keeps the legacy mapper semantics and write format, also after a cluster upgrade and through merges.
- An index created at or after it uses the null-free semantics and the new format. A data stream adopts them on rollover.
- A new index gets the lower of the current index version and the highest one every data node supports, so no node receives the new format before all data nodes can read it.
- The codec keeps reading every older format version, including segments with null slots. A merge follows the format version of its target writer (#167451).

ColumNAR ships in 9.6 and is enabled by default for `keyword`, `text` and `match_only_text` in `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar`, so its null-slot representation is a persisted format.

A temporary feature flag gates the development and is removed before the change ships. The `IndexVersion` gate is permanent. The `IndexVersion` constant is added with the implementation.

- #165909: the null semantics, their observable behavior and the muted tests of #165791.
- #167450: enforce the null semantics in the mappers, for regular and batch indexing. Implements #165909.
- #167451: stop writing null slots in a new ColumNAR format version. Depends on #167450.
- #166868: order and duplicate preservation, starting with `version` and `geo_point`. Parallel to the null issues.

- All sub-issues are resolved.
- The tests of #165791 and of #166868 pass without mutes across the applicable configurations.
- A change of codec for a field type does not change its reconstructed `_source`.
- Indices keep or adopt the behavior according to their creation version (#167450, #167451).
- The temporary feature flag is removed, and the index mode and the `IndexVersion` decide.

Drop null array elements at indexing in strict columnar index modes

Strict columnar modes keep the position of a null array element so `_source` can return it. Most readers ignore these positions, so the same document gives different answers: an indexed `keyword` with `[null]` matches `exists`, but the `missing` aggregation counts it as missing, `value_count` and ES|QL `COUNT` count zero values, and ES|QL `MV_COUNT` of `["a", null]` is 1.

This issue owns the observable behavior. The mappers implement it in #167450 and ColumNAR follows in #167451. Part of #166867.

In `columnar`, `logsdb_columnar` and `vectordb_columnar`, indexing drops a null array element after any `null_value` is applied. `exists` matches when a field has at least one value after mapping. The order and the duplicates of the remaining values do not change (#166868).

| Input | `exists` | `_source` |
|---|---|---|
| `null`, `[]`, field missing | no | absent |
| `[null]`, `[null, null]` | no | absent |
| `["a", null, "b"]` | yes | `["a", "b"]` |
| `[null, "a"]`, `["a", null]` | yes | `"a"` |
| `null` with `null_value: NA` | yes | `"NA"` |
| `[null, null]` with `null_value: NA` | yes | `["NA", "NA"]` |
| `["a", null, "b"]` with `null_value: NA` | yes | `["a", "NA", "b"]` |
| `["a", null, "a"]` | yes | `["a", "a"]` |
| `[""]` | yes | `""` |

A field with no value after mapping has no doc values, no norm, no terms and no point for the document. `columnar_stored` builds the same source at index time, so it drops null elements too. `dense_vector`, `sparse_vector` and `constant_keyword` keep rejecting a null. Other index modes do not change.

The behavior applies to indices created at or after the new `IndexVersion` planned for 9.7. An index created before it keeps preserving null elements. The compatibility rules are in #166867.

The tests are in #165791. Each muted case was run without its mute and failed for the reason below.

- **`_source` reconstruction (71 cases):** null elements are preserved. Expected: they are dropped, so `["a", null, "b"]` returns `["a", "b"]`, also after repeated values and in `columnar_stored`.
- **`exists` and counts (29 cases):** a null-only field is treated as present. Expected: a document with `[null]` does not match `exists`, and has no doc values and no norm, on both `IndexWriter#addDocument` and `#addBatch`.
- **`flattened` (2 cases):** null keys and elements are preserved. Expected: they are dropped.

The counts come from the annotations in #165791 and change as tests are fixed.

Two related reports:
- #166893 (`exists` on `text` differs between the indexing paths) is fixed by the shared policy of #167450.
- #165521 (`exists` total smaller than the hits for documents that hold only nulls) assumed that such a document matches `exists`. It is reassessed per index version:
  - On the new `IndexVersion`, such a document has no doc values and no term, so the term count and the scorer should agree. The two `exists` count cases muted for #165521 in #165791 are the check once #167450 lands. This is not verified yet.
  - An index created before the new `IndexVersion` keeps its previous field-presence behavior, including the inconsistencies of #165521 and #166893. The result depends on the field type and the indexing path. A merge does not change it, because such an index keeps writing null slots. #165521 stays open for these indices unless it is fixed separately.

Evaluate null preservation in ColumNAR numeric fields without the `.offsets` companion

Tracked in `numeric/meta` (#164320). Depends on `numeric/wiring` (#164321).

Superseded by the null semantics of #166867: null elements are dropped (#167450), so numeric columns keep no null positions. Kept as history. It is not required work.

Optional, not a release gate. The `.offsets` companion that `numeric/wiring` writes is correct and is enough for the initial integration. This issue evaluates storing null positions in the ColumNAR column, so that synthetic `_source` does not need a second field in a second codec.

#165669 writes only non-null values to the ColumNAR payload and records null positions in `.offsets`, a `SORTED` field stored with `ES819`. In-payload nulls were tried there and reverted, because Lucene rejects a document that has doc values but no point for a field that declares points.

That constraint is narrow:

- `index` defaults to false in strict columnar modes. The field then has only `BINARY` doc values, and there is no conflict.
- An `index_terms` field can use the valueless-document handling that keyword uses (`ColumnarBinaryDocValuesField#typeWhenValueless`).
- With points, only a document with no non-null value, such as `[null]`, has the conflict. `[1, null, 2]` writes a point.

So `.offsets` is needed only for valueless documents of point-indexed fields.

- Carry the null positions of a document in the payload, as a trailer after the values.
- Store them in the column as an optional sparse stream, separate from the value stream. The value stream stays compact and non-null, and a column without nulls is written as today, byte for byte.
- Lazy access: queries, aggregations, sorting and ES|QL block loading must not read or decode the null positions. Only synthetic `_source` reconstruction and merges open the stream. A small amount of shared metadata at reader initialization is acceptable.
- `exists` keeps using numeric-value presence. A document that holds only nulls does not match. The doc-values iterator that Lucene queries see covers only documents with a value.
- Write `.offsets` only for a valueless document of a point-indexed field.
- Fix value addressing for a document with zero values. `NumericColumnWriter` tables value addresses only when `numValues > numDocsWithField`, so one document with zero values and one with two cancel out. Reproduced at the library level in #165522. No writer produces a zero-value payload today. This change makes it reachable, so decide the empty-payload contract in #165522 first.
- Bump the column format version. No BWC coverage is needed while the codec is behind `columnar_numeric_codec`. After the flag is removed this is a persisted-format change, so decide before then.

Open decision for point-indexed valueless documents: keep `.offsets` for them (proposal), change Lucene, or stop preserving `[null]` for these fields.

Write the columnar_stored _source blob directly from mapped values in batch indexing

Follow-up to #161466, which lets `columnar_stored` indices use columnar batch indexing. That PR rebuilds each row's `_source` blob by reassembling the row's Lucene fields and running the synthetic source loader, so it is correct but still pays per-document loader cost. This issue tracks writing the blob directly from the mapped values.

Based on two CPU profiles (async-profiler) of a bulk indexing benchmark on a `columnar_stored` index through the batch path.

The profile shows `SourceFieldMapper.postColumnarParse` at 22.0% (001) and 19.2% (002) of all samples. About 16 of those points are fixed per-document loader overhead (`reset`, `advanceToDoc`, `prepare`, `repopulate`, `RowCursor`), and only about 4 points are decoding and writing values. This design skips the loader pass for each row. Mappers hand the `_source` mapper a small writer over the data they already computed, and `postColumnarParse` writes the blob straight from those writers.

We call it a success when all of these hold:

- The blob is byte-for-byte equal to what the current loader path writes, for every supported mapper.
- `postColumnarParse` drops to roughly 6% of samples or less on the same benchmark. This is an estimate from the profile, not a promise.
- Docs per second on the benchmark improve end to end. We measure this separately, because CPU shares do not always match throughput.

The documented contract says columnar `_source` keeps leaf-array order, duplicates and nulls. Two rules in the current loader decide the output, and we copy each into exactly one shared place so they cannot drift:

1. **Scalar or array.** `CompositeSyntheticFieldLoader.write` sums the value counts of a field's layers. One value is written as a scalar and anything else as an array. A keyword payload with no non-null slot also counts as an array (`valueCount()` returns 2), and a single slot counts as a scalar.
2. **Layer order.** The document-values layer is written first, then the fallback layers (`ignore_above` originals, `ignore_malformed`, `on_failure`). A value dropped by `ignore_above` therefore comes after the indexed values in the array, not at its original position. We keep that behaviour.

Field keys come out sorted by path, as `ObjectMapper`'s loader does today. Columnar modes are flat, so there are no objects to open and close, and nested mappings already fall back before this point.

**1. A small `SourceColumn` interface.** It answers two questions per document: how many values the field contributes, and how to write them into an `XContentBuilder`. A `CompositeSourceColumn` holds a field's layers in loader order and implements the scalar-or-array rule once. Every writer is forward-only per document, so it can keep a cursor and never searches.

**2. Registration at map time.** `FieldMapper` gets `supportsColumnarSource()`, which defaults to `false`. A supporting mapper registers its writer from `doMapColumnBatch`, using the data it already built (for example, the keyword payload column, or the sortable-long column for numbers). That data is in the original source order, and the mapper has already applied `null_value`, `coerce` and `ignore_above`, so the writer reads the same values the loader would decode. No second pass over the input and no copy of values.

**3. Assembly in `SourceFieldMapper#postColumnarParse`.** If every mapped field registered a writer, we sort the writers by key once per batch. Then, per document, we write each column's values into one reusable builder, encode with `XContentDataHelper.encodeXContentBuilder`, and build the `_ignored_source` columns as the PR does today. If any field has no writer, the whole batch takes the existing loader path. The current implementation stays as the reference and as the fallback.

Eligibility works by default-deny. `FieldMapper#mapColumnBatch` marks the batch "direct source unavailable" whenever a non-multi-field mapper does not support it. This means a new mapper added later is correct without any change, only slower.

- Unknown layers: for each field we check its `syntheticFieldLoaderLayers()` against a short allow-list. A mapper that adds a layer we do not know falls back.
- Source filters (`includes`, `excludes`) and synthetic vector exclusions do not get a direct path in the first stages. Any mapping with those falls back.
- An exception from a writer is caught by the existing `catch` in `ShardBatchMapper#mapColumnBatch`, which falls back to the sequential path.
- An escape hatch: a dynamic node setting that forces the loader path, so support can switch it off without a release.

| Stage | Content | Why this order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Run the existing `*ColumnarCompatibilityTests` with `columnar_stored` settings against the current implementation. | Widens the oracle before we change anything. |
| 1 | `SourceColumn`, `CompositeSourceColumn`, eligibility and assembly, plus keyword and `long`. | Smallest set that exercises the whole design, and the likely dominant columns. |
| 2 | Re-profile. | Decides whether to continue (see below). |
| 3 | boolean, date, `ip`, then `double`, `float`, `half_float`, `scaled_float` and the other numeric types. | Each reuses the loader's own value writer, for example `NumberType::writeValue`, so formatting stays shared. |
| 4 | Fallback layers: `ignore_above`, `ignore_malformed`, `on_failure`, `null_value` cases. | The most likely place for subtle differences, so it gets its own stage and tests. |
| 5 | `text`, `match_only_text`, `wildcard`, `constant_keyword`, `geo_point`. | Less common, and some need the field's own formatter. |
| 6 | `flattened` (group mapper) and filter support, only if profiles justify them. | Most complex; may stay on the loader path. |

After stage 2 we compare against the estimate. If the gain is well below the roughly 14-point target, we stop and look at trimming the shared loader instead.

- **Differential:** for each stage, run the same documents through the loader path and the direct path and require equal blob bytes. The existing `AbstractColumnarMapperCompatibilityTestCase` already compares against the row path, so each mapper test class runs in `columnar_stored` mode.
- **Randomized:** one generator mixing scalars and arrays, nulls, empty arrays, absent fields, duplicates, over-long keywords, malformed values and `null_value`, across several field-type mixes.
- **Mapping-level:** a mapping with one unsupported field must fall back for the whole batch and still produce a correct blob.
- **End to end:** extend `BatchBulkIT#testColumnarStoredSourceBatchMode` with several field types and read the source back with a get, a search and a source filter.
- **Performance:** same benchmark and settings as the two profiles; report CPU share and docs per second.

- A writer and its mapper's loader can drift over time. The differential tests catch this for the cases they generate, and sharing the value writers where possible lowers the risk.
- A mapper's output data may not keep source order in some paths (for example when Lucene sorts values and a separate offsets column restores the order). For numbers the sorted order is rebuilt from offsets, so the writer must read the pre-sort data. We confirm this per mapper before writing its writer.
- The workload in the profiles has an unknown field mix. If it is mostly types we only add in stage 3 or later, the first gain is smaller than expected.

- What is the field mix of the benchmark used for the profiles? This decides the order inside stages 1 and 3.
- Is all-or-nothing per mapping acceptable, or do we need per-field mixing of loader and direct writers in one blob? Mixing is possible, because both emit sorted keys, but it adds merging logic.
- Should the escape hatch be a node setting or an index setting?
- Do we need a direct path for source filters at all? `columnar_stored` with `includes` and `excludes` may be rare enough to leave on the loader path for good.
- Should we reuse one `BytesStreamOutput` for the builder across documents? It looks safe, but I have not checked how `XContentDataHelper.encodeXContentBuilder` handles the buffer's lifetime.

ColumNAR adoption for `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar`

ColumNAR is a standalone doc-values library. This issue tracks adopting it for qualified field types in `index.mode=columnar` and `index.mode=logsdb_columnar`.

Field types qualify independently, by showing a measurable improvement over their current codec without regressing storage, indexing, merge, or query performance. Adoption is per index mode: once a field type is enabled for ColumNAR in a mode, all new indices in that mode use ColumNAR for it. The codec is fixed at index creation time and stays consistent across all segments of that index, so different field types in the same index may use different codecs.

ColumNAR is initially adopted for `keyword`, `text`, and `match_only_text` fields, while `ES819` remains the codec for other field types.

---

Required to enable ColumNAR by default in `columnar` and `logsdb_columnar` index modes.

Shared codec infrastructure required by numeric and keyword support.

---

Implement and benchmark keyword support. Depends on `codec/core`.

ColumNAR must support low- and high-cardinality keyword fields and select the encoding automatically at flush time from the observed distribution, with no mapping changes or user intervention.

---

Wire ColumNAR keyword into the server layer. Depends on `codec/core` and `codec/keyword`.

---

End-to-end Rally validation on representative LogsDB datasets; JMH qualification is covered by `codec/keyword`. Merge throughput is a first-class acceptance criterion alongside storage, indexing, and query performance. Depends on `server/keyword`.

---

New indices adopt the codec policy defined for their index mode and `IndexVersion`. Existing indices retain the policy they were created with, and data streams migrate through rollover. Rolling upgrades must preserve read compatibility for indices created with either policy. Depends on `validation/logsdb`.

---

Extend ColumNAR adoption to additional field types and ensure consistent semantics across strict columnar index modes. Each initiative owns its requirements, implementation, validation, compatibility and adoption readiness.

**Columnar GA:** Multivalued semantics (#166867) is required for GA of the `columnar` index mode. The other Phase 2 initiatives are not GA blockers and may be delivered independently.

Cross-cutting correctness for multivalued fields in the strict columnar index modes: consistent null, order and duplicate semantics across codecs. Tracked in `semantics/meta` (#166867), which holds the contract, the compatibility rules and the sub-issues.

---

Adopt ColumNAR for mapped `flattened` fields and the `_unmapped` sink, qualifying storage and performance against `ES819`. Depends on `codec/keyword` and `server/keyword`.

---

Adopt ColumNAR for numeric and date fields, qualifying each field type independently against `ES95`. Depends on `codec/core`.

---

Cross-cutting `_source` retrieval performance in the strict columnar index modes, independent of field-type qualification. Sets a baseline for synthetic `_source` reconstruction, with `columnar_stored` as comparison, and detects regressions as more field types adopt ColumNAR.

---

Independent optimization candidates. Optimizations that belong to one field type are tracked in that field type's initiative.

---

Native ColumNAR columns for further field types. Not required for the current initiatives.

Extend OTel and Prom entrypoints to columnar indexing

These protobuf entrypoints currently create docs using xcontent (cbor) that are then passed to data nodes and indexed one at a time. As we're adding columnar indexing capabilities, they can be adjusted to avoid unnecessary conversions to xcontent and index protobuf contents in bulk.

- **Read-path microbenchmark.** `FlattenedFieldExtractBenchmark` (#155925, made quicker in #157251) runs nightly in the `periodic-micro-benchmarks` pipeline. It compares three reads of a sub-key: the fused keyed doc-values load (`field_extract(root, "constant")`), loading the whole flattened root as a JSON blob and extracting the key per row, and loading the root alone as a baseline. The benchmark showed that the fallback is bound by doc-values term lookups, not JSON parsing.
- **Fusion widened** to `DISSECT`/`GROK`, `URI_PARTS`, `REGISTERED_DOMAIN`, `USER_AGENT` and `IP_LOCATION` (#156633), measured with the benchmark above.

   - the fallback path, which loads the whole flattened root per row: many documents with large flattened objects and a non-constant key, or a consumer that fusion doesn't cover;
   - `FIELD_EXTRACT` on a key with many values per document, since it returns all of them as a multi-value;
   - the dotted path, once it lands.
   The query should either finish or trip the circuit breaker cleanly, never OOM the node.
2. **End-to-end benchmark.** No Rally track contains an ES|QL query on a flattened field (elastic/rally-tracks has no `FIELD_EXTRACT` usage). Add ES|QL operations on realistic flattened data, for example Okta `okta.target` or HTTP headers, covering filter, `STATS ... BY` and `SORT` on a sub-key. Run them nightly so regressions show up in esbench. When the dotted path lands, add the same queries written with the path and compare.
3. **No regression for queries without flattened fields.** The PRD requires this. Once the dotted path changes name resolution, check that the existing ES|QL nightly benchmarks don't slow down. Cover queries on indices with and without flattened fields in the mapping.

ES|QL: IN subquery can fail when index.max_terms_count is below 100

An `IN` subquery with up to 100 values (`esql.in_subquery_hash_join_threshold`) keeps the values as an `IN` list. The data node can push the list to Lucene as a `terms` query. A shard rejects a `terms` query longer than `index.max_terms_count`, so the query fails when that setting is below the value count.

#167525 caps the threshold at that limit, but only for a positive `IN` on a plain key directly on a local index.

- A key behind `EVAL`, `KEEP`, `RENAME` or `SORT`. The data node moves the filter down and pushes it, but the planner does not see through those nodes.
- `NOT IN`.
- Remote indices. The remote limit is unknown on the coordinator.

Example (not reproduced yet, found by reading the code):

```
FROM idx | EVAL x = 1 | WHERE k IN (FROM other | KEEP k)
```

with `index.max_terms_count: 50` and 75 values.

- Look through those nodes in `AbstractInSubqueryJoin#indexedFilterSource`.
- Retry with a hash join when the shard rejects the query.
- Get the remote limit during resolution.

Relates to #167525, #166605, #165551

ES|QL: `MATCH` on dense `semantic_text` after `INLINE STATS` runs unfiltered KNN search

9.7.0 / Serverless (any build with `FULL_TEXT_FUNCTIONS_AFTER_INLINE_STATS`)

When `MATCH()` targets a dense `semantic_text` field (e.g. `.jina-embeddings-v5-text-small`, `.jina-embeddings-v3`, E5) **after `INLINE STATS`**, the underlying KNN search executes without any pre-filters across the entire shard.

Because the vector search ignores:
- filters before `INLINE STATS` (e.g. tenant/user/space filters, or the REST `filter` parameter),
- the `INLINE STATS` filter itself (e.g. keeping only the latest revision per `id` in an append-only data stream), and
- adjacent `WHERE` predicates,

it fetches only the global top `k = 10` nearest documents across the whole unfiltered shard (see also #137538) and then intersects them with the rows that survived the earlier stages. Any 10 higher-scoring filtered-out documents (other users, deleted/expired items, or older revisions) crowd out valid matches and cause the query to return **0 hits**.

`MATCH()` on a dense `semantic_text` field after `INLINE STATS` searches only within the documents that survived the earlier pipeline stages (or falls back to exact scoring over the surviving rows, as `KNN()` does when not pushed down).

`MATCH()` runs an unfiltered top-10 approximate KNN search over the entire shard and returns 0 rows whenever 10 filtered-out documents score higher than the matching document(s).

Because filters above `InlineJoin` cannot be pushed down, `MATCH()` runs via `LuceneQueryExpressionEvaluator` / `LuceneQueryScoreEvaluator` using a standalone `SemanticQueryBuilder` outside any `BoolQueryBuilder`. That leaves `KnnVectorQueryBuilder`'s `autoPrefilteringScope` empty, so HNSW runs completely unfiltered. (For comparison, `Knn#evaluatorQueryBuilder` avoids this by falling back to `ExactKnnQueryBuilder` when not pushed down.)

Use any dense embedding endpoint (e.g. `.jina-embeddings-v5-text-small`)

      "id": { "type": "keyword" },
      "user_id": { "type": "keyword" },
[... 7 more lines]
```

ES|QL: task descriptions include the full plan and shard list and are unbounded

The tasks that ES|QL registers expose very large descriptions through the Tasks API (see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167535 and https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/167717). They are built eagerly when the task is registered, kept for the lifetime of the task, and written out in full by every detailed `GET _tasks` / `GET _tasks/<id>`. For example:

- `DataNodeRequest#getDescription()` returns `"shards=" + shards + " plan=" + plan + ...`: the whole physical plan and the whole shard list for every data-node request. There is one such task per in-flight data-node request.
- `ClusterComputeRequest#getDescription()` returns `"plan=" + plan`.
- The user-facing query task (`EsqlQueryRequest#createTask`) is created with `queryDescription()`, the query text.
- etc.

A large query, a wide plan or many shards makes each description large, and a detailed task list multiplies it: the description on every node, the serialized node reply, the deserialized copy on the coordinating node, then the REST response. Repeated or concurrent `GET _tasks?detailed=true` against a cluster running many ES|QL queries can exhaust the heap of the coordinating node.

- #167717: general bound on task descriptions in the Tasks API
- #162349, #162131: same problem for reindex / update-by-query, fixed per request type
- #167535: charges node task replies to the in-flight breaker on the coordinating node (mitigates the coordinator side only)

Potential directions to consider:

1. Make the descriptions of `DataNodeRequest` and `ClusterComputeRequest` and other ES|SQL classes/stasks short summaries: for example the shard count and a bounded or hashed plan identifier, rather than the full plan and shard list.
2. Review the descriptions of the driver, group and query tasks for size on large plans, and bound them too.
3. Build descriptions lazily where the plan is only needed on request.
4. Check that the plan and query are still available where ES|QL needs them (the query/profile APIs, logs), so no diagnostics are lost.
5. Add a test with a large plan and many shards that checks the description stays under a fixed size.

Bound the size and number of task descriptions and details exposed by the Tasks API

Task descriptions are built eagerly from `TaskAwareRequest#getDescription()`, kept on the `Task` for its whole lifetime, and written out in full by every `GET _tasks?detailed=true` / `GET _tasks/<id>` call. Nothing bounds their size in general. Request types have been capped one at a time:

- #162349 / #162131: reindex and update-by-query script params (capped at 1024 chars after OOMEs when listing tasks)
- #22832: `IndexRequest#toString()`
- `BulkRequest` / `BulkShardRequest` return a short summary
- `SearchRequest` builds its description lazily
- `MasterService` caps pending-task descriptions at `MAX_TASK_DESCRIPTION_CHARS = 8 * 1024`
- ES|SQL ticket https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/167718

but any new action, or an existing one that has not been audited, can reintroduce the problem. Repeated or concurrent `GET _tasks?detailed=true` can exhaust the heap of the coordinating node. https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167535 attempts to at least account for that memory in a circuit breaker.

- Capping every description (for example at 1 KiB) bounds one task but not the response: there can be numerous tasks, and a detailed listing still scales with their number.
- The Tasks API is not intended to carry this level of detail. Long-standing needs for better ways to inspect and manage specific kinds of running work (such as ES|QL queries) are better served by their own APIs than by task descriptions.
- Fixing individual request types, as above, is whack-a-mole.

We do not have a settled solution yet. Directions to evaluate:

1. A general upper bound on the description exposed through the Tasks API (truncate with a marker, applied when building `TaskInfo` or at `Task` construction), so a new action cannot reintroduce the problem.
2. Build descriptions lazily (a supplier, as `SearchRequest` does) so they are not retained per task for the lifetime of the task.
3. Bound the size of one `_tasks` response: for example a node-level budget for the detailed reply, with a clear indication when it was cut short, or pagination.
4. A guard in the test framework that fails when a registered action returns an unbounded description.
5. Dedicated APIs for inspecting long-running work such as ES|QL queries, so the Tasks API does not have to carry plans and query text.

- Truncate silently, or flag truncation in the `TaskInfo` output?
- Does anything (Kibana, other tooling, support workflows) depend on the full description text? ES|QL descriptions in particular may be parsed or read by people.
- Is a bound on the number of tasks or on the response size acceptable for `GET _tasks`, which is currently unbounded?

ESQL: A common model for the children of maps and structs

Follow-up to #166713, which is being fixed in the smallest way first (keys from lookup indices and enrich policies).

ES|QL has no model for columns that have children. Objects are flattened into dotted column names with no parent, `flattened` keys are names that each shard answers on its own, and `nested` fields, Parquet `MAP` and `LIST<STRUCT>` are unsupported. Each new feature in this area has had to invent its own answer to the same questions.

One schema model, one type model and one resolution strategy for the children of maps and structs:

- **Maps** (`Map<K, V>`): an open set of keys and one value type. `flattened` today; later `rank_features`, `sparse_vector`, Parquet `MAP`.
- **Structs**: fixed fields, each with its own type. `nested` (a list of structs), Parquet `LIST<STRUCT>`. `object` and Parquet `STRUCT` are structs that ES|QL already flattens into columns.

What it has to answer:

- #167529: a tree model behind `SET map_types=true`. Children follow their parent through every command.
- #167714: the same model amended so that columns keep their names and win over keys. It needs no opt-in in a differential test against the behavior from before keys, at the price of a restriction under `unmapped_fields="load"`.
- A prefix rewrite before analysis (`middle_one.c.d` → `a.b.c.d`, each shard answers by its own mapping, an existing column wins) was proposed as a lighter alternative. It should be compared with the two drafts on the examples above.

- Syntax for keys that a dotted name cannot express (keys that contain dots, keys that are not strings).
- Performance of reading a key from a value: #150363.

PromQL: binary operator between aggregations fails with `Unknown column [value]` once a downsampled index is in the data stream

9.5.7

_bundled_

We ingest Prometheus metrics with remote write into `metrics-*.prometheus-*` data streams (built-in `metrics-prometheus@template`: one metric per document, `__name__` as a dimension) and query them from Grafana through `_prometheus/api/v1/query`.

As soon as a downsampled backing index (metrics mapped as `aggregate_metric_double`) became part of one of these data streams, **every binary operator between two aggregations started failing**, whatever the metrics or the time range:

```
sum(a) / sum(b)
sum(a) - sum(a)
max by (hostname) (a) / max by (hostname) (b)
```

**Expected:** the same results as before the downsampled index was added (e.g. `0.5` for `sum(a) / sum(b)` in the reproduction below), as `sum(a) / sum(b)` is documented as supported.

**Actual:**

```
{"status":"error","errorType":"bad_data","error":"Found 1 problem\nline 0:1: Unknown column [value]"}
```

- A single aggregation (`sum(a)`) and an aggregation with a number (`sum(a) / 2`) still work.
- The query fails even when the queried time range does not overlap the downsampled index.
- It also fails for metrics stored in *other* data streams: `_prometheus/api/v1/query` covers every `metrics-*` data stream, so a single downsampled index anywhere breaks binary operators for all metrics (reproduced by querying a freshly created data stream with no downsampled index while another data stream had one).
- On our cluster, the same query succeeds when the `PROMQL` command targets only the non-downsampled backing indices, and fails as soon as the downsampled one is included.
- Possible hint: with the downsampled index present, `scalar(sum(a)) / scalar(sum(b))` fails with `Unknown column [value], did you mean any of [value_$4, value_$3]?` (without it, this shape is rejected with the documented "grouping key [] cannot be used as an aggregate" limitation), as if the per-operand `value` columns were renamed while the binary operator still refers to `value`.

The same happens with the ES|QL `PROMQL` command:

```

Get settings `include_defaults` ignores node-derived index setting defaults

Index settings whose default is derived from node settings may report the wrong default in `GET /<index>/_settings?include_defaults=true`.

`TransportGetSettingsAction` computes defaults with `indexScopedSettings.diff(indexMetadata.getSettings(), Settings.EMPTY)`, so node settings never reach the default function. For example, `index.data_stream.bloom_filter_for_id_field.enabled` (#167554) reports `false` on a node whose `node._internal.bloom_filter_for_id_field.data_stream_timestamp.enabled` is `true`. Other settings (`index.disable_sequence_numbers`, `index.mapping.combine_dynamic_updates`) with node-derived defaults are affected the same way.

Found in review of #167554.

Note that the node level settings that determine the defaults were added for stateless. Maybe instead of the node settings, the default should have been be based on `DiscoveryNode.isStateless(settings)` instead.
