Cache can keep entries in its LRU list after removing them from the map

9.7.0-SNAPSHOT

OpenJDK 27.0.1.1

While benchmarking ways to reduce `lruLock` contention in `Cache`, I found that entries removed from the segment map can stay in the LRU list. I'll call these **ghost entries**.

**Expected:** every entry in the LRU list is also in the segment map, so `get()` finds it, and a replaced entry is reported once as `REPLACED`.

**Actual:** a ghost is in the LRU list but not in the map. It still counts toward `count()` and `weight()`, so a bounded cache evicts live entries too early. `get()` can't find it, `keys()` returns it, and its value stays in memory until eviction reaches it. With no size limit and no expiry, only `invalidateAll()` removes it.

`put()` [updates the segment map first](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L590-L609) and takes `lruLock` afterwards to link the entry. Until then the entry is `NEW`: mapped but not linked. I found two ways a ghost is created in that gap.

**Case 1: a `put` replaces an entry that isn't linked yet**

1. `put` A of key K maps e1 and waits for `lruLock`.
2. `put` B of K replaces e1 with e2 and gets `lruLock` first.
3. B should unlink e1 and report it as replaced, but [`put()`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L596) and [`unlink()`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L965) both skip `NEW` entries.
4. A then [links e1](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L913), which is no longer in the map. The removal listener is never told e1 was replaced.

`invalidate(key)` during the gap leaves a ghost the same way.

**Case 2: eviction removes a newer entry with an equal value**

[`evictEntry()`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L936) and the [iterator's `remove()`](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L860) remove the map entry with `segment.remove(key, value, false)`, which [compares values](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/common/cache/Cache.java#L323), not entries.

1. The cache is full and K maps to e1.
2. `put` A of K with an equal value replaces e1 with e2 and waits for `lruLock`.
3. `put` B of another key gets `lruLock` first and evicts e1. The values are equal, so e2's mapping is removed instead.
4. A links e2, which is no longer in the map. `get(K)` returns null right after A's `put`.

**How often:** in a stress test with a tiny cache (8 threads, 20% puts, about 250 entries, 2,000 keys), the window in case 1 opened 3,800 to 4,200 times per million puts. Eviction removes most ghosts quickly, but some were still there at the end of 326 of 600 one-second rounds. With no size limit they pile up: in one run, 8 threads putting 64 keys for about a second left about 157,000 ghosts next to 64 live entries. With the fixes below there were none.

**Fix** ([both commits](https://github.com/danfaer/elasticsearch/compare/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2...3e90820effd7d30d1c9675bb3d2ddd74c27a8c8d)):

- [Case 1](https://github.com/danfaer/elasticsearch/commit/3e90820effd7d30d1c9675bb3d2ddd74c27a8c8d): `unlink()` marks a `NEW` entry `DELETED`, so its own `put` doesn't link it, and the replaced entry is reported as `REPLACED`.
- [Case 2](https://github.com/danfaer/elasticsearch/commit/a7e7347ae063577c6c321a137e8b2895accfbbbd): eviction and the iterator remove the mapping only if it holds the entry being removed. `invalidate(key, value)` still compares values, as documented.

Both fixes are cheap: no new locks, and nothing changes on the `get()` path. I can open a PR if this approach looks right.

These are unit tests in `CacheTests` on top of c508ded ([diff](https://github.com/danfaer/elasticsearch/compare/c508ded59bd9ccb13235c156ad26e75c40c9f9d2...fadf165b8f06fe209e49bef7415ca392acb1fc5f)). Apart from the tests, the commit only adds a package-private `getLruLock()` to `Cache`.

```
git remote add danfaer https://github.com/danfaer/elasticsearch.git
git fetch danfaer cache-ghost-repro
git checkout fadf165b8f06fe209e49bef7415ca392acb1fc5f
```

4 tests below hold `lruLock` on the test thread, so a `put` stops after updating the segment map but before linking the entry. They fail every time on `main`:

```
./gradlew :server:test \
  --tests 'org.elasticsearch.common.cache.CacheTests.testPutReplacing*' \
  --tests 'org.elasticsearch.common.cache.CacheTests.testInvalidateEntryNotYetLinked' \
  --tests 'org.elasticsearch.common.cache.CacheTests.testEvictionKeepsReplacementWithEqualValue'
```

The other 2 use only the public Cache API and don't touch the lock . They run puts from 8 threads, then check that `count()` matches the entries in the segment maps and that no key is listed twice. The first puts 64 keys into a cache with no size limit; the second evicts from a cache of maximum weight 32, with values equal to their keys. Both failed 50 of 50 runs on my M1 Max:

```
./gradlew :server:test --tests 'org.elasticsearch.common.cache.CacheTests.testGhostEntries*' -Dtests.iters=50
```

```
testGhostEntriesFromConcurrentPuts   (CacheTests.java:1003)

  largest of 50:  AssertionError: ghosts 152792, count 152856 expected:<0> but was:<152792>

ESQL: FILLNULL does not warn about a column of type unsupported

`FILLNULL` leaves a column of type `unsupported` unchanged without the warning that the docs say lists every skipped column.

The documentation for the command says that a column the value cannot be applied to "is left unchanged and a warning lists the skipped columns". `WarnUnfillableFillNull` lists the unfillable targets, but a column of type `unsupported` is not among them.

I found it with the new `CsvFillNullIT` (#167574), which appends `| FILLNULL DEFAULT ON *` to csv-spec queries. For the `inlinestats.csv-spec` test `ImplicitCastingMultiTypedDateTruncInlinestats_ByWithEval`:

```
FROM employees, employees_incompatible
| KEEP emp_no, hire_date
| EVAL yr = DATE_TRUNC(1 year, hire_date)
| INLINE STATS c = count(emp_no::long) BY yr
| SORT yr DESC, hire_date DESC
| LIMIT 10
| FILLNULL DEFAULT ON *
```

The two indices disagree on `emp_no`, so the column is `unsupported` and holds nulls. The values are unchanged, which is expected, but the warning names only the other columns without a default:

```
Line 8:3: [FILLNULL] the following fields have no default fill value for their type and were left unchanged: [hire_date, yr]; provide an explicit value
```

I expected `[emp_no, hire_date, yr]`. I have not tried the query in isolation outside that test, or with an explicit value instead of `DEFAULT`.

Either the warning should name the column, or the docs should say that `unsupported` columns are skipped silently. `CsvFillNullIT` currently models the silent behaviour, with a comment pointing here.

Bulk needs an option to not create a missing index

A race: the index exists when ES|QL `INTO` plans its write, but is deleted before the first bulk reaches it, and the bulk then creates it again. Bulk needs an "if not exists" option, so that it fails instead of creating the index.

Found in #167344.

Batch indexing falls back to the row path on an empty object nested in a flattened field or the _unmapped sink

main (9.7.0-SNAPSHOT), reproduced at 2e28f827cf9f

_bundled_

With `indices.batch_indexing: true`, the columnar batch path cannot handle an empty object (`{}`) that sits below a flattened field's root. The batch is abandoned and re-indexed on the row path, with a WARN and a full stack trace for every chunk:

```
WARN o.e.i.m.ShardBatchMapper columnar batch mapping failed on [PRIMARY], falling back
java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException: utf8Cursor: unsupported ESCF value type [KEY_VALUE] for string conversion
    at org.elasticsearch.escf.EscfColumnTransforms$StringifyingCursor.nextDoc(EscfColumnTransforms.java:262)
    at org.elasticsearch.index.mapper.flattened.FlattenedFieldMapper.mapColumnGroupBatch(FlattenedFieldMapper.java:2178)
    at org.elasticsearch.index.mapper.flattened.UnmappedSinkFieldMapper.mapColumnGroupBatch(UnmappedSinkFieldMapper.java:154)
    at org.elasticsearch.index.mapper.ShardBatchMapper.mapColumnBatch(ShardBatchMapper.java:580)
    at org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.ShardBatchIndexer.doBatchIndexOnPrimary(ShardBatchIndexer.java:132)
```

The indexed data is correct (the row path produces it), but the batch work is wasted and indexing takes the slow path.

It affects:
- the `_unmapped` sink under root `dynamic: flattened`: any unmapped field whose value is `{}`, for example `{"temp": {}}`;
- a mapped `flattened` field with a nested empty object, for example `{"attrs": {"x": {}}}`.

`{"attrs": {}}` (the empty object is the flattened field's own value) is not affected: `FlattenedFieldMapper#doMapColumnBatch` already skips it via `EscfColumnTransforms.allNullOrEmptyObject`.

**Cause.** The ESCF encoder stores an empty object as a zero-byte `KEY_VALUE` leaf at the object's own path, so it stays distinct from an absent field (`EscfEncoder`, `EscfRowBuffer#emptyObject`). `FlattenedFieldMapper#mapColumnGroupBatch` reads every column of the group through `EscfColumnTransforms.utf8Cursor`, and `StringifyingCursor.nextDoc` throws on `KEY_VALUE`. The row path indexes nothing for a nested empty object (`FlattenedFieldParser#parseObject` returns on the immediate `END_OBJECT`), so the batch path should skip a zero-entry `KEY_VALUE` row and emit nothing, as it already does for an empty array.

Open question: a non-empty `KEY_VALUE` (an object inside an array, `EscfDocumentHandler`) may reach the same cursor. Not checked.

**Impact.** In the `elastic-logs-logsdb-columnar-dynamic-flattened` nightly benchmark (elastic/logs track, `logsdb_columnar`, root `dynamic: flattened`), the 2026-11-24 run logged 246,784 of these fallbacks, all with this exception. Every `mysql.slowlog` document has `"temp": {}`, and 0.3-0.7% of application-log documents have `"json": {}`; one such document is enough to send its whole chunk to the row path. In a local test-mode run, 63% of documents were indexed on the row path. Bulk indexing throughput was 29% lower than in `elastic-logs-logsdb-columnar` (same data with mapped fields, no fallbacks), although the two runs are not a strict A/B comparison.

Start a snapshot build with `./gradlew run -Drun.license_type=trial`, then:

```
PUT _cluster/settings
{"persistent": {"indices.batch_indexing": true, "logger.org.elasticsearch.action.bulk.ShardBatchIndexer": "trace"}}

PUT sink-repro
{"settings": {"index.mode": "logsdb_columnar", "number_of_replicas": 0},
 "mappings": {"dynamic": "flattened", "properties": {"@timestamp": {"type": "date"}}}}

PUT flat-repro
{"settings": {"index.mode": "logsdb_columnar", "number_of_replicas": 0},
 "mappings": {"properties": {"@timestamp": {"type": "date"}, "attrs": {"type": "flattened"}}}}
[... 16 more lines]
```

Server log:
1. first `sink-repro` bulk: a `batch indexed [...] operations` trace line (batch path);
2. second `sink-repro` bulk (`temp: {}`): the WARN above, then the row path;
3. first `flat-repro` bulk (`attrs.x: {}`): the same WARN;
4. second `flat-repro` bulk (`attrs: {}`): `batch indexed [1] operations`.

All bulk requests return `"errors": false`.

Change mutateInstance overrides that replace the whole instance

`mutateInstance` exists so a serialisation test can prove `equals` and `hashCode` notice a change. A correct implementation copies the object and changes only one field. As each run picks a different field at random, over many test runs every field is checked in isolation. If there is a bug that the `equals` or `hashCode` methods ignore a field, the test will fail deterministically, and you can see which field was missed.

Two shortcuts hide that bug. Building a brand new random object, or calling `randomValueOtherThan` to get any other object, only proves that two different objects are not equal. They can differ in several fields at once, so a field that `equals` ignores never gets caught.

This ticket is to fix existing tests that break this convention. [CoordinationMetadataWireSerializingTests](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/main/server/src/test/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/coordination/CoordinationMetadataWireSerializingTests.java) is an example of a correctly implemented test suite

Updatable doc-values

Updatable doc-values lets a `doc_values: { updatable: true }` field be changed in place with `IndexWriter.updateDocValues` instead of reindexing the whole document, on columnar indices. The first version landed in #157749, behind the `doc_values_updatable` feature flag.

Uncharged per-clause bit sets can OOM a node

main

_bundled_

Query cache population is now charged to the request circuit breaker (#165667), and so is scoring for `PointRangeQuery` and costly `MultiTermQuery`s (`ContextIndexSearcher#chargingExecutionMemory`). Several other queries and aggregations still build a `FixedBitSet`/`LongBitSet` of `maxDoc` (or of the field's ordinal count) for each clause, without telling any breaker. A single `bool` with a few thousand such clauses, which is under the default clause limit, or a few thousand aggregations, can then exhaust the heap.

Points/shape queries are not charged in `ContextIndexSearcher#chargingExecutionMemory`. Their scorers are built all at once for a disjunction, so every clause's bit set is alive at the same time.

Aggregation-time bit sets:

ES|QL: IN subquery above 100 values scans the whole outer source instead of filtering

Above `esql.in_subquery_hash_join_threshold` (default 100) an `IN` subquery becomes a hash join that reads every row of the outer source, even when the outer side is an indexed field and the value set is selective. Up to the threshold it's inlined as `WHERE field IN (...)` and pushed to Lucene.

Repro on 9.7.0-SNAPSHOT: one index, 2M events, 200k values of a `keyword` field `session.id`, 10 docs each.

```
FROM idx
| WHERE session.id IN (FROM idx | WHERE marker < ? | STATS c = COUNT(*) BY session.id | KEEP session.id)
| STATS events = COUNT(*)
```

| Subquery values | Default threshold (100) | Threshold 10,000 |
|---|---|---|
| 50 | 1,000 rows read | 1,000 rows, 36 ms |
| 500 | 2,005,000 rows, 1.6 s | 10,000 rows, 40 ms |
| 5,000 | 2,050,000 rows, 0.9 s | 100,000 rows, 115 ms |

On a 29M-event index, 10,000 values read 7.39M rows in 4.6 s through the subquery, against 576k rows in 0.7 s as a literal `IN` list.

Choose between the `IN` filter and the hash join on cost, for example the value count against the estimated outer rows, up to `index.max_terms_count`. Or raise the default. Callers on Serverless can't change the setting.

ES|QL: `_score` doesn't honor pipe order and behaves differently on runtime expressions in some cases

Found on main (9.6.0-SNAPSHOT) but everything here should behave the same on 9.5 (and earlier, where applicable) as well.

ES|QL documents that "each processing command works on the output table of the previous command", which is pipe
order. For `_score`, that would mean a reference sees only the scores from searches written *before* it. Neither kind
of search follows that consistently today:

- **Searches on indexed fields** (`MATCH` etc. pushed down to Lucene) never follow pipe order. Lucene scores at the
  source, so every reference to `_score` sees the final score, even one written before the search.
- **Runtime searches** (`MATCH`/`MATCH_PHRASE`/runtime `KNN` on an expression, or on a field of a federated dataset,
  #156097, #160785) score in a `ScoreOperator` after the filter holding them has run. Some shapes follow pipe order,
  and others behave like indexed fields.

So for scoring support on runtime expressions, we can either choose to have consistency with indexed fields, or to follow pipe order, but not both.

The existing implementation in main currently attempts to maintain pipe order, since it can't leverage pushdown (by definition). However, there are (at least) shapes of queries that don't currently honor pipe order:

before is 2.0, but pipe order gives 0.0.

```
  FROM books METADATA _score
  | EVAL before = _score, content = TO_TEXT(CONCAT(title, " ", description))
  | WHERE MATCH(content, "Tolkien Rings")
  | STATS max_before = MAX(before), max_score = MAX(_score)
```

Note that in this example, changing the EVAL from a simple alias to any sort of computation results in pipe order being honored. 😬

For example, this query is handled correctly: before is 0.0, which is what pipe order gives.
```
  FROM books METADATA _score
  | EVAL before = _score + 0.0, content = TO_TEXT(CONCAT(title, " ", description))
  | WHERE MATCH(content, "Tolkien Rings")
  | STATS max_before = MAX(before), max_score = MAX(_score)
```

s is 2.0, but pipe order gives 0.0.

```
  FROM books METADATA _score
  | EVAL content = TO_TEXT(CONCAT(title, " ", description))
  | RENAME _score AS s
  | WHERE MATCH(content, "Tolkien Rings")
  | STATS max_s = MAX(s)
```

In this example, the result is 1463, 2714, 4023 (all 2.0), but pipe order gives 1463, 2130, 2301. Under pipe order every row ties at 0.0 when it's sorted, so book_no decides.
```
  FROM books METADATA _score
  | EVAL content = TO_TEXT(CONCAT(title, " ", description))
  | SORT _score DESC, book_no ASC
  | WHERE MATCH(content, "Tolkien Rings")
  | LIMIT 3
  | KEEP book_no, _score
```

`_score` is a single attribute, with one id, whose value changes partway through the plan.

- **Indexed search:** the search is pushed into the Lucene query at the source, so `_score` already holds the final score when the first command sees it.
- **Runtime search:** a runtime-scoring filter's `ScoreOperator` overwrites the `_score` column. The logical optimizer assumes each attribute has one value, so some of its rewrites change the answer:
  - **Alias and `RENAME`:** `ReplaceAliasingEvalWithProject` turns `EVAL before = _score` into a projection, and the filter is then pushed below it. In the optimized plan `MAX(before)` becomes `MAX(_score)`, read after the search.
  - **`SORT`:** `PushDownAndCombineFilters` swaps the filter below the `OrderBy`, and the sort and `LIMIT` merge into a `TopN` above the search.
  - A computed `EVAL` and a `_score` filter keep pipe order only because nothing substitutes or reorders them here.

Which semantics should `_score` **on a runtime expression** have? Should it always be the final score, as indexed fields do as a side effect of pushdown? For runtime search, it would mean making a reference see a search written *after* it, which is hard in general (across `LIMIT`, `STATS`, ...).

- #160804: a `_score` filter *after* a runtime search compares the score from before it. Its fix keeps the pipe order that the last row of the table shows for a `_score` filter written before a runtime search.
- #160650: `SORT _score ASC` is pushed down to Lucene as descending.
- #159746: `_score` across sub-queries with and without `METADATA _score`; a runtime search above a multi-branch `UnionAll` doesn't score at all.
- #156097 (runtime search scoring), #160785 (scoring on federated datasets).

ES|QL COMPLETION command fails with 400 when inference connector returns extended-thinking content array

When an ES|QL `COMPLETION` command calls an inference connector that uses Anthropic's extended-thinking feature, the request fails with a 400 error. Extended thinking causes the model to return `choices[0].message.content` as an **array of blocks** (a `thinking` block followed by a `text` block) rather than a plain string. The EIS `CompletionResult`/`Choice` deserialiser expects `content` to be a required string field and cannot handle the array form.

```
status_exception: Failed to send Elastic Inference Service chat completions request.
  Cause: [1:1302] [CompletionResult] failed to parse field [choices]
    Caused by: x_content_parse_exception: [1:1302] [Choice] failed to parse field [message]
      Caused by: illegal_argument_exception: Required [content]
```

`[1:1302]` is the character offset in the raw EIS response body where the array value is encountered. EIS successfully receives a complete, well-formed response from the model — it fails only at deserialisation of the `content` field.

1. Configure an Anthropic inference endpoint that supports extended thinking (e.g. Claude Fable / claude-3-7-sonnet with `thinking` enabled).
2. Use `COMPLETION` in an ES|QL query with a prompt complex enough to trigger extended thinking in the model.
3. Observe the `status_exception` 400 returned from Elasticsearch.

The error is deterministic for prompts that reliably trigger extended thinking. Simpler prompts that do not trigger extended thinking succeed on the same connector.

Anthropic's extended-thinking API returns `message.content` as a structured array:

```
{
  "choices": [{
    "message": {
      "content": [
        { "type": "thinking", "thinking": "<internal reasoning>" },
        { "type": "text",     "text": "<actual model response>" }
      ]
    }
  }]
}
```

EIS's `CompletionResult` / `Choice` parser treats `content` as a required `string` field. When it encounters the array, it cannot find the string value and throws `Required [content]`.

Possible fixes:
- Detect when `content` is an array; concatenate or extract the `text`-type block's `.text` value.
- Make `content` nullable/optional and fall back to reading from the first `text`-typed block.
- Handle the extended-thinking response schema as a distinct `Choice` variant alongside the standard one.

- Elastic 9.5.4 (self-managed)
- ES|QL `COMPLETION` command with an Anthropic inference connector

`COMPLETION` returns the model's text response (the content of the `text`-type block) even when the model activates extended thinking.

`COMPLETION` throws a 400 `status_exception` and the query fails.

Move ReservingResponseHandler and ShardResponseReservation out of the search package

`ReservingResponseHandler` and `ShardResponseReservation` live in `org.elasticsearch.action.search`. With #167535, `TransportTasksAction` (used by `GET _tasks`) uses them as well, so the generic tasks fan-out depends on classes owned by search. The two callers also treat a trip differently: a shard reservation trip fails the search, a task reply trip fails only one node.

Move both classes to `org.elasticsearch.transport` (and drop "Shard" from the reservation name), so search can change its shard policy without touching the shared code. No behaviour change. It touches about 20 files, mostly imports and the rename, which is why it was kept out of #167535.

ES|QL: SET with an identifier or pattern parameter as value returns a 500

﻿ES|QL returns a 500 `unresolved_exception` when the value of a `SET` setting is an identifier or pattern parameter. It should be a 400 with a clear message that the setting needs a constant value.

Tested on 9.5.7:

```
POST /_query
{
  "query": "SET unmapped_fields = ?i; ROW a = 1",
  "params": [{ "i": { "identifier": "x" } }]
}
```

Response: `500`, `unresolved_exception`: `Invalid call to dataType on an unresolved object ?x`.

The same happens with other settings (`SET time_zone = ?i`) and with a pattern parameter (`{ "p": { "pattern": "x*" } }`, `Invalid call to data type on an unresolved object ?x*`).

A plain value parameter works (`SET time_zone = ?v` with `{ "v": "UTC" }`).

An identifier or pattern parameter becomes an `UnresolvedAttribute`, and the settings validation calls `dataType()` on the value before checking that it is a constant.

Azure repository: cancel() racing onNext leaks a ByteBuf in CancellableRateLimitedFluxIterator

main (f64ea0cbb0a). The class is unchanged since #158936 (4e553c2eae7); the race exists since at least #104259.

repository-azure (module)

_bundled_ (reproduced with Temurin 21.0.12)

`CancellableRateLimitedFluxIterator.onNext` checks the done state and then offers the element to the queue. `cancel()` sets the done state and then clears the queue. Nothing stops `cancel()` from running entirely between the check and the offer:

| | SDK thread: `onNext(buf)` | reader: `AzureInputStream.close()` → `cancel()` |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `doneState.get().done()` is false | |
| 2 | | set done (CancellationException) |
| 3 | | `cancelSubscription()`; `clearQueue()` finds the queue empty |
| 4 | `queue.offer(buf)` succeeds | |

After step 4 the buffer is in the queue of a closed stream. Nothing polls it again, so `ReferenceCountUtil::safeRelease` never runs and the `ByteBuf` from `NettyAllocator` leaks (one chunk per affected close). With the pooled allocator its memory is not returned to the pool.

Expected: every element that reaches `onNext` is either returned by `next()` or passed to the cleaner, as the comment in `onNext` intends ("we just clean the resources"). `testCancellation` covers elements that arrive after `cancel()` returns, but not ones that arrive during it.

#104259 moved the done flag before `clearQueue()`, which made the window smaller but did not close it.

Put this in `org.elasticsearch.repositories.azure` (the constructor is package-private) and run it. A downloader thread delivers one chunk while the reader closes the stream, two million times, and counts chunks that are never released:

```
package org.elasticsearch.repositories.azure;

import org.reactivestreams.Subscription;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

/**
 * A blob download is still delivering a chunk when the reader closes the stream.
 *
[... 81 more lines]
```

Output on main (16-core Linux machine, JDK 21):

```
download 276: the chunk was never released; it is still in the closed stream's queue: [chunk of download 276]
download 998: the chunk was never released; it is still in the closed stream's queue: [chunk of download 998]
download 1976: the chunk was never released; it is still in the closed stream's queue: [chunk of download 1976]
2000000 downloads closed while a chunk was arriving, 328 chunks never released
```

Across runs it loses between 43 and 336 chunks per two million.

None. Netty's leak detector may report `LEAK: ByteBuf.release() was not called` when it samples one of these buffers.

ESQL: EQL source command should distinguish between older and newer nodes when checking responding shards

Follow up to https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/pull/167558/changes#r4710090605

An EQL response from an older remote node means the shard counts are unknown, not that no shard succeeded. If that branch returns no matching rows and a newer branch reports only failed shards, the query-wide check can incorrectly throw “all shards failed” even though the older branch searched healthy shards. Preserve the unknown state for the failure check.

[ML] Datafeeds: skip long empty gaps before real-time for search-query datafeeds

After a lookback over old sparse data, the first real-time flush of a search-query (DSL) datafeed advances the model clock to now. Autodetect then writes one empty bucket result per bucket span. With a 1m bucket span and a gap of years, that is about 300,000 documents in one refresh window, which can exhaust the heap of the results index shard.

#167704 fixes this for ES|QL datafeeds only. Before real-time extraction and before each `advance_time` flush, it skips gaps of more than 10,000 bucket spans with a `skip_time` flush. The `DatafeedJob` logic does not depend on the datafeed type, so search-query datafeeds can use it by dropping the ES|QL gate.

Open question: skipped buckets have no results, so `count` and `low_count` detectors do not report the skipped gap. Decide whether that is acceptable by default for search-query datafeeds, or whether the threshold should be configurable.

A long empty gap inside the lookback history, or inside a catch-up window after a failed lookback, still writes every bucket for all datafeed types.

[ES|QL] INLINE STATS aggregate multivalue collapses when the column is re-evaluated by a downstream EVAL

main (reproduced on `9.7.0-SNAPSHOT`)

When `INLINE STATS` is grouped by a **multivalued** key, the aggregate is joined back to each source row as a per-row multivalue (one value per distinct group the row belongs to). That multivalue is **silently collapsed to its first value** as soon as a downstream `EVAL` re-evaluates that aggregate column (for example `EVAL c = COALESCE(c, 0)`, as emitted by `FILLNULL ... ON *`).

The result of the aggregate column therefore depends on whether a later command happens to reference it, which is a correctness bug. Aggregate columns that are *not* re-evaluated keep their multivalue in the same query, and a trailing `EVAL` that does not reference the column leaves it untouched — so only the re-evaluated column is affected.

Using the standard `employees` dataset (where `is_rehired` is multivalued), these three queries differ only in the trailing command:

**1. Baseline — aggregate is a per-row multivalue (correct):**

```
FROM employees
| INLINE STATS count = COUNT(height.float) + 2 WHERE false BY job_positions, is_rehired
| SORT emp_no DESC | LIMIT 2 | KEEP emp_no, count, is_rehired
```
`emp_no 10100` → `count = [2, 2]`, `is_rehired = [false, false, true, true]`

**2. Trailing EVAL that does not reference `count` — multivalue preserved (correct):**

```
FROM employees
| INLINE STATS count = COUNT(height.float) + 2 WHERE false BY job_positions, is_rehired
| EVAL probe = 1
| SORT emp_no DESC | LIMIT 2 | KEEP emp_no, count, is_rehired
```
`emp_no 10100` → `count = [2, 2]` (unchanged)

**3. Trailing EVAL that re-evaluates `count` — multivalue collapses (bug):**

```
FROM employees
| INLINE STATS count = COUNT(height.float) + 2 WHERE false BY job_positions, is_rehired
| EVAL count = COALESCE(count, 0)
| SORT emp_no DESC | LIMIT 2 | KEEP emp_no, count, is_rehired
```
`emp_no 10100` → `count = 2` ❌ (expected `[2, 2]`)

In case 3, an untouched aggregate column (e.g. a second `count_distinct = ... BY ...`) keeps its multivalue while only the re-evaluated `count` collapses, confirming the collapse is per-column and tied to the re-evaluation.

`COALESCE` is not the cause: both its eager and lazy evaluators copy whole positions (`result.copyFrom(block, p, p + 1)`), preserving multivalues. A scalar out of `COALESCE` means its input was already scalar, i.e. the `INLINE STATS` / inline-join side produced the aggregate as a single value for that column once it is consumed by a downstream `EVAL`, bypassing the per-row multivalue reconstruction that the untouched columns still go through.

Surfaced by the `FILLNULL` comparative csv-spec test (`CsvFillNullIT`, elastic/elasticsearch#167574, elastic/elasticsearch#163195): appending `| FILLNULL DEFAULT ON *` to `inlinestats.csv-spec` / `inlinestatsWithFalseFiltersAndGroups_DropEvaledValue` changed the aggregate multivalues to scalars.

Split time-series queries by `_tsid` range

Time-series aggregations run in two passes: first by `_tsid` and time bucket, then by the user's groups. With many time series, the coordinator has to hold all `(_tsid, bucket)` groups from the first pass, which can take GBs. Spilling to disk would help, but it's slower and we don't have it yet.

Instead, we can split the query, either by time bucket or by `_tsid`. Splitting by time bucket is simpler, but it doesn't work for `rate` (the most memory-hungry) or window functions, since they need samples across tbucket boundaries. So this issue splits by `_tsid` range. Each branch handles its own set of series, and the coordinator only needs to hold the groups of the branches that are running.

- On clusters with little memory, queries that used to fail with a circuit breaker error now complete, but slower. Some users may prefer the error as a signal to scale up.
- The estimate can be off. Overestimating causes unnecessary splits, and underestimating can still trip the circuit breaker.
- A split query can be slower than an unsplit one, since each branch has fixed costs (planning, setup, coordinator, and execution overhead).
- Splitting can sometimes use a bit more memory than not splitting, because of per-branch overhead.
- Queries that get probed but not split still pay for the probe (a few ms).

Updatable doc-values

Updatable doc-values lets a `doc_values: { updatable: true }` field be changed in place with `IndexWriter.updateDocValues` instead of reindexing the whole document, on columnar indices. The first version landed in #157749, behind the `doc_values_updatable` feature flag.

ES|QL: support `fields` option in QSTR

QSTR has no way to set the fields to search, other than a single `default_field`. `QSTR("hello", {"fields": ["title"]})` fails with `Invalid option [fields]`.

Accept a `fields` option and pass it to the `query_string` query, with the same syntax as the DSL:

```
FROM books
| WHERE QSTR("hobbit", {"fields": ["title^2", "desc*"]})
```

- `fields` together with `default_field`: the `query_string` query rejects the combination, but only on the shard.
- HIGHLIGHT: it checks `default_field` against its `ON` fields and does not know about `fields`.
- Score combination across fields: `type` and `tie_breaker` are not QSTR options, so it would always be `best_fields` with a tie breaker of 0.
- Validation: non-finite or negative boosts, and non-string values such as `{"fields": [true]}`, should fail at verification.

ES|QL: Add min competitive optimization for lucene operators

We currently only push ES|QL conditions that have an exact equivalent to a Lucene query.

Take as example, where all conditions are pushed down to lucene and we use a SORT that's also pushed down:
```
FROM wikipedia METADATA _score
| WHERE title:"europe"
| sort _score desc
| limit 10
```
This query will use the `LuceneTopNSourceOperator` and should be close in performance to a running a match query in the DSL. The `LuceneTopNSourceOperator` will emit at most 10 rows that need to be processed on the compute service side.

The moment we have a filter condition that is not pushed down, we no longer use the `LuceneTopNSourceOperator`, but `LuceneSourceOperator`. We will still push down the match query, but `LuceneSourceOperator` will output all docs that match the query string. These docs will then be processed on the compute service side to apply the non-pushable filter and then sorted to get the the top 10.

```
FROM wikipedia METADATA _score
| WHERE title:"europe" and length(title) > 10
| sort _score desc
| limit 10
```

~~We should look into whether we can push down more WHERE conditions as filters.
We will likely need a custom Lucene query for this that can evaluate an ES|QL expression.
We can start with something simple such as pushing down only conditions that depend on the Literals and indexed fields (not other runtime columns resulted from EVALs).
If we want to first validate if this would improve things, we can start with a simple prototype that pushes down a set conditions like `length(title) > 10` as a painless script query and then run a simple benchmark on a larger dataset (where it is more likely that we will see an improvement).~~

EDIT: We should look into adding a min competitive optimization.
For example we can have a callback between the `LuceneSourceOperator` and `TopNOperator` such that we can set a min competitive score back in `LuceneSourceOperator` once we fill the priority queue in `TopNOperator`

ESQL: push down filters past STATS

Follow-up to https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/115281

The current [push down optimization](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/c7f53ff3b639555736e2b6d0864e537cacbc2d59/x-pack/plugin/esql/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/xpack/esql/optimizer/rules/logical/PushDownAndCombineFilters.java#L44-L52), where we transform `... | STATS ... BY field | WHERE field > 10` into ` WHERE field > 10 | STATS ... BY field` (and similarly for more complex filters), does not yet take into account that `field` could be multivalued. In case it is, the correct push down result is `EVAL field = MV_DEDUPE(field) | MV_EXPAND field | WHERE field > 10 | STATS ... BY field`.

Let's make our filter push down multi-values aware.

ES|QL: IN subquery should derive per-column filters on the outer source

**Problem.** A multi-column `IN` subquery often compares keys that are renamed or computed before the filter:

```
FROM orders
| EVAL store = store_id, sku = product_code, day = DATE_TRUNC(1 day, created_at), tier = TO_STRING(customer_tier)
| WHERE (store, sku, day, tier) IN (FROM recalls | WHERE severity == "high" | KEEP store, sku, day, tier)
```

The subquery runs first. Its tuples are then either inlined as an `OR` of `AND`s over `MvSingleValueOrNull(key) == literal` (up to 100 tuples), or joined through a hash join (above 100). Neither form reaches the source:
- the keys are produced by `EVAL`;
- they are wrapped for multi-value semantics;
- a tuple condition is not a single-column predicate.

So the outer source is read in full. A Lucene index gets no `TermsQuery`, and an external source gets no row-group pruning.

The usual workaround is a hand-written prefilter on raw columns, for example `product_code IN (FROM recalls | KEEP sku)`. In one workload over an external Parquet archive, that cut bytes read by about 40%. Every row that matches a tuple must also satisfy weaker per-column conditions on the raw columns, and the planner already holds the values needed to express them.

**Goal.** Positive `IN` subqueries prune the outer source without a user-written prefilter. This applies to single- and multi-column keys, renamed or computed by invertible expressions, on both the inline path and the hash-join path.

**Passing criteria.**
- Renamed keys produce per-column filters at the source: a `TermsQuery` for an index, pushed predicates for an external source. Verify with plan tests and the profile's read counts.
- Keys with an exact inverse (type conversions) or a range inverse (`DATE_TRUNC`) are covered. Non-invertible keys are skipped.
- Hash-join-path queries also prune the outer source.
- Results and warnings are identical across the existing `IN` subquery specs, including NULL tuples and multi-valued keys.
- `NOT IN`, mark joins, and any other form where dropping rows changes the result stay untouched.
- Planning cost stays bounded for large subquery results.

**Related.**
- #166605: moves the semi-join past row-preserving commands. It is complementary, since it does not cover computed keys or per-column decomposition.
- #165551: above the threshold, the hash join scans the whole outer source.

Metric attributes are rebuilt and revalidated on every instrument call

`OtelHelper` started showing up in various profiles at 4–7% of CPU. Partial investigation points to the attribute preparation done on every recording call, rather than to export.

**Problem.** Every attribute-carrying call (`incrementBy`, `add`, `record`) goes through `OtelHelper.fromMap`. Each time, it builds a new `Attributes` from the caller's `Map`, even when that map is a constant. With assertions enabled, `MetricValidator.assertValidAttributeNames` also regex-checks every key on every call.

On hot paths this becomes a per-operation cost and a source of garbage. One example is `ChildMemoryCircuitBreaker`'s held-memory counter, which is updated on every breaker adjustment. Under assertions, the validation cost also skews profiles and slows down tests.

**Goal.** Recording with a fixed attribute set costs about the same as recording without attributes.

**Passing criteria.**
- Callers can prepare attributes once and reuse them; existing `Map`-based call sites keep working.
- Recording with prepared attributes allocates nothing per call, verified with JMH and an allocation profiler.
- Attribute validation runs once per (metric, key set), and invalid names are still rejected.
- The breaker's held-memory counter uses prepared attributes, and the exported metrics are unchanged.
- No unbounded caches keyed by caller-provided maps.

Split time-series queries by `_tsid` range

Time-series aggregations run in two passes: first by `_tsid` and time bucket, then by the user's groups. With many time series, the coordinator has to hold all `(_tsid, bucket)` groups from the first pass, which can take GBs. Spilling to disk would help, but it's slower and we don't have it yet.

Instead, we can split the query, either by time bucket or by `_tsid`. Splitting by time bucket is simpler, but it doesn't work for `rate` (the most memory-hungry) or window functions, since they need samples across tbucket boundaries. So this issue splits by `_tsid` range. Each branch handles its own set of series, and the coordinator only needs to hold the groups of the branches that are running.

- On clusters with little memory, queries that used to fail with a circuit breaker error now complete, but slower. Some users may prefer the error as a signal to scale up.
- The estimate can be off. Overestimating causes unnecessary splits, and underestimating can still trip the circuit breaker.
- A split query can be slower than an unsplit one, since each branch has fixed costs (planning, setup, coordinator, and execution overhead).
- Splitting can sometimes use a bit more memory than not splitting, because of per-branch overhead.
- Queries that get probed but not split still pay for the probe (a few ms).
